0.title: The Letter to the Ephesians
0.overview:
Paul wrote this letter from a Roman prison, around AD 60–62, awaiting trial before Caesar. He was chained to a guard. And from that cell he wrote what has often been called the most majestic letter Paul ever penned — a letter so vast in its theological vision, so soaring in its doxology, that it feels less like correspondence and more like a window thrown open onto eternity.

The letter may have been circular — several early manuscripts omit the words “in Ephesus” from 1:1, suggesting it was passed between the churches of Asia Minor. Tychicus carried it personally (6:21). Whether it reached one church or many, it was written for the whole church in every age — including yours.

Did Paul really write it? Many modern scholars think a follower wrote it in his name, pointing to its long sentences and unusual vocabulary, its close overlap with Colossians, and phrases such as his holy apostles and prophets (3:5) that they take to look back on an earlier generation. But the letter names Paul twice (1:1; 3:1), the early church received it as his without dissent, and the differences are well explained by its subject and setting: a letter of praise and teaching rather than controversy, written at the same time as Colossians and carried by the same man (6:21; Col 4:7). A letter claiming to be Paul’s that was not would be a forgery, and the church of that day rejected such letters. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote it.

The heartbeat phrase is in Christ, appearing over thirty times. Everything God has done, is doing, and will do for his people is located in the person of his Son. Chosen in him. Redeemed in him. Raised with him. Seated with him. Built together in him. The letter is not primarily about what Christians must do; it is about who Christians already are — and the doing flows from the being.

The grand theme is God’s eternal purpose to unite all things in Christ — things in heaven and things on earth (1:10). The church is not a human institution that God blesses; it is the centrepiece of his cosmic plan, the body through which the manifold wisdom of God is displayed to the watching principalities and powers (3:10). To be part of this church is to be enrolled in the most significant project in the universe.

The structure is clean and powerful. Chapters 1–3 are the great indicative: what God has done in Christ from before the foundation of the world to the present moment. Chapters 4–6 are the great imperative: how the people of God now walk, in every relationship and in every spiritual battle. The hinge is the word “therefore” in 4:1 — one of the most consequential words in Christian ethics. The imperative is always grounded in the indicative. We do not obey in order to be accepted; we obey because we already are.

Preach this letter and you will give your congregation the full panorama of God’s saving purpose, from the eternal counsel of the Trinity before creation to the armour for the battle they face this week. There is nothing higher in Paul. There may be nothing higher in Scripture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Every Spiritual Blessing in Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul greets the saints with grace and peace, then blesses God for every spiritual blessing in Christ. Before the world was made, the Father chose his people in Christ to be holy, and in love destined them to be his adopted children, for the praise of his grace given in the Beloved. In Christ they have redemption by his blood and the forgiveness of sins, poured out generously, and God has made known his plan to bring everything in heaven and earth together under Christ. In him believers have received an inheritance by the purpose of the God who works all things by his will: first Jewish believers, then Gentiles who heard the gospel and believed, sealed with the promised Spirit as the guarantee of their inheritance until God’s possession is fully redeemed. Everything leads to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, Grace, and the Glory of God

These twelve verses are the biblical locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of election. "He chose us in him before the foundation of the world" (v.4) — the election is personal, particular, and prior to anything in us. It is not based on foreseen faith; it is the ground of faith. God chose us before we existed, before we believed, before we had done anything good or bad (Romans 9:11). The choice was made in eternity, rooted in the sovereign good pleasure of his will (v.5), and directed toward the praise of the glory of his grace (v.6).

The purpose of election is not merely the salvation of individuals; it is the display of grace. "So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus" (2:7). We are saved so that the universe — angels, principalities, and powers — might see what grace looks like. The church is God's exhibit A: the living demonstration that mercy triumphs over judgment, that the undeserving can be made heirs, that the dead can be raised.

John Calvin wrote that the knowledge of election is not given to breed pride or speculation but to ground assurance. The believer who knows they were chosen before the foundation of the world — not because of what they would become but because of God's sovereign love — has a security that no circumstance can shake. This is the pastoral gold of Ephesians 1: your standing before God does not depend on your spiritual performance today. It was settled in eternity, sealed by the Spirit, and guaranteed by the inheritance that awaits.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian Christians lived in the shadow of the great temple of Artemis — one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, a monument to a goddess who offered fertility, protection, and blessing to her devotees. The mystery religions of Ephesus promised spiritual elevation through initiation rites, secret knowledge, and ritual participation. Against all of this, Paul announces something infinitely more magnificent: you already possess every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places — not through ritual, not through initiation, not through any human achievement, but through your union with Christ. You have been chosen, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, enlightened, and sealed. The goddess in the marble temple has nothing to offer you. You are already heirs of the universe.

Now: We live in an age of spiritual seeking. The bookshops are full of self-help and spirituality. People curate their own spiritual experiences, their own moral codes, their own pathways to meaning and blessing. Against all of this noise, Ephesians 1 speaks with clarifying force: every spiritual blessing is in Christ, and in Christ alone. The person who has Christ has everything. The person who lacks Christ lacks everything that ultimately matters, however enriched their life may appear. The church's task is not to offer a slightly better version of what the world already has, but to announce that in Christ, the one thing that actually satisfies every longing of the human heart is freely and fully given.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to the saints who are in Ephesus, and are faithful in Christ Jesus:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to the saints who are in Ephesus, and are faithful in Christ Jesus:

Meaning first. Ephesians 1 has two parts. Verses 3–14 are one long outburst of praise, a single sentence in Greek, celebrating every blessing God has given his people in Christ: the Father chose them before creation and adopted them as his children (vv. 4–6); the Son redeemed them by his blood and revealed God’s plan to bring everything together under Christ (vv. 7–12); and the Spirit, received when they believed, seals them as God’s own and guarantees their future inheritance (vv. 13–14). Verses 15–23 turn that praise into prayer: Paul asks God to open their eyes to know him better, to grasp the hope he has called them to, how precious they are to him, and the power at work for them, the same power that raised Christ from the dead and set him above every power in the universe as head over all things for the church. The chapter tells believers who they are and what they have, before the rest of the letter tells them how to live.

Setting and background. Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome about AD 60–62, chained to a soldier (3:1; 4:1; 6:20). Ephesus was the great city of the province of Asia (western Turkey): a busy port, home of the vast temple of the goddess Artemis, and famous for magic and spells (Acts 19:19). Paul had spent nearly three years there (Acts 20:31). Most of the believers were Gentiles who had come out of that world of idols, magic and fear of spiritual powers. Much of the letter answers that fear: Christ is above every power (1:21), and his people are safe in him.

Paul, an apostle. Key words. “Apostle” (apostolos, one sent): a messenger with the authority of the one who sends him. Paul was one of those personally commissioned by the risen Christ to lay the church’s foundation (2:20; Galatians 1:1). His words carry Christ’s authority; that is why this letter is Scripture.

By the will of God. Not his own choice or ambition. The former persecutor of the church is an apostle only because God willed it (1 Timothy 1:12–16). It sets the tone of the letter: everything begins with God’s will.

To the saints. Key words. “Saints” (hagioi, holy ones). In the New Testament this is not a special class of exceptional or canonised Christians but every believer. “Holy” means set apart for God, belonging to him. They are saints not because they have reached perfection, but because God has claimed them in Christ.

And are faithful in Christ Jesus. Key words. “Faithful” (pistois) can mean trusting (believers) or trustworthy. Here it means the same people described from another angle: those who trust Christ.

In Christ. Key words. The key phrase of Ephesians, used about thirty-five times in different forms (in him, in the Beloved). It means union with Christ: believers are joined to him, so that what is true of him becomes true of them. Every blessing in this chapter comes in him.

Textual note. Some of the earliest manuscripts (P46, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) omit “in Ephesus”. The letter has no personal greetings, though Paul spent three years there. Verdict: probably a circular letter to the churches of Asia, carried by Tychicus (6:21), with Ephesus as its chief destination.

Where Christians differ: did Paul write it? Many modern scholars think a follower wrote it, citing its style and its overlap with Colossians. Verdict: Paul is the author. The letter claims Paul twice (1:1; 3:1), the early church received it without dispute, and its differences fit a letter of praise written at the same time as Colossians.

What it does not mean. Calling every believer a saint does not mean that how we live does not matter. Paul will spend half the letter calling saints to live like saints (4:1).

In a sentence. From Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus because God willed it, to God’s holy people in Ephesus, who trust in Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. You are a saint, not because of how holy you feel today, but because you are in Christ. Live up to your name.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62. The ESV notes that some early manuscripts omit “in Ephesus”; the letter may have been meant to circulate among several churches of the region.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Grace. Key words. “Grace” (charis). The ordinary Greek greeting was chairein, greetings; Paul changes it to a word that sounds like it and means far more. Grace is God’s free, undeserved favour: kindness given to people who deserve the opposite (2:8–9). It is the source of everything in this letter.

Peace. Key words. “Peace” (eirēnē, translating the Hebrew shalom, the Jewish greeting). More than calm feelings: wholeness and right relationship. First peace with God, since we were once under his wrath (2:3), and then peace between people once divided (2:14–17).

The order. Always grace first, then peace. Peace is the fruit of grace; there is no peace with God without it.

From God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. One source, two persons. Paul puts Jesus beside the Father as the giver of divine gifts, something no Jew would say of a mere man: a quiet witness to Christ’s deity.

What it does not mean. Not a polite formula. It is a prayer and a blessing, spoken with apostolic authority.

In a sentence. May God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ give you their undeserved kindness and the peace it brings.

For worship. Receive the greeting as God’s word to you today: grace, and then peace.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.

One great sentence. Verses 3–14 are a single sentence in Greek, the longest in the New Testament, from a man too caught up in praise to stop. It is shaped by the Trinity: the Father chooses and adopts (vv. 4–6), the Son redeems (vv. 7–12), the Spirit seals (vv. 13–14). Three times it ends with the refrain to the praise of his glory (vv. 6, 12, 14).

Blessed be God … who has blessed us. Key words. One word, two directions. When we bless God (eulogētos), we praise him, speaking well of him. When God blesses us (eulogēsas), he does good to us: his word gives what it speaks (Genesis 1:28). We bless him because he has first blessed us.

The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is known as the Father of Jesus. We know him truly only through his Son.

Every spiritual blessing. Key words. “Every”: not one is missing; a believer is not waiting for some further blessing to make them complete in Christ. “Spiritual” (pneumatikē) does not mean vague, inner or unreal, and it is not the opposite of material. It means given and applied by the Holy Spirit (the Spirit is named in v. 13). The blessings are listed in what follows: being chosen, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, given wisdom and an inheritance, and sealed by the Spirit.

In the heavenly places. Key words. “The heavenly places” (en tois epouraniois, in the heavenlies). This puzzles many readers: how can blessings be in heaven when we live on earth? The phrase appears five times in Ephesians (1:3, 20; 2:6; 3:10; 6:12), and those uses explain it. It is where Christ now sits at God’s right hand (1:20); where believers are already seated with him (2:6); where spiritual powers, good and evil, operate (3:10; 6:12). It is not a place far away that we reach only after death, but the unseen realm of God’s rule, the real world behind the visible one, which in Christ has already broken into this age. Our blessings are there because Christ is there, and we are joined to him. That is why they are secure: they are kept where Christ is, beyond the reach of anything on earth.

In Christ. Every blessing comes only in union with him. Outside Christ, none; in Christ, all.

Has blessed. Key words. Past tense (eulogēsas): already given, not merely hoped for. Much is still to be enjoyed in full (vv. 14, 18), but it is already ours.

What it does not mean. Not a promise of earthly comfort, health or wealth. Paul writes this in chains. None of the blessings that follow is a circumstance, so none can be lost in a redundancy, a diagnosis or a prison.

In a sentence. Praise the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, by joining us to Christ, has already given us every blessing his Spirit brings, kept safe where Christ reigns.

On a Tuesday. When someone asks how you are on a bad day, you may say honestly that the day is hard, and that you are blessed.

For worship. Bless the God who has blessed you.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 3–14 are a single long sentence of praise in the Greek. “The heavenly places” is the unseen realm where Christ reigns.

verseByVerse.quote: Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him.

Even as. Key words. “Even as” (kathōs, just as, because). The first blessing explains all the others: they come to us because God chose us.

He chose us. Key words. “Chose” (exelexato, picked out for himself, middle voice: for his own sake, to be his). This is election: God’s free decision to save particular people. The choice is God’s, and it is personal: us.

In him. Election is never apart from Christ. God chose a people in his Son, as their head and Saviour. That is why the right place to look for assurance of your election is not into God’s secret decrees but at Christ: all whom the Father gives him come to him, and he will never cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37).

Before the foundation of the world. Before anything existed, before we were born or had done anything good or bad (Romans 9:11; 2 Timothy 1:9). God’s love for his people is older than the universe.

That we should be holy and blameless before him. Key words. “Holy” (hagious): set apart and pure. “Blameless” (amōmous): without blemish, the word for a perfect sacrifice. This is the purpose of election: God chose us for holiness, not because of it. When does it happen? In Christ we are already counted blameless (Colossians 1:22); we are being made holy now; and one day we will be presented faultless (5:27; Jude 24). Before him: in God’s presence and sight.

Where Christians differ: why did God choose? Arminians hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe (citing Romans 8:29; 1 Peter 1:2). Verdict: unconditional election (Westminster Confession 3.5). Paul roots the choice in God’s love, will and purpose (vv. 5, 9, 11), never in anything foreseen in us; and he says we were chosen to be holy, which would make no sense if God chose us because he foresaw our holiness. Faith is the result of election (Acts 13:48), not its cause. It is not unfair, because no one is owed salvation; it is mercy given freely.

Where Christians differ: chosen as individuals, or as a group? Some (following Karl Barth, and some Arminian scholars) hold that God chose Christ, and that the church is elect only as a group, in him; individuals become elect when they join themselves to Christ by faith. Verdict: God did choose a people, the church, and he chose them in Christ; but the people are made up of persons. Paul says he chose us, and v. 5 says he predestined us for adoption, which is personal. Elsewhere election is clearly of individuals: Jacob, not Esau (Romans 9:11–13); names written in the book of life (Revelation 13:8). The corporate and the personal belong together.

Common questions. If God has chosen, why preach the gospel? Because God chose the means as well as the end: the chosen come to faith through hearing the gospel (v. 13; Romans 10:14). Election is the reason evangelism will succeed (Acts 18:10). How can I know I am chosen? Not by looking for a secret sign, but by trusting Christ and seeing the fruit of holiness he produces (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5; 2 Peter 1:10).

Textual note. “In love” may end verse 4 (holy and blameless in love) or begin verse 5 (in love he predestined us). The ESV links it with verse 5, which fits Paul’s stress on God’s motive.

What it does not mean. Not fatalism, as if it does not matter what we do. Nor a reason for pride: election leaves no room for boasting (2:9). And it is not meant to make anyone anxious. Scripture gives it to comfort believers that their salvation rests on God, not on themselves.

In a sentence. For before the world was made, God chose us to belong to Christ, so that we would stand before him holy and without fault.

On a Tuesday. If you sinned badly this week, you are not less chosen. Repent and go on in the holiness you were chosen for.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “in love” may go with verse 4: “holy and blameless before him in love.”

verseByVerse.quote: In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will.

In love. The motive behind election is not cold decree but love (see the textual note on v. 4).

He predestined us. Key words. “Predestined” (proorisas, marked out beforehand, set a boundary in advance; our word horizon comes from the same root). Election (v. 4) is God choosing whom; predestination is God deciding what he would make of them, and here Paul names it: his children. In Scripture, predestination is almost always spoken of to comfort believers about their destiny, not to make people speculate about others.

For adoption to himself as sons. Key words. “Adoption” (huiothesia, placing as a son). In Roman law, an adopted son received a new father and name, had his old debts cancelled, and gained full rights of inheritance, equal to a natural son. Wealthy Romans adopted adult heirs. We were by nature children of wrath (2:3), outsiders; God brings us into his family as heirs (Galatians 4:4–7; Romans 8:15–17). “To himself”: not merely to a status, but to belong to him.

Why adoption and not only forgiveness? God could have pardoned us and left us as forgiven servants. Instead, he makes us his children. Forgiveness deals with our guilt; adoption gives us a Father, a family, a home and an inheritance. The Westminster Shorter Catechism (Q. 34) calls it an act of God’s free grace whereby we are received into the number, and have a right to all the privileges, of the sons of God.

As sons. In that world sons inherited. The word includes daughters: every believer, man or woman, receives the full inheritance (Galatians 3:26–28).

Through Jesus Christ. God has one eternal Son by nature; we become children by grace, through union with him.

According to the purpose of his will. Key words. Literally the good pleasure (eudokian) of his will: God delighted to do it. It was not reluctant; it made him glad. Nothing outside God moved him to it.

What it does not mean. Not that all people are God’s children in this sense. All are his creatures and his offspring as their Creator (Acts 17:28), but adoption comes through Christ, received by faith (John 1:12).

In a sentence. In love he decided beforehand that, through Jesus Christ, we would be adopted as his own children, because this was what he gladly willed.

For worship. Pray Our Father today knowing what it cost to make it true.
verseByVerse.note: In Roman law an adopted son received the full rights and inheritance of a natural son.

verseByVerse.quote: To the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved.

To the praise of his glorious grace. Key words. The first of three refrains (vv. 6, 12, 14). The ultimate purpose of salvation is God’s glory: that his grace be seen and celebrated. Our good and his glory are not rivals: we are saved for our joy and his praise. “Glory” (doxa) is God’s weight, his splendour made visible. His grace is glorious: it displays how great and good he is.

With which he has blessed us. Key words. Literally which he graced us with (echaritōsen, from the word grace): he freely favoured us. The same verb is used only once elsewhere, of Mary, the favoured one (Luke 1:28). It describes what God does for someone, not a quality they have of their own.

In the Beloved. Key words. “The Beloved” (tō ēgapēmenō): Christ, the Son the Father loves (Matthew 3:17). We are accepted because we are in him. God sees his people in the Son he delights in, and his love for them is his love for his Son, extended to all who are joined to him (John 17:23).

What it does not mean. Not that God saved us because he needed praise. He lacks nothing. He shows his grace because it is good, and we flourish by seeing and enjoying it.

In a sentence. He did this so that his glorious grace would be praised, the grace he freely gave us by uniting us to his beloved Son.

For worship. You are loved because you are in the Beloved. Praise the grace that put you there.
verseByVerse.note: “The Beloved” is Christ, echoing the Father’s voice at his baptism.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace.

In him we have. Present tense: a possession now, not only a future hope.

Redemption. Key words. “Redemption” (apolytrōsis, release by payment of a ransom). The word was used for buying a slave’s or prisoner’s freedom. Israel was redeemed from Egypt by the blood of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12–15). We were slaves to sin and under its penalty (2:1–3); Christ bought our freedom.

Through his blood. “Blood” means his life given in a violent, sacrificial death (Leviticus 17:11). The price was not silver or gold but Christ himself (1 Peter 1:18–19).

The forgiveness of our trespasses. Key words. “Forgiveness” (aphesis, release, sending away). “Trespasses” (paraptōmatōn, false steps, crossing God’s boundaries). Paul defines redemption first as forgiveness. Our deepest slavery was guilt before God, and Christ dealt with it.

Where Christians differ: how does the cross save? Some modern writers deny that Christ’s death was a substitute bearing our penalty, seeing it only as an example of love or a victory over evil. Verdict: penal substitution is central to the atonement: Christ bore the punishment our sins deserved, in our place. Scripture joins blood, redemption and forgiveness: a price paid, a penalty borne (Romans 3:24–25; Galatians 3:13; Hebrews 9:22). His victory over evil (Colossians 2:15) and his example of love (5:2) belong with it, not instead of it.

According to the riches of his grace. Not measured by our need but by his wealth. No sin is too great for riches like these.

What it does not mean. Not that the ransom was paid to Satan, as some early writers suggested. It satisfied the justice of God himself, who provided the payment in love (Romans 3:25–26).

In a sentence. In Christ we have been set free at the cost of his blood, and our sins are forgiven, as fully as God’s rich grace can forgive.

For worship. Name a sin you have been forgiven, and thank him for the blood that paid for it.
verseByVerse.note: Redemption was the word for buying a slave’s freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: Which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight.

Which he lavished upon us. Key words. “Lavished” (eperisseusen, made it overflow, more than enough). Grace is not rationed.

In all wisdom and insight. Key words. “Wisdom” (sophia): seeing things as God sees them. “Insight” (phronēsei): practical understanding, knowing how to live by it. Whose wisdom? It may describe God’s wisdom in planning salvation, or the wisdom he gives us to understand it. Probably the second: the next verse says he made his plan known to us, and Paul prays for this very wisdom in v. 17. Grace not only forgives; it opens our eyes.

Why this matters. God does not save us and leave us in the dark. He wants his children to understand his purposes, which is why he goes on to reveal his plan (vv. 9–10).

In a sentence. He poured this grace out on us in abundance, and with it gave us wisdom and understanding.

On a Tuesday. Ask God for wisdom when you read Scripture. He is glad to give it (James 1:5).

verseByVerse.quote: making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth in him.

Making known. God has told us what he is doing; it is not hidden from his people.

The mystery of his will. Key words. “Mystery” (mystērion). In Paul, a mystery is not a puzzle or something unknowable, but a truth once hidden in God and now revealed (3:3–6; Romans 16:25–26). The Old Testament gave hints; in Christ the plan is laid open.

According to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ. Christ is the centre of God’s plan from the beginning.

As a plan for the fullness of time. Key words. “Plan” (oikonomia, the management of a household; our word economy comes from it): God is administering history like a wise steward running an estate. “The fullness of time” is the moment when history reaches its goal. It began with Christ’s coming (Galatians 4:4) and will be completed at his return.

To unite all things in him. Key words. “Unite” (anakephalaiōsasthai, to sum up, to bring together under one head). An ancient writer would add up a column of figures and put the total at the top: Christ is the sum and head of everything. Sin broke the universe apart: people from God, people from each other (Jews and Gentiles in chapter 2), creation into frustration (Romans 8:20–22), spiritual powers into rebellion. God’s plan is to bring it all back into order and harmony under Christ.

Things in heaven and things on earth. The whole created order, seen and unseen.

How this shapes the letter. Chapter 2 shows this happening now: Jews and Gentiles made one in Christ. Chapter 3 says the church displays it to the heavenly powers (3:10). Chapter 4 calls the church to live in that unity.

Where Christians differ: will everyone and everything finally be saved? Some, from Origen in the third century to modern universalists, read uniting all things as a promise that every person, and even the devil and fallen angels, will finally be reconciled to God. Verdict: no. To unite under one head means to bring everything under Christ’s rule, not that everything will be saved. In the same letter Paul warns that the immoral have no inheritance in the kingdom and that God’s wrath comes on the disobedient (5:5–6), and that Christ’s enemies are subdued (1:21–22). Some things are brought under Christ in joyful worship, and others in defeat (1 Corinthians 15:24–28; Philippians 2:10–11). Everything will be put in order; not everything will be saved.

In a sentence. He has let us in on the secret of his plan, which he purposed in Christ to carry out when history reaches its goal: to bring everything in heaven and on earth together under Christ as its one head.

On a Tuesday. Your fractured world, family, nation or church, has a future in Christ. Work for reconciliation now as a sign of what is coming.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we who were the first to hope in Christ might be to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we who were the first to hope in Christ might be to the praise of his glory.

In him we have obtained an inheritance. Key words. “Obtained an inheritance” (eklērōthēmen, were allotted, were given a share). The Greek can mean we were given an inheritance, or we were made his inheritance. Both are true: we receive God’s promised future, and we are God’s own possession (v. 18; Deuteronomy 32:9). In the Old Testament Israel’s inheritance was the promised land; in the New Testament it widens to the whole renewed creation and life with God for ever (Matthew 5:5; 1 Peter 1:4).

Having been predestined. As in v. 5: decided beforehand by God.

According to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will. Key words. “Works” (energountos, is actively at work in, carries out). “All things” (ta panta). “Counsel” (boulēn, deliberate decision). God’s plan for us is part of his rule over everything. He is not reacting to history; he is carrying it out, every event, according to his own wise decision (Romans 8:28; Proverbs 16:33).

Where Christians differ: does God govern all things, or only some? Many Christians hold that God sets the overall direction of history but leaves most events to human free choices, which he foresees and responds to. Open theists go further and say God does not know free choices in advance. Verdict: Paul says God works all things according to his will: not most things, not the big things only. Scripture shows God governing the fall of a sparrow (Matthew 10:29), the roll of dice (Proverbs 16:33), the decisions of kings (Proverbs 21:1) and even the wicked acts that crucified Christ (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). This does not make human choices unreal: people choose freely and are responsible, and God works through their choices, not around them. How both are true is a mystery, but Scripture teaches both. It is the deepest comfort a believer has: nothing in your life is outside God’s purpose.

We who were the first to hope in Christ. Key words. “First to hope” (proēlpikotas, hoped beforehand). Probably Jewish believers, Paul included, who had hoped for the Messiah and believed in Jesus first; verse 13 then turns to “you also”, the Gentiles. Some take it as all believers, who hope now before Christ’s return; but the switch from “we” to “you” in v. 13 favours the first reading.

To the praise of his glory. The second refrain.

What it does not mean. Not that God is the author of sin. He governs evil without doing evil or approving it, and turns it to good, as at the cross (Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23).

In a sentence. In Christ we too were given a share in God’s inheritance, as God decided beforehand, the God who carries out everything according to his own will, so that we Jewish believers, who were the first to put our hope in Christ, might bring praise to his glory.

On a Tuesday. Whatever happens today, the God who works all things is working in it for his glory and your good.

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory.

In him you also. Now the Gentiles: you who were outsiders share fully in everything just described (2:11–22).

When you heard … and believed. How God’s eternal choice becomes real in history: through ordinary preaching and real faith (Romans 10:14–17). Election never bypasses the gospel; it works through it.

The word of truth, the gospel of your salvation. The gospel is true and it saves. “Gospel” (euangelion) means good news: the announcement of what God has done in Christ.

Were sealed. Key words. “Sealed” (esphragisthēte). In the ancient world a seal pressed into wax showed ownership, guaranteed authenticity and protected the contents. Documents, sacks of goods and even slaves were sealed. God sets his seal on believers: the Holy Spirit. He marks them as God’s property, proves they are genuine and keeps them safe until the end (4:30).

With the promised Holy Spirit. Promised by the prophets (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Joel 2:28) and by Jesus (Acts 1:4–5).

Who is the guarantee of our inheritance. Key words. “Guarantee” (arrabōn), a business word: a down payment, the first instalment that pledges the rest and is of the same kind. In modern Greek the word means an engagement ring. The Spirit is the first taste of heaven now, and God’s promise that the rest will certainly come.

Until we acquire possession of it. Literally until the redemption of the possession: until God fully takes possession of his people at the resurrection, and they possess their inheritance.

To the praise of his glory. The third refrain closes the great sentence.

Where Christians differ: when are believers sealed? Some Pentecostal teaching, and some older Reformed writers such as Martyn Lloyd-Jones, treat the sealing as a further experience after conversion, an overwhelming assurance to be sought. Verdict: the text ties it to believing: having heard and believed, you were sealed. The Greek participle describes what happened together with believing, not a later stage. Every believer is sealed with the Spirit at conversion (Romans 8:9). Believers may still seek to be filled afresh (5:18), and God may give special seasons of assurance; but no Christian is unsealed.

Where Christians differ: can a sealed believer be lost? Those who hold that true believers can finally fall away read the seal as a mark that can be broken. Verdict: the seal is God’s, set until the day of redemption (4:30), and the guarantee pledges the full inheritance. A pledge God gives is not withdrawn. This is one of the clearest grounds for the perseverance of the saints: those God seals, he keeps. Warnings elsewhere are real, and those who abandon Christ show they were never truly his (1 John 2:19); but the sealed are kept.

What it does not mean. Not that the seal depends on feeling the Spirit. It is God’s act, whether felt strongly or not.

In a sentence. And you Gentiles too, when you heard the true message, the good news that saves you, and believed in Christ, were marked as God’s own with the Holy Spirit he had promised, who is the down payment guaranteeing our full inheritance until God completes the redemption of his people, so that his glory is praised.

For worship. Thank God that he has given you his Spirit as the pledge of your inheritance, and that he does not take back his pledge.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and security. The “guarantee” was a first instalment, pledging full payment later.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having heard of their faith and love, Paul never stops thanking God for them and praying that the Father of glory will give them the Spirit of wisdom and revelation to know him better. He prays that the eyes of their hearts will be opened to grasp the hope of God’s call, the wealth of his inheritance in his people, and the vast power at work for believers. That power is the strength God exerted when he raised Christ from the dead and seated him at his right hand, above every ruler and name in this age and the next, putting all things under his feet and giving him as head over all things to the church, his body, the fullness of the one who fills everything.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit of Wisdom and Revelation

Paul prays for "the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him" (v.17). This single phrase encapsulates the Reformed understanding of how divine truth moves from the page to the heart. The Spirit who inspired the Scripture is also required to illuminate the reader of Scripture. Without the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, the words of God remain external — true, but not transforming; known about, but not known. Calvin devoted a famous section of the Institutes to this: the Scripture needs no external proof of its authority, because the Spirit who produced it also produces the certainty of it in the heart of the believer.

The practical implication is that Bible reading and prayer are inseparable disciplines. To open the Scripture without asking the Spirit to open our eyes to it is to work without our most essential tool. The Puritans understood this, and habitually prayed for illumination before they opened the book. The eyes of the heart do not open themselves. This prayer of Paul's is therefore not only a prayer about the Ephesians — it is a prayer for every reader of Scripture in every age who wants not merely to know about God but to know God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul writes this prayer from prison. He cannot visit the Ephesians; he cannot lay hands on them; he cannot preach to them in person. What he can do is pray — and his prayer from chains is not for his own release but for their illumination. This is one of the most searching things in the letter: the imprisoned apostle, whose situation would seem to give him every right to focus on his own needs, pours his intercession entirely outward, toward the people he loves. His joy is in their knowledge of Christ, not in his own circumstances. This is the mind of Christ (Philippians 2:5) applied to prayer.

Now: We live in an age of unprecedented access to biblical content. More sermons, commentaries, podcasts, and Bible apps exist today than at any point in history. And yet spiritual blindness remains our greatest problem. We have more information about God than any previous generation, and arguably less experiential knowledge of him. Paul's prayer cuts through all of this: what we need is not more content but opened eyes — the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, granting us not information but encounter. The Ephesians had Paul's letter. We have the whole Bible. Both of us need the same thing: the Spirit who makes the word alive.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers,

For this reason. Because of vv. 3–14. Doctrine leads to prayer. Knowing God’s purposes does not make prayer unnecessary; it gives prayer its confidence.

Because I have heard. Paul hears reports of these churches, many of them perhaps founded after he left.

Your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints. The two marks of genuine Christianity: trust towards Christ and love towards his people. Faith that does not produce love is not real (Galatians 5:6; 1 John 3:14). All the saints: not only those you like.

Textual note. Some early manuscripts omit “your love”, reading “faith… toward all the saints”. The longer text is probably original (compare Colossians 1:4).

I do not cease to give thanks for you. Paul thanks God, not the believers, for their faith and love, because these are God’s gifts.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul prayed every moment without stopping. He prayed regularly and often for them, and they were never left out.

In a sentence. That is why, since I heard of your trust in the Lord Jesus and your love for all God’s people, I keep thanking God for you and mentioning you when I pray.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for specific Christians you know, and tell them.

verseByVerse.quote: That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him.

The God of our Lord Jesus Christ. As a man, Jesus worshipped and prayed to the Father (John 20:17).

The Father of glory. The glorious Father, the source of all splendour.

May give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation. Key words. “Wisdom” (sophias): seeing things as God sees them. “Revelation” (apokalypseōs, unveiling). Paul’s first request is not for new blessings but for a deeper knowledge of God himself.

Where Christians differ: the Holy Spirit, or a spirit of wisdom? Some translations read “a spirit of wisdom”, meaning a wise attitude or disposition. Verdict: the Holy Spirit. Wisdom and revelation are his work (Isaiah 11:2; 1 Corinthians 2:10–12), and only God can give revelation. But they already have the Spirit (v. 13), so Paul is not praying for them to receive him again; he is praying for the Spirit’s ongoing work in their understanding.

Revelation without new revelation. “Revelation” here means God opening their eyes to what he has already revealed in Christ, not new truths beyond Scripture. The canon is complete; but every believer still needs the Spirit to make what is written clear and real to the heart (1 Corinthians 2:14).

In the knowledge of him. Key words. “Knowledge” (epignōsei, full, personal knowledge). Not just facts about God, but knowing him, as a child knows a father.

Why this prayer? They have every blessing (v. 3), but they need to see what they have. A man who does not know he has inherited a fortune lives like a pauper.

What it does not mean. Not a request for secret knowledge or private visions, the kind of thing Ephesian magic offered. It is understanding of the God revealed in Christ.

In a sentence. I ask that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glorious Father, will give you his Spirit, who brings wisdom and opens your eyes, so that you come to know him better.

On a Tuesday. Pray first that you and others will know God better. Ask the Spirit to open your eyes before you read the Bible.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding

verseByVerse.quote: Having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints.

Having the eyes of your hearts enlightened. Key words. “Heart” (kardia). In Scripture the heart is the centre of the person: thinking, willing and feeling, not only emotion. Paul wants them to see with the inner person, to understand and be gripped. “Enlightened” (pephōtismenous, flooded with light). Only God can do this (2 Corinthians 4:6).

The hope to which he has called you. Key words. “Hope” (elpis). Christian hope is not wishful thinking but certain expectation of what God has promised: resurrection, Christ’s return, the new creation, life with God. God’s call brought them into it.

The riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints. Whose inheritance is meant: ours, or God’s?

Where Christians differ: our inheritance, or God’s? Some read this as the inheritance believers receive, kept among the saints. Verdict: most likely God’s own inheritance, which is his people. Paul says his inheritance, and the Old Testament calls Israel the LORD’s portion and inheritance (Deuteronomy 32:9; Malachi 3:17). Paul wants them to grasp how much God values them. For Gentiles who had been without God (2:12), this was astonishing. Both truths are biblical (v. 14 speaks of our inheritance), but here the wonder is that they are God’s treasure.

What it does not mean. Not that God gains something he lacked. He chooses to treasure his people.

In a sentence. I pray that the eyes of your heart will be opened, so that you know the sure hope God has called you to, and how rich and glorious a treasure he has in his people.

For worship. You are part of God’s inheritance. He values you.

verseByVerse.quote: and what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places,
verseByVerse.commentary:
and what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places,

The immeasurable greatness of his power. Key words. “Immeasurable” (hyperballon, surpassing, beyond measuring). The third thing Paul prays they will see.

Four words for power. Paul piles them up: power (dynamis, ability), working (energeia, power in action), great (kratos, strength that prevails) and might (ischys, inherent strength). Words fail him.

Toward us who believe. This power is directed at believers: for our salvation, holiness and endurance (3:16, 20).

When he raised him from the dead. The measure of the power. Death is the one enemy no human can overcome. God reversed it. That same power has raised believers from spiritual death (2:5–6) and is at work in them now.

And seated him at his right hand. Key words. “Right hand”: the place of supreme honour and authority beside a king (Psalm 110:1). It is not a physical location, as if God the Father had a body with a right side; it means Christ shares God’s throne and rule. Being seated means his saving work is finished (Hebrews 10:12).

In the heavenly places. See on v. 3.

For the Ephesians. They had lived in fear of spiritual powers, curses and fate. Paul wants them to know that the power working for them is greater than all of it.

What it does not mean. Not that believers will always feel powerful or see miracles. God’s power is often seen in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9), in endurance and change of heart.

In a sentence. And that you may know how immeasurably great is his power for us who believe, the same mighty power he used when he raised Christ from the dead and enthroned him at his right hand in heaven.

On a Tuesday. The habit you think you cannot break, the grief you think you cannot bear: the power that emptied the tomb is at work in you.

parallels.desc: sit at my right hand

verseByVerse.quote: Far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.

Far above. Key words. “Far above” (hyperanō): not merely above, but immeasurably above, in a different league.

All rule and authority and power and dominion. Key words. Terms Jews and Greeks used for ranks of spiritual beings, including hostile ones (6:12), and also human rulers. Whatever powers there are, good or evil, visible or invisible, Christ is over them.

Every name that is named. In Ephesus, magicians invoked the names of gods and spirits to gain power (Acts 19:13–19). There is no name, spirit or power that Christ does not outrank. No curse, horoscope or spirit has a claim on those who belong to him.

Not only in this age but also in the one to come. Key words. Jews divided history into two ages: this present age, marked by sin and death, and the age to come, when God would put everything right. Christ’s resurrection has brought the age to come into the present; the two now overlap until his return. His rule covers both: now, and for ever.

What it does not mean. Not that evil powers have vanished. They are still active (6:12), but they are defeated and subject to Christ (Colossians 2:15).

In a sentence. Christ now sits far above every ruler, authority, power and lordship, above every name anyone can name, in this age and in the age to come.

On a Tuesday. There is no power anywhere that Christ is not above. Whatever you fear today is beneath him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church,

He put all things under his feet. Key words. From Psalm 8:6, where God gives humanity rule over creation. Adam lost it; Christ, the true man, has received it (Hebrews 2:6–9). Under his feet pictures total subjection, as conquered kings bowed before the victor.

And gave him as head over all things to the church. Key words. “Gave” (edōken). The sentence is easy to misread. It does not say Christ is head over the church and also over all things, though both are true. It says God gave the church a gift: Christ, who is head over all things. The one who rules the universe has been given to the church. He rules everything for the sake of his people.

Head. Key words. “Head” (kephalē). Here it clearly means authority, ruler, since it stands alongside putting all things under his feet. In 4:15–16 it also carries the idea of source of life and growth for the body.

Where Christians differ: the head of the church. Roman Catholic teaching sees the pope as Christ’s visible vicar and head on earth. Verdict: Christ alone is head of the church (Westminster Confession 25.6), ruling by his word and Spirit through local elders. No human being shares that headship.

In a sentence. God put everything under Christ’s feet, and gave him, the head over everything, to the church.

For worship. The Lord of everything is the head of your church. Worship him as the one who rules all things for his people.

parallels.desc: you have put all things under his feet

verseByVerse.quote: which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.

Which is his body. The church is not a club or an organisation that admires Christ, but the body of Christ: united to him, living from him, the means by which he acts in the world.

The fullness of him who fills all in all. Key words. “Fullness” (plērōma). One of the hardest phrases in Paul. What does it mean to call the church Christ’s fullness?

Where Christians differ: does the church fill Christ, or does Christ fill the church? There are two main readings. First, the church completes Christ, as a body completes a head. Calvin took this view and found it moving: Christ, who lacks nothing in himself, counts himself in some sense incomplete without his people. Second, the church is filled by Christ: it is the place he fills with his presence, life and gifts. Verdict: the second is more likely. Paul consistently speaks of Christ filling (4:10, he ascended that he might fill all things) and of believers being filled (3:19; 5:18), never of Christ being filled up by us; and Colossians 2:9–10 says the fullness of deity dwells in Christ and you have been filled in him. The church is the community Christ fills, his fullness on earth. Yet Calvin’s point remains true in its own way: Christ is not ashamed to be joined to his people as a head to its body.

Who fills all in all. Key words. Christ’s presence and rule extend through all creation (4:10; Jeremiah 23:24). He fills the universe by his power; he fills the church by his saving presence.

What it does not mean. Not that the church is perfect or that Christ depends on it. It means the church is precious and has a dignity far above how it often looks.

In a sentence. The church is his body, filled by him who fills everything everywhere.

On a Tuesday. When church life seems small and ordinary, remember what it is: the body of the risen King, filled with his presence.

1.overview:
Ephesians opens with the longest sentence in the New Testament (vv. 3–14), a single breathless act of praise for every spiritual blessing God has given his people in Christ. The Father chose them before creation to be holy, predestined them in love for adoption, and freely gave them grace in his beloved Son. In Christ they have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, and they have been let into the secret of God’s plan: to unite all things in heaven and on earth under Christ. Jews who first hoped in Christ and Gentiles who later believed have both been sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, the down payment of their inheritance, all to the praise of God’s glory.

Then Paul prays (vv. 15–23). He does not ask for new blessings, but that they may see the ones they have: the hope of God’s calling, the riches of his inheritance in his people, and the immeasurable power at work in believers, the same power that raised Christ from the dead and seated him far above every power in this age and the next. God has made Christ head over everything for the sake of the church, which is his body. The chapter teaches that salvation begins in God’s eternal choice, rests on Christ’s blood, is sealed by the Spirit, and ends in praise.

2.title: Dead in Sin, Alive in Christ
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And you were dead in the trespasses and sins <sup>2</sup>in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience — <sup>3</sup>among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. <sup>4</sup>But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, <sup>5</sup>even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved — <sup>6</sup>and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, <sup>7</sup>so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. <sup>8</sup>For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, <sup>9</sup>not a result of works, so that no one may boast. <sup>10</sup>For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them. <sup>11</sup>Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands — <sup>12</sup>remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. <sup>13</sup>But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. <sup>14</sup>For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility <sup>15</sup>by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace, <sup>16</sup>and might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility. <sup>17</sup>And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. <sup>18</sup>For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father. <sup>19</sup>So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, <sup>20</sup>built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, <sup>21</sup>in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. <sup>22</sup>In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reminds them that they were spiritually dead in their sins, living by the world’s ways and under the power of the spirit at work in the disobedient. All of us once lived for the flesh and were by nature deserving of wrath. But God, rich in mercy and great in love, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead: by grace we are saved. He raised us and seated us with Christ in the heavenly realms, to show for ever the riches of his kindness. Salvation is by grace through faith, God’s gift, not earned by works, so that no one can boast. We are God’s handiwork, created in Christ for the good works he prepared for us.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total Depravity, Sovereign Grace, and the New Creation

"Dead in trespasses and sins" is the Reformed doctrine of total depravity in its most direct biblical expression. Total depravity does not mean that fallen human beings are as evil as they could possibly be — common grace restrains the full expression of human sin. It means that every faculty of the human person — mind, will, affections, conscience — has been corrupted by the fall, so that no part of us naturally seeks God or is capable of saving itself. The will is not neutral, waiting to choose God if only given sufficient reason; it is enslaved, "following the prince of the power of the air" (v.2), "carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind" (v.3).

Against this backdrop, the "but God" of v.4 is the hinge of history. God does not respond to a seeking sinner; he acts on a dead one. This is irresistible grace — not grace that overrides the will by force, but grace that transforms the will, making the dead alive, making the unwilling willing, making the seeking possible. If we seek the cause of our salvation, we find it not in ourselves but in God alone. The new birth is entirely God's work, and the faith through which we receive it is itself his gift (v.8).

The closing verse — "we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works" — is the Reformed answer to the charge that grace produces passivity. It does not. Grace produces the very thing that law could only demand. The person who knows they are entirely saved by grace, not by works, is freed from self-justifying performance and freed for genuine, joyful, Spirit-empowered good works — the works that God prepared beforehand for them to walk in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The recipients of Paul's letter knew exactly what he meant by "dead in trespasses and sins" — it was their autobiography. Many had been worshippers of Artemis, practitioners of occult arts (Acts 19:19 tells us that converted Ephesians burned their magic books, worth fifty thousand pieces of silver). The darkness, the slavery to spiritual powers, the restless seeking for blessing through ritual and charm — they had lived it. The "but God" of v.4 was the turning point of their actual lives. The grace Paul describes was not theological theory to them; it was the story of what had happened to them, written in their own experience. This is why the passage carries such heat — Paul is describing something he and his readers have lived through, not merely thought about.

Now: "Dead in trespasses and sins" describes every human being outside of Christ, however educated, however moral, however spiritually sincere. The kind CEO, the generous philanthropist, the sincere seeker of truth — apart from Christ, all share the same condition: spiritual death, living under the dominion of the one who still holds sway over "the sons of disobedience" (v.2). This is not a comfortable diagnosis, but it is a necessary one — because a person who thinks they are merely ill will never seek the cure appropriate to death. The church must have the courage to declare both the diagnosis and the remedy with equal clarity: dead — but God.

verseByVerse.quote: You were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Christ, Paul’s readers were not sick or struggling people who needed a little help: they were spiritually dead, and their whole way of life was steered by the world around them and by the devil behind it.

The connection. Chapter 1 ended with God’s power raising Christ from the dead and seating him above every power (1:19–23). Chapter 2 shows the same power at work in us. To see how great it is, Paul first shows how dead we were. The sentence that begins in verse 1 does not reach its main verb until verse 5: “God … made us alive.” Verses 1–3 are the grave; verses 4–7 are the resurrection.

You were dead. Not physically: the readers had been walking, working and worshipping idols. Spiritual death means being cut off from the life of God (4:18). A dead body cannot hear, see, feel or respond. So a person spiritually dead cannot hear God’s voice with love, see his glory with delight, or turn to him by their own power. This is what God warned of in Eden: in the day you eat of it you shall surely die (Genesis 2:17). Adam did not drop dead that day, but he hid from God, and death began.

In the trespasses and sins. Two words for wrong. A trespass (paraptōma) is a false step, crossing a line God has drawn. A sin (hamartia) is missing the mark, falling short of what God made us for. Together they cover every way we fail: doing what God forbids, and not being what he commands. The dead are dead “in” them: sin is both the cause of the death and the sphere it is lived in.

In which you once walked. “Walk” is the Bible’s word for a way of life (4:1, 17; 5:2, 8, 15). The paradox: the dead were busy. Spiritual death is not inactivity but activity without God: careers, families, religion, pleasure, all lived as if God were not there.

Following the course of this world. Literally “according to the age of this world”. “The world” here is not the planet or people as God’s creatures, but human society organised without God: its values, assumptions, fashions and pressures. It tells us what to want and whom to admire, and the dead go along with it without noticing, the way fish do not notice water (1 John 2:15–17).

The prince of the power of the air. Satan, called elsewhere the ruler of this world (John 12:31) and the god of this age, who blinds unbelieving minds (2 Corinthians 4:4). In the ancient world the air, the space between earth and the heavens, was thought to be the home of spirits. Paul uses the language his readers knew: the spiritual powers they feared are real, and they are ruled by one evil prince. He is not equal to God; he is a creature already defeated (1:21; Colossians 2:15).

The spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience. Satan works inside the disobedient. The word “at work” (energeō) is the same Paul used of God’s power in raising Christ (1:20). Two powers are at work in the world: the devil’s in the disobedient, God’s in those he raises. “Sons of disobedience” is a Hebrew way of saying people characterised by disobedience.

Three enemies. Verses 1–3 name the three enemies the church has long called the world, the flesh and the devil: the world outside us (v. 2), the devil above us (v. 2), and the flesh inside us (v. 3). They work together. Culture makes sin normal, the devil makes it attractive, and our own nature wants it.

What it does not mean. Not that unbelievers are as bad as they could possibly be, or that they cannot do kind or good things in a human sense. Many are honest, generous and brave. Total depravity means that sin has reached every part of human nature, mind, will and desires, so that nothing in us is untouched, and nothing in us can turn us back to God. Nor does it mean that everyone outside Christ is consciously serving Satan. Most simply follow the crowd; that is the point. And it does not remove responsibility. The dead “walked” in sins; they did what they wanted.

Where Christians differ: how dead? Semi-Pelagian and Arminian traditions hold that the fall left people weakened but still able, with God’s general help (called prevenient grace), to accept or refuse the gospel. Reformed theology holds total inability: the fallen will is free to choose what it wants, but it does not want God, and no one can come to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44; Romans 8:7–8). Paul’s image decides it: a corpse does not cooperate with its resurrection. Verdict: total depravity and inability (Westminster Confession 9.3). This is why everything turns on “But God” (v. 4).

In a sentence. Without Christ we were spiritually dead, busy in sin, carried along by the world, driven by the devil, and unable to save ourselves.

On a Tuesday. When you share the gospel, argue clearly, but pray first: you are speaking to people who need resurrection, not merely persuasion. And no one is too far gone, because God raises the dead.
verseByVerse.note: “The prince of the power of the air” is Satan. The air was thought to be the realm of spiritual powers.

verseByVerse.quote: among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now includes himself and every Jew: “we all” once lived for our own desires, and we were all, by our very nature, under God’s just anger, exactly like everyone else.

Among whom we all once lived. Verses 1–2 said “you” (the Gentile readers). Now Paul says “we”. A Jew might think that, with the law, the temple and circumcision, he was in a different position from pagans. Paul, the strictest of Pharisees (Philippians 3:4–6), says no: Jew and Gentile alike were dead. This prepares for verses 11–22: if both were equally lost, both are saved the same way, and neither can look down on the other (Romans 3:9, 22–23).

The passions of our flesh. “Flesh” (sarx) in Paul often means not the body but human nature as fallen and turned in on itself: the self living for the self, apart from God. The “passions” are its cravings.

The desires of the flesh and the mind. Literally “the wills of the flesh and of the thoughts”. Paul deliberately adds “the mind”. Sin is not only bodily appetite, food, sex, drink. It is also the sins of the thinking self: pride, ambition, envy, unbelief, the respectable sins of clever and moral people. A man can be sober, chaste and hard-working and still live entirely in the desires of the mind.

And were by nature children of wrath. The deepest statement of the problem. Not only did we do wrong, we were wrong. “By nature” means by birth, by what we are as children of Adam, before and beneath any choice (Psalm 51:5). “Children of wrath” is again a Hebrew idiom: people who belong to wrath, on whom wrath rests (John 3:36).

Wrath. Not a fit of temper, and not something unworthy of a loving God. God’s wrath is his settled, holy, just opposition to evil (Romans 1:18). A God who was not angry at child abuse, cruelty and betrayal would not be good. His wrath is the response of his holiness to sin, and it is always fair: no one receives more than they deserve.

Like the rest of mankind. No exceptions. This is the universal human condition.

What it does not mean. Not that the body or physical desire is evil in itself. God made the body and called it good (Genesis 1:31); hunger and sexual desire are his gifts. “Flesh” means those desires, and the mind’s too, captured by the self and pursued outside God’s will. Nor does “children of wrath” mean God hates his creatures or takes pleasure in their ruin (Ezekiel 33:11). The very next words are “But God, being rich in mercy”. Wrath is real, but it is not God’s last word to those who come to Christ.

Where Christians differ: original sin. Pelagius (fifth century) taught that each person is born innocent and sins only by following bad examples. Eastern Orthodoxy teaches that we inherit mortality and a tendency to sin from Adam but not his guilt. Augustine and the Reformers taught that we inherit both a corrupt nature and the guilt of Adam’s first sin, because Adam acted as the representative head of the race (Romans 5:12–19). “By nature children of wrath” fits only the last: wrath rests on us by nature, not only after we choose. Verdict: original sin as both inherited corruption and imputed guilt (Westminster Confession 6.3). The same principle of representation is what saves us: as Adam’s sin was counted to us, so Christ’s righteousness is counted to those in him.

In a sentence. Every human being, the respectable as much as the rebel, has lived for self and stands by nature under God’s just wrath.

On a Tuesday. The sins of your mind, the pride you feel when you compare yourself with others, are as much “flesh” as any sin of the body. Bring both to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole gospel turns on two words, “But God”. Into our death, when we could do nothing, God acted, moved by his own rich mercy and great love, and gave us new life together with Christ.

But God. After three verses of death, the main subject of the sentence finally appears. Everything depends on these two words. If the story were “But we”, there would be no hope, because dead people cannot act. Martyn Lloyd-Jones called them the gospel in two words. Notice where the change begins: not in us, but in God.

Being rich in mercy. Mercy is God’s pity for those in misery. Grace gives what we do not deserve; mercy withholds what we do deserve and relieves our distress. God is “rich” in it (compare 1:7; 2:7; 3:8): his mercy does not run out, however great the need or however many come.

Because of the great love with which he loved us. The reason God acted lies in him, not in us. Paul piles up the words: love, great love, love with which he loved. And he loved us as we were, not as we would become: even when we were dead (Romans 5:8). We were not lovable; he loved us anyway, and his love made us lovely.

Made us alive together with Christ. The main verb of the whole sentence. One Greek word, synezōopoiēsen, “made alive with”. This is regeneration, the new birth (John 3:3–8; Titus 3:5): God giving spiritual life to the spiritually dead. It is God’s act alone. A dead man does not assist his resurrection; Lazarus did not help Jesus raise him (John 11:43–44). The first sign of the new life is that the dead begin to hear, believe and repent.

Together with Christ. Our new life is not a separate miracle but a share in his. When the Father raised Jesus (1:20), he raised all who are united to him. Our new birth is the power of Easter reaching us.

By grace you have been saved. Paul cannot wait until verse 8 to say it, so he breaks into his own sentence. “Have been saved” is a perfect tense in Greek: a completed act with lasting results. Saved, and still saved. “Salvation” here includes everything God has done: rescue from death and wrath into life with Christ.

The order of salvation. Reformed theology reads this as showing that regeneration comes before faith in order (not necessarily in time). God first makes us alive; then we believe. We do not believe in order to be born again; we believe because we have been born again (John 1:12–13; 1 John 5:1).

What it does not mean. Not that we are passive in the Christian life: once alive, we believe, repent, fight sin and walk in good works (v. 10). The point is that the first move, from death to life, is God’s alone. Nor does “mercy” mean that God overlooks sin. His mercy reaches us “with Christ”: through the death and resurrection of the one who bore the wrath of verse 3 in our place.

Where Christians differ: does God’s life-giving work depend on our consent? Arminians hold that God’s grace enables every person to believe, but that grace can be resisted, so the decisive factor in who is saved is the human response. Reformed theology holds that God’s regenerating grace is effectual: when God makes alive, the dead live (John 6:37; Acts 16:14, where the Lord opened Lydia’s heart). Verdict: effectual calling (Westminster Confession 10.1–2). God does not drag the unwilling; he makes them willing by giving them new hearts (Ezekiel 36:26).

In a sentence. When we were dead and could do nothing, God, out of his own mercy and love, made us alive with Christ: salvation is his work from the start.

For worship. Write or tell your own “But God” story: what you were, and what he did.

verseByVerse.quote: And raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because believers are joined to Christ, what happened to him has happened to them: God has not only given them life, but raised them with Christ and seated them with him on his throne, already, now.

Three “with” words. In Greek, Paul makes up compound words: made alive with (v. 5), raised with, seated with. Each matches a step in Christ’s story in 1:20: the Father raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand. Our story is his story. This is union with Christ: he is our representative head, and we are “in” him, so his history becomes ours (Romans 6:4–5; Colossians 3:1–3).

Raised us up with him. Spiritually, now: we have passed from death to life (John 5:24). Physically, later: our bodies will be raised at his return (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). The first guarantees the second.

Seated us with him in the heavenly places. To be seated is to be at rest, finished, and in a position of authority. Christ sat down because his work was complete (Hebrews 10:12). The “heavenly places” (see 1:3) are the unseen realm where Christ reigns over every power (1:20–21). The very powers that once ruled the Ephesians (v. 2) are now beneath the one with whom they are seated. They have changed sides of the throne.

In Christ Jesus. The reason for all of it. We are not seated there by our own spiritual height, but because we are in him.

Already and not yet. Paul uses past tenses: he raised us, he seated us. This is our position, settled in God’s eyes. Our experience does not yet match it: we still struggle, suffer and die. Ephesians holds both together. We are seated (2:6), yet we must stand and fight (6:10–13). The fight is real, but it is fought from victory, not for it.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians are already beyond struggle, sickness or sin, or that they can claim earthly power or success by their status. Paul writes this in chains. Nor is it an escape from earthly life: the seated church is sent to walk in good works on earth (v. 10).

In a sentence. In Christ you already share his resurrection life and his throne, though you do not yet see it.

On a Tuesday. Face the day from where you sit in Christ, not from where your circumstances put you. The boss, the diagnosis and the fear are real, but they are beneath your Lord’s feet, and you are seated with him.

verseByVerse.quote: So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is God’s purpose in saving us: that throughout eternity he might put the boundless wealth of his grace on display, in the kindness he has shown us in Christ.

So that. Paul gives the reason for verses 4–6. God saved us for our good, yes, but above all for the display of his own glory. This is the same goal as the refrain of chapter 1: to the praise of his glory (1:6, 12, 14). God’s glory and our good are not rivals: he is glorified precisely by being kind to us.

In the coming ages. Not one coming age but “ages”, one after another without end. Salvation is not a temporary rescue but an eternal exhibition.

He might show. The word means to demonstrate or exhibit, like a public display (Romans 9:22–23). The audience includes the angels and powers: through the church, God’s wisdom is made known to the rulers in the heavenly places (3:10). Each saved sinner is a living exhibit of what God’s grace can do.

The immeasurable riches of his grace. “Immeasurable” (hyperballon) means surpassing, beyond all measuring, the same word used of his power in 1:19. Grace is not merely sufficient; it overflows. Eternity will not exhaust it.
