In kindness toward us. Grace is not cold or grudging, like a judge reluctantly granting a pardon. It comes with kindness (chrēstotēs): warm, generous, gentle goodness (Titus 3:4). God does not merely tolerate the forgiven; he delights in them.

In Christ Jesus. All of this kindness reaches us through one channel. Outside Christ, God’s kindness calls people to repentance (Romans 2:4); in Christ, it becomes an eternal inheritance.

What it does not mean. Not that God saves us as mere objects to make himself look good, as though we were trophies on a shelf. The display is of kindness toward us: it is a display of love. Nor does it mean that grace runs out after conversion; it will be shown, and grow brighter, for ever.

In a sentence. God saved you so that for all eternity the universe would see in you how rich and kind his grace is.

For worship. You will be a trophy of grace for ever. Begin the praise now.

verseByVerse.quote: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now spells out what he blurted out in verse 5: salvation is God’s gift from first to last, received through faith, and in no way earned by anything we do, so that no human being will ever be able to boast before God.

For. Verses 8–9 explain verses 4–7. If God saved the dead, then salvation cannot be our achievement.

By grace. The source. Grace (charis) is God’s free, undeserved favour: not a substance poured into us, but God’s attitude and action of kindness toward those who deserve wrath (v. 3). If it is deserved in any way, it is no longer grace (Romans 11:6).

You have been saved. Again the perfect tense (see v. 5): a finished rescue with lasting effect. Saved from death (v. 1), from the world, the flesh and the devil (vv. 2–3), and from wrath (v. 3).

Through faith. The means, the empty hand that receives the gift. Faith is not a contribution, a small payment, or a virtue that earns God’s approval. It is trust: relying on Christ and what he has done, instead of on ourselves. Its value is entirely in its object. Weak faith in a strong Christ saves; strong faith in anything else does not. Note the preposition: we are saved through faith, never because of faith.

And this is not your own doing. In Greek “this” (touto) is neuter, while “grace” and “faith” are both feminine. So “this” does not point to faith alone, nor to grace alone, but to the whole thing just described: salvation by grace through faith. Paul’s point is that no part of it, including our believing, originates with us. It is the gift of God.

Not a result of works. “Works” here means anything we do to put God in our debt: law-keeping, religious rituals, moral effort, good deeds. Paul’s Jewish background had in view the works of the law, but the principle covers every human attempt to earn salvation (Romans 4:4–5; Titus 3:5).

So that no one may boast. God designed salvation this way on purpose. If we contributed even one per cent, we could boast of that one per cent: “I chose wisely when others did not.” God removes every ground of pride, so that the only boast left is in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:29–31). This gives a simple test of any version of the gospel: does it leave room for anyone to boast?

What it does not mean. Not that faith is unnecessary because God does everything: no one is saved without believing. Not that good works do not matter: verse 10 follows immediately. And “not of works” does not mean that God saves people while they remain unchanged. He saves us from sin, not in it. Works are excluded as the ground of salvation, not as its fruit.

Where Christians differ: is faith itself a gift? Arminians hold that God offers salvation and gives everyone the ability to believe, but that faith itself is the human response. Reformed theology holds that faith, too, is God’s gift, granted to those he has made alive (Philippians 1:29; Acts 13:48; 2 Peter 1:1). Even if “this” in verse 8 refers to the whole package rather than to faith alone, faith is part of the package. Verdict: faith is God’s gift; we believe, but we believe because God has given us life (v. 5).

Where Christians differ: justification. Roman Catholic teaching (Council of Trent, 1547) holds that justification includes the inner renewal of the person, begins at baptism, can be increased by good works, and can be lost by mortal sin. The Reformers taught that justification is a legal declaration: God pronounces the sinner righteous, not because of any righteousness in them, but because Christ’s righteousness is counted to them, received by faith alone (Romans 3:24–28; 4:5). Renewal (sanctification) always follows, but it is not the ground of our standing with God. Verdict: by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone (Westminster Confession 11.1). Verses 8–10 together say it exactly: saved not by works, but for works.

In a sentence. Salvation is a gift from beginning to end: God gives it by grace, we receive it by faith, and nobody earns it, so nobody can boast.

On a Tuesday. When you feel you have been a good Christian this week and God must be pleased with you, or a bad one and he must be finished with you, come back to this verse. Your standing rests on his gift, not on your week.
verseByVerse.note: “This” most naturally refers to the whole of salvation by grace through faith.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good works cannot save us, but they are the very purpose for which God saved us: we are his handiwork, newly created in Christ, and he has already prepared a life of good works for us to walk in.

For. Paul explains why salvation cannot come from our works (v. 9): because we ourselves are God’s work. A painting does not make the painter.

His workmanship. Greek poiēma (from which comes our word “poem”): something made, a work of craftsmanship or art. The same word describes creation in Romans 1:20. The emphasis in Greek falls on “his”: his work we are, not our own. You are not a self-made person; you are God’s masterpiece, still being finished (Philippians 1:6).

Created in Christ Jesus. Salvation is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17; Galatians 6:15). As God created the first world out of nothing by his word, so he creates new people in Christ. It is not a renovation of the old self but a new beginning.

For good works. The purpose of the new creation. “Good works” are actions that please God: done in faith, according to his commands, from love, for his glory. They include the large and visible (missions, justice, generosity) and the small and hidden (patience with a child, honesty at work, a kind word, a meal for a neighbour).

Which God prepared beforehand. As God planned our salvation before the foundation of the world (1:4), he planned the good works that would follow. We do not invent the Christian life; we discover it. Each day has works God has already prepared.

That we should walk in them. “Walk” again (see v. 1). Before, we walked in trespasses and sins (vv. 1–2); now we walk in good works. The same word marks the change: a new way of life. Chapters 4–6 will spell out what this walk looks like (4:1, 17; 5:2, 8, 15).

Not by works, but for works. Verses 8–10 together are the whole Reformation in miniature. Works are the fruit of salvation, never the root. The Reformers put it this way: we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone. Faith that produces no works is not saving faith (James 2:17–18).

What it does not mean. Not that good works are optional extras for keen Christians: they are what we were created for. Nor that good works earn us anything: they are God’s gift too, since he prepared them and works in us to do them (Philippians 2:13). And “prepared beforehand” does not make us puppets. God’s plan works through our real choices, not around them.

In a sentence. God made you new in Christ for a life of good works, which he has already planned for you to walk in.

On a Tuesday. Ask God this morning to show you the good works he has prepared for you today, and expect to find them in ordinary places: your desk, your kitchen, your street.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gentile believers should remember what they were: called uncircumcised, without Christ, excluded from Israel, strangers to God’s covenants, hopeless and godless. Now in Christ, those who were far away have been brought near by his blood. He is our peace: he has made Jew and Gentile one, demolishing the wall of hostility by setting aside the law’s commands and regulations, creating one new humanity and reconciling both to God through the cross. He came preaching peace to those far and near, and through him both have access to the Father by one Spirit. So Gentiles are no longer foreigners but fellow citizens with God’s people and members of his household, built on the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone, growing into a holy temple, a dwelling for God by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Atonement and the New Community

This passage reveals the ecclesiological dimensions of the atonement — a dimension often underemphasised in evangelical theology. We tend to think of Christ's death in purely individual terms: He died for me, my sins are forgiven, I am reconciled to God. All of this is gloriously true. But Paul insists that the cross accomplished something more: it created a new community. Christ died not only to reconcile individuals to God (vertical reconciliation) but to reconcile estranged human beings to one another (horizontal reconciliation). He "reconciled us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility" (v.16).

This means that the unity of the church is not merely a practical or organisational goal; it is a theological reality purchased by Christ's blood. To live in division, to maintain the walls that Christ has torn down, to prefer the company of people like us over the diverse community Christ has created — this is a denial of the atonement. Every genuinely reconciled, cross-cultural Christian community is a proclamation of the gospel: not with words but with existence. Its very existence says: the cross is real, the wall is down, God has made one new man.

The metaphor of the temple (vv.19–22) carries the further implication that the church's holiness matters. The old temple was the place where God dwelt, and its holiness was fiercely guarded. The new temple — the church — is also the dwelling place of God by his Spirit. The community of believers is not merely a gathering of like-minded people; it is the sacred space where the Holy God has chosen to make his home on earth. This gives both dignity and responsibility to every local church: you are the temple of God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The stone wall of the Jerusalem temple — the soreg — was not a metaphor. Inscriptions warning Gentiles that entry beyond it meant death have been found by archaeologists. The barrier was physical, legal, and deadly. When Paul says Christ has broken down "the dividing wall of hostility," his Jewish and Gentile readers understood exactly what wall he meant. They may have stood on opposite sides of it. Now they sat side by side at the Lord's table, eating and drinking together, addressed as fellow citizens and members of the same household. The sociological miracle was visible and daily, and it pointed to a theological reality: the cross had accomplished what no social programme could.

Now: The church in our age still struggles with the walls that Christ has torn down. Racial segregation in churches persists in many places. Class divisions shape congregational culture in ways we rarely examine. Political tribalism has entered sanctuaries and split families of faith. Against all of this, Ephesians 2 speaks with prophetic force: the wall is down. Christ killed the hostility. The new humanity he created is more fundamental than any human division that preceded it. The church that reflects this — that is visibly, sacrificially, joyfully diverse across the lines that divide the surrounding world — is not merely being socially progressive. It is being theologically faithful. It is showing the world what the cross actually accomplished.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands —
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now turns from salvation as rescue from death to salvation as reconciliation between peoples. He asks his Gentile readers first to remember what they were, outsiders despised by the Jews, so that they never forget the grace that brought them in.

Therefore. Because of verses 1–10. If God saved both Jew and Gentile by grace alone, with no works to boast of, then the wall between them has no ground left to stand on.

Remember. In Scripture, remembering is not mere recall but a spiritual discipline. Israel was told again and again to remember that they had been slaves in Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15). Remembering where we came from produces humility and gratitude, and kills pride. Christians who forget what they were saved from soon look down on those who are still there.

You Gentiles in the flesh. “Gentiles” (ethnē, “the nations”) was the Jewish word for everyone else. “In the flesh” here means physically, by birth: they were not born into God’s covenant people.

Called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision. These were labels, and insults. Circumcision was the sign God gave Abraham of his covenant (Genesis 17:9–14), and it had become the badge of Jewish identity. Many Jews called Gentiles “the uncircumcision” with contempt, as unclean outsiders. Paul says “so-called” of both labels: both are names given by people, not God’s final verdict.

Which is made in the flesh by hands. A pointed phrase. In the Greek Old Testament the phrase “made with hands” is regularly used of idols, as in Leviticus 26:1 and Isaiah 46:6. Paul hints that circumcision of the body, valued for itself, is merely human. God always wanted circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4), and in Christ believers receive a circumcision made without hands (Colossians 2:11). The true Jew is one inwardly (Romans 2:28–29).

What it does not mean. Not that circumcision was a mistake or that God’s covenant with Israel was worthless: it was his gift and pointed to Christ (Romans 3:1–2; 9:4–5). Paul objects to the outward sign being treated as the ground of standing with God, and used to despise others.

In a sentence. Gentile believers must remember that they were once despised outsiders, so that they live in humble gratitude for grace.

On a Tuesday. Think back to what you were before Christ. Then think of the people your church tends to look down on, and remember that you once stood where they stand.

verseByVerse.quote: remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Christ, the Gentile readers were outsiders in every way that mattered: no Messiah, no place in God’s people, no share in his promises, no hope and no true God. Paul lists five losses so they feel the size of what they now have.

At that time. Before they believed: the “once” of verses 2–3.

1. Separated from Christ. “Christ” means Messiah, the anointed King God promised to Israel. The hope of the Messiah belonged to Israel (Romans 9:5). Gentiles had no share in it; they were not looking for him or waiting for him.

2. Alienated from the commonwealth of Israel. “Commonwealth” (politeia) means citizenship, membership of a nation with its rights. Israel was the people God had formed, ruled and lived among. Gentiles were foreigners to it, with no rights of citizenship.

3. Strangers to the covenants of promise. God made covenants with Abraham (Genesis 12; 15; 17), with Israel at Sinai, and with David (2 Samuel 7), and promised a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34). All of them carried one great promise: I will be your God, and you will be my people, and through Abraham’s offspring all nations will be blessed. Gentiles were outside these binding agreements; God had made no such promise to them.

4. Having no hope. Not that they had no wishes or plans, but no sure hope beyond death. Ancient tombstones often carried grim inscriptions expressing that death was the end. Paul says the same elsewhere of those who grieve with no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

5. Without God in the world. Greek atheoi, from which comes our word “atheist”. Ironically, Ephesus was crowded with gods: Artemis, the emperor, a host of others. Paul does not mean they had no religion, but that they did not know the one true God. Gods everywhere, and God nowhere. Many religions, no relationship with the Creator.

The logic. The list moves from the specific to the total. Without the Messiah, they had no place in God’s people; without a place, no promises; without promises, no hope; without hope, no God. Everything hangs on the first: being separated from Christ is the root of every other loss. So, in verse 13, being brought near in Christ restores them all.

What it does not mean. Not that Gentiles were outside God’s rule or care: he gave them rain and harvests and did not leave himself without witness (Acts 14:17). Nor that every Jew was automatically saved: Paul says elsewhere that not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel (Romans 9:6). The point is the privileged position of Israel as the people of the promises, a position the Gentiles did not share.

In a sentence. Without Christ, the Gentiles had no Messiah, no people, no promises, no hope and no God.

On a Tuesday. This describes many of your neighbours and colleagues. Pray for them with compassion, not contempt, and be ready to tell them about the hope that is in you.

verseByVerse.quote: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything in verse 12 has been reversed: those who were far from God and his people have been brought near, not by their own efforts, but by the blood of Christ.

But now. The second great turning point of the chapter, matching “But God” in verse 4. There the change was from death to life; here, from distance to nearness. The same Christ makes both possible.

In Christ Jesus. The exact reversal of “separated from Christ” (v. 12). The first loss is undone, and with it all the others.

Far off … brought near. Paul borrows the words of Isaiah 57:19: peace to the far and to the near. In the Old Testament, “near” described Israel, the people with access to God at his temple, and “far” described the nations. Proselytes, Gentiles who converted to Judaism, were spoken of as being “brought near”. Paul says the Gentiles have been brought near, not by becoming Jews through circumcision, but in Christ.

By the blood of Christ. “Blood” in Scripture means life violently given up in death, especially in sacrifice (Leviticus 17:11). Under the old covenant, sacrifices allowed the priest to come near to God. Christ’s death is the final sacrifice: it removes the guilt that kept us far from God (1:7; Colossians 1:20). The distance between us and God was not geography but sin, and only sacrifice could remove it.

Have been brought. Passive: someone else did it. We did not travel the distance; we were carried.

What it does not mean. Not that Gentiles now join Israel by becoming Jewish, nor that Jews remain near without Christ. The rest of the passage shows that both come near to God in exactly the same way: through Christ, by the Spirit (v. 18).

In a sentence. In Christ, those who were far from God are brought near by his sacrificial death.

For worship. Thank God that you, once far away, have been brought near: not by your effort, but by his blood.

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ is not only the one who makes peace: he is our peace. By his death he has done away with the barrier and the hostility that divided Jew from Gentile, and has made the two one.

For he himself. The Greek puts “he” in the emphatic position. Peace is not a treaty, a programme or a feeling; it is a person. Micah promised a ruler from Bethlehem of whom it would be said, he shall be their peace (Micah 5:5), and Isaiah named the Messiah the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6).

Our peace. Peace here has two dimensions, which the passage takes in turn: peace between peoples (vv. 14–15), and peace with God (v. 16). The second is the foundation of the first.

Has made us both one. Jew and Gentile, the deepest religious division of the ancient world, are now one. Jews thanked God daily that they were not Gentiles; many Gentiles despised Jews as odd and antisocial. In Christ the two are a single people.

The dividing wall of hostility. In the Jerusalem temple, a stone balustrade about one and a half metres high separated the outer Court of the Gentiles from the inner courts. Notices in Greek and Latin warned that any foreigner who went beyond it would be responsible for his own death. One of these inscriptions was found in 1871 and can be seen today in Istanbul. Paul himself was nearly lynched when he was accused of bringing a Gentile, Trophimus, an Ephesian, past it (Acts 21:28–29). The Ephesians would know the story. When Paul wrote, the wall was still standing; it fell with the temple in AD 70. But in God’s eyes it had already fallen at the cross.

Of hostility. The literal wall stood for a deeper reality: mutual hatred, contempt and suspicion. The wall in stone expressed a wall in hearts.

In his flesh. In his physical body, in his death on the cross. The wall was not torn down by education, negotiation or goodwill, but by the sacrifice of Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that ethnic, cultural or national differences disappear, as if all believers must become culturally the same. In Revelation people of every tribe and language worship together, still distinct (Revelation 7:9). What disappears is the hostility and the barrier: the idea that any group stands nearer to God, or is more worthy of his people, than another. Nor does it mean that peace among people is possible without the cross. Christ is our peace; peace without him is a truce.

In a sentence. Christ himself is our peace: by his death he has destroyed the wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile and made them one.

On a Tuesday. Racism, ethnic contempt and snobbery in the church deny what the cross has done. If Christ has torn the wall down, no Christian may rebuild it, whether by a joke, a seating pattern, or a cold welcome.
verseByVerse.note: The temple courts had a stone barrier with inscriptions forbidding Gentiles, on pain of death, to go further.

parallels.desc: he shall be their peace

verseByVerse.quote: by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul explains how Christ tore the wall down: by doing away with the law as a system of commandments and regulations that fenced Israel off from the nations. In its place he created something new: not Gentiles turned into Jews, but one new humanity in himself.

By abolishing. The word (katargeō) means to make ineffective, to put out of action. Christ did this in his death: the cross brought the old arrangement to its end.

The law of commandments expressed in ordinances. Paul piles up words for a legal system: law, commandments, ordinances (decrees, regulations). He means the Mosaic law as a whole covenant arrangement, especially the parts that marked Israel off from the nations: circumcision, food laws, sacrifices, the calendar of feasts and Sabbaths, purity rules (Colossians 2:14–17). These were God-given and good, a fence to keep Israel distinct until the Messiah came (Galatians 3:23–25). But they also made Jew and Gentile two peoples who could not eat together. Christ fulfilled what they pointed to, and so their dividing role is over.

What it does not mean. Not that God’s moral will has been abolished. Paul quotes the fifth commandment in this very letter (6:2–3), and chapters 4–5 are full of moral commands. Reformed theology distinguishes the moral law, which reflects God’s character and binds all people at all times, from the ceremonial law (sacrifices, priesthood, purity), fulfilled in Christ, and the civil law of Israel as a nation, which expired with that nation (Westminster Confession 19.3–5). Jesus came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17). What is abolished is the law as a covenant that divided and condemned, not God’s holy will. Nor does it mean that Christians become lawless: believers now keep God’s law from a new heart, by the Spirit (Romans 8:4).

That he might create in himself. Creation language again (see v. 10). Unity in the church is not a human achievement or an agreement between parties; it is God’s new creation in Christ.

One new man in place of the two. “Man” here (anthrōpos) means a humanity, a new kind of people. This is not Jews absorbing Gentiles (they need not be circumcised), nor Gentiles absorbing Jews; it is a third thing, a new humanity in Christ, in which the old division no longer defines anyone (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11). Early Christians were sometimes called a “third race”.

So making peace. Peace was made, not merely announced. It is an accomplished fact, not just a goal.

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church. Dispensationalists hold that Israel and the church are two distinct peoples with distinct promises: the church is a parenthesis, and God will resume his earthly plan for national Israel in a future millennium. Covenant theology holds that there is one people of God throughout history, the one olive tree of Romans 11, now including believing Jews and Gentiles together, and that the promises to Israel find their fulfilment in Christ and his church. Paul’s “one new man” and “one body” fit the second. Verdict: one people of God in Christ. This does not mean God has finished with the Jewish people: Paul expects many Jews to come to faith in Christ (Romans 11:25–26), and they will come into the same one body, not a separate one.

In a sentence. By his death Christ ended the law as a dividing wall and created one new people out of Jew and Gentile.

On a Tuesday. Do not add extra rules, cultural habits or preferences as conditions for belonging to the church. Christ died to remove such walls.

verseByVerse.quote: And might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The deepest peace the cross makes is not between people but between people and God. Christ reconciled Jew and Gentile together to God in one body, and in his death he put the hostility itself to death.

And might reconcile. To reconcile is to turn enemies into friends by removing the cause of the hostility. The word here (apokatallassō) is strengthened: a complete reconciliation. It is used only here and in Colossians 1:20–22.

Us both to God. Here is the logic of the whole passage. Jew and Gentile could not be at peace with each other while both were at war with God. The vertical problem lies beneath the horizontal one. Both were children of wrath (v. 3). When both are reconciled to God through the same cross, they find themselves standing side by side.

Whose hostility? Our hostility to God is real (Romans 8:7; Colossians 1:21). But Scripture also speaks of God’s just opposition to us: we were children of wrath (v. 3). Reconciliation deals with both. At the cross, God’s wrath against sin was borne by Christ as our substitute (Romans 5:9–10; 2 Corinthians 5:21), and so the cause of the enmity is removed from God’s side; and through the gospel our hearts are won, so the enmity is removed from ours.

In one body. Probably a double meaning. First, Christ’s physical body on the cross, in which he reconciled us (Colossians 1:22). Second, the church, the one body of Christ (1:23; 4:4) into which both are brought. One body died, so that one body might live.

Through the cross. Not through Christ’s teaching or example alone, but through his death. Reconciliation is costly.

Thereby killing the hostility. A striking contrast. Human hostility usually kills people. At the cross, the hostility itself was killed. Christ did not kill his enemies; he died for them, and in doing so put enmity to death.

What it does not mean. Not that the cross changed God from hating to loving: God’s love sent Christ (Romans 5:8). God himself provided the sacrifice that satisfied his own justice. Nor does it mean that everyone is automatically reconciled whether they believe or not: reconciliation is received through faith, which is why the next verse speaks of preaching (v. 17; 2 Corinthians 5:20).

In a sentence. The cross reconciles us first to God, and in doing so to one another, by putting the hostility to death.

On a Tuesday. If you cannot be at peace with a fellow believer, begin by remembering that both of you were God’s enemies, and both have been reconciled at the same cross.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having made peace at the cross, Christ came and announced it to everyone, to the Gentiles far away and the Jews nearby. Now both have the same access: through the Son, by the one Spirit, into the presence of the Father.

He came and preached peace. Christ preached peace during his ministry, but Paul probably means chiefly after the resurrection: the risen Christ preached through his apostles and his church, by his Spirit. His first words to the disciples after rising were “Peace be with you” (John 20:19–21). When the gospel is preached faithfully, Christ himself is speaking.

Peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. Isaiah again: how beautiful the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace (Isaiah 52:7), and peace, peace, to the far and to the near (Isaiah 57:19). The repeated “peace” stresses that both groups need it equally. The near (Jews) were as much in need of reconciliation as the far.

For through him. The evidence that peace has been made: we have access.

We both have access. “Access” (prosagōgē) was used of being introduced into the presence of a king, a privilege few had. Under the old covenant, Gentiles could go no further than the outer court; even Israelites could not enter the holy place; only the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place, once a year, with blood (Hebrews 9:7). Now every believer, Jew or Gentile, can come directly to God, at any time, with confidence (3:12; Hebrews 10:19–22). The torn curtain (Mark 15:38) meant the same thing as the broken wall.

In one Spirit. The same Holy Spirit lives in Jew and Gentile believers alike (1 Corinthians 12:13). There is not a Jewish route and a Gentile route to God, but one Spirit giving both the same welcome.

To the Father. The goal of access is not merely forgiveness but family: we come to God as Father (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6).

The Trinity. Through the Son, in the Spirit, to the Father. This is the shape of all Christian prayer and worship. We pray to the Father, in the name of Christ (on the ground of his work), helped by the Spirit (Romans 8:26).

What it does not mean. Not that every religion or every sincere seeker has access to God. Access is “through him”, through Christ alone (John 14:6). Nor does it mean we need no mediator: we need exactly one, and we have him (1 Timothy 2:5). No priest, saint or ritual stands between the believer and the Father.

In a sentence. Christ has announced peace to all, and now every believer, Jew or Gentile, can come freely to the Father through him, by the one Spirit.

For worship. Come to the Father now, through Christ, by the Spirit. You need no appointment.

verseByVerse.quote: So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conclusion: the Gentile believers are no longer outsiders but full citizens of God’s people and members of his own household. And they belong to a building whose foundation is the teaching of the apostles and prophets, with Christ himself as the cornerstone that sets the line of everything.

So then. Paul draws the result of verses 11–18, and reverses the losses of verse 12 one by one.

No longer strangers and aliens. Two words for outsiders. A “stranger” (xenos) is a foreigner passing through, with no rights. An “alien” (paroikos) was a resident foreigner: allowed to live in the city, but a second-class inhabitant without citizen rights. The Gentiles had been both in relation to God’s people. Now neither.

Fellow citizens with the saints. “The saints” are God’s people (see 1:1), including believing Israel of old and the Jewish believers now. Gentiles are not second-class members or guests; they have full and equal citizenship. Ephesus was a free city under Rome, and its people prized citizenship. Our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20).

Members of the household of God. A step further than citizenship. A citizen belongs to a state; a household member belongs to a family. God is not only our King but our Father (v. 18). The church is his family (1 Timothy 3:15).

Built on the foundation. Now the picture changes again: from a city and a family to a building. The foundation is laid once, at the start, and everything rests on it.

Of the apostles and prophets. The apostles were those personally commissioned by the risen Christ as his authoritative witnesses (see 1:1). The prophets here are most likely New Testament prophets, not the Old Testament prophets: the order is apostles then prophets, and Paul says in 3:5 that the mystery has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets, and in 4:11 lists them together as gifts of the ascended Christ. They are the foundation in the sense of their teaching: the revelation of Christ they received and passed on, now preserved in the New Testament.

Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone. In ancient building, the cornerstone (akrogōniaios) was the first stone laid, at the corner of the foundation. It was cut and placed with great care, because every other stone was lined up by it: it fixed the angle of the walls and the level of the whole building. Isaiah 28:16 speaks of a precious cornerstone laid in Zion, and Psalm 118:22 of the stone the builders rejected becoming the chief cornerstone; Jesus applied it to himself (Matthew 21:42; 1 Peter 2:4–7). Christ is the one by whom everything in the church is measured and held together.

What it does not mean. Not that the apostles and prophets are more important than Christ: the foundation is their witness to him, and he is the stone that determines it. Nor that new apostles and prophets with the same foundational authority continue in the church today. A foundation is laid once; the building rises on it. This is one reason the canon of Scripture is closed: the foundation is complete, and the church is built on it, not added to it. Some use “prophets” to claim ongoing revelation of the same authority as Scripture; this verse suggests the opposite.

Where Christians differ: the continuation of prophecy. Continuationists hold that the gift of prophecy continues, often as a lesser, fallible gift distinct from the foundational prophets of this verse. Cessationists hold that apostles and prophets belonged to the foundation-laying period and ceased with it, and that God now speaks through the completed Scriptures. Verdict: cessationist, held charitably. Whatever view one takes, no claimed word today may add to or stand alongside the apostolic foundation.

In a sentence. Gentile believers are full citizens and family members in God’s people, built on the apostles’ and prophets’ teaching, with Christ as the cornerstone that sets everything.

On a Tuesday. Treat the new believer, the refugee and the stranger in your church as family, because they are. And test every teaching you hear by the apostolic foundation, the Scriptures.
verseByVerse.note: A cornerstone was the first, carefully placed stone that set the line of the whole building.

parallels.desc: a precious cornerstone

verseByVerse.quote: in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is a building still under construction. In Christ, every part is being fitted together, and the whole is growing into a holy temple, the place where the Lord lives.

In whom. In Christ, the cornerstone. The building has no unity or life apart from him.

The whole structure. Every part, Jew and Gentile, every congregation, every believer.

Being joined together. A builder’s word (synarmologoumenē), used again of the body in 4:16. It describes stones cut, shaped and fitted precisely to one another so that they hold without gaps. Each believer is a stone (1 Peter 2:5), and God shapes us to fit with others. This shaping often comes through the friction of living with very different people.

Grows. A mixed picture: buildings do not normally grow, living things do. The church is a living building, growing in number as people come to Christ, and in maturity as they are built up (4:15–16).

Into a holy temple. The word Paul uses (naos) means the inner sanctuary, the place of God’s presence, not the whole temple complex. In Ephesus, the great temple of Artemis was one of the seven wonders of the world, four times the size of the Parthenon. Paul says the true temple is not made of marble but of people. And in Jerusalem, the temple whose wall had kept Gentiles out (v. 14) is replaced: Gentiles are now not only allowed in, they are part of the building itself (1 Corinthians 3:16–17; 2 Corinthians 6:16).

In the Lord. The temple is holy because the Lord is in it, and it belongs to him.

What it does not mean. Not a church building of bricks: the temple is the people. Nor a single congregation alone: Paul speaks of the whole church across the world and through history, which each local church expresses.

In a sentence. In Christ, believers are being fitted together into a living, growing temple for God.

On a Tuesday. The people you find hardest in your church are stones God is fitting next to you. Being shaped together is part of how the temple is built.

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul brings it home to his readers personally: you also, you Gentiles, are being built together with everyone else into the place where God himself lives by his Spirit.

In him you also. The emphasis falls on “you also”: you who were far off, without God (v. 12), are now part of his dwelling. The outsiders have become the house.

Are being built together. Present tense: an ongoing process. The church is not finished. Each conversion adds a stone; each act of love and teaching builds up.

Into a dwelling place for God. The great theme of the Bible is God living with his people. He walked with Adam in Eden; he filled the tabernacle with his glory (Exodus 40:34); he filled Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 8:10–11); he came in the flesh and “tabernacled” among us (John 1:14). Now he dwells in his church by his Spirit, and one day the whole new creation will be his dwelling: the dwelling place of God is with man (Revelation 21:3). The gathered church is the present stage of that story.

By the Spirit. God dwells in the church not symbolically but really, by the Holy Spirit. This completes the Trinitarian pattern of the chapter: the Father (v. 18), in Christ (vv. 13–21), by the Spirit (vv. 18, 22).

What it does not mean. Not that God is absent from individual believers: each believer’s body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19). But here the emphasis is corporate: God dwells among his people together. A Christian who stays away from the church is like a stone lying in a field instead of being built into the wall.

In a sentence. Together with all believers, you are being built into God’s home, where he lives by his Spirit.

For worship. When the church meets, God is at home. Come expecting him.

2.overview:
Chapter 2 tells the gospel twice. First as the story of every believer (vv. 1–10): we were dead in sin, ruled by the world, the devil and our own desires, and by nature under God’s wrath. “But God”, rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ, raised us and seated us with him, so that for ever he may display the riches of his grace. Salvation is entirely by grace through faith, God’s gift and not our achievement, and its fruit is a life of the good works God prepared for us.

Then as the story of two peoples (vv. 11–22). Gentiles were once outsiders, without Christ, without the covenants of promise, without hope and without God. Now, by Christ’s blood, they have been brought near. Christ himself is our peace: in his flesh he has torn down the wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile, ending the law’s regulations as a barrier, creating one new humanity and reconciling both to God in one body through the cross. Through him both have access to the Father by one Spirit. Gentile believers are no longer foreigners but fellow citizens and members of God’s household, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone, growing into a holy temple where God lives by his Spirit.

3.title: The Mystery of Christ and the Fullness of God
3.text: <sup>1</sup>For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles — <sup>2</sup>assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, <sup>3</sup>how the mystery was made known to me by revelation, as I have written briefly. <sup>4</sup>When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, <sup>5</sup>which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. <sup>6</sup>This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel. <sup>7</sup>Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. <sup>8</sup>To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, <sup>9</sup>and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things, <sup>10</sup>so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. <sup>11</sup>This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, <sup>12</sup>in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him. <sup>13</sup>So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory. <sup>14</sup>For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, <sup>15</sup>from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, <sup>16</sup>that according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being, <sup>17</sup>so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith — that you, being rooted and grounded in love, <sup>18</sup>may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, <sup>19</sup>and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. <sup>20</sup>Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us, <sup>21</sup>to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, a prisoner for the Gentiles, explains that God entrusted to him the administration of grace for them: the mystery revealed to him, which he has briefly described. In past generations it was not made known as it now has been by the Spirit to the apostles and prophets: through the gospel the Gentiles are co-heirs with Israel, members of one body and sharers in the promise in Christ. Paul became its servant by God’s gracious gift and power. Though the least of all God’s people, he was given grace to preach Christ’s boundless riches to the Gentiles and to make plain to all how this long-hidden mystery works out, so that through the church God’s manifold wisdom should now be shown to the heavenly rulers, according to his eternal purpose in Christ, in whom we approach God with freedom and confidence through faith. So they should not be discouraged by his sufferings for them, which are their glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery Hidden and Revealed

The concept of "mystery" (mysterion) in Pauline theology is not something puzzling or obscure. It is a technical term for a secret previously hidden in God that has now been disclosed in the gospel. The mystery of Christ — the inclusion of the Gentiles as co-heirs — was not absent from the Old Testament, but it was not fully clear. It was there in the Abrahamic promise ("in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed," Genesis 12:3), in the prophets (Isaiah 49:6; 60:3), in the Psalms (Psalm 87; 96:3). But the full disclosure awaited the coming of Christ and the apostolic proclamation of the gospel.

This "already hidden, now revealed" pattern is the structure of all biblical revelation. The Old Testament is full of types, shadows, and partial disclosures that only become fully visible in the light of Christ. This is why the Reformers insisted on the unity of the two Testaments — they are one revelation progressively unfolding, not two contradictory religions. And it is why reading the Old Testament through the lens of Christ is not an imposition on the text but the fulfilment of its own internal logic. The mystery of the Gentiles was always there; the church is now living in the age of its full disclosure.

Paul's description of himself as "the very least of all the saints" (v.8) has been the theme of Reformed meditation on gospel humility. The man who had been the church's most zealous persecutor, who had dragged men and women to prison and consented to their deaths, now counts himself the least worthy recipient of the grace he proclaims. This is not false modesty; it is the grammar of genuine encounter with grace. The closer you are to Christ, the more clearly you see how far you fall short — and the more marvellous it becomes that grace extends even to you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul describes his ministry as the proclamation of "the unsearchable riches of Christ" (v.8). The Greek word for "unsearchable" (anexichniastos) means literally "untraceable" — riches so vast that you cannot find their boundary, cannot trace their perimeter, cannot reach their end. To the Ephesian church, surrounded by the very traceable riches of Artemis and the mystery cults — gods who could be appeased, blessing that could be earned, secrets that could be unlocked for a price — Paul announces something of a different order entirely. The riches of Christ are boundless. They cannot be exhausted. The more you receive, the more remains to be given. No mystery religion could offer this.

Now: Paul is in prison when he writes this, and he explicitly tells the Ephesians not to lose heart because of his sufferings (v.13). The apostle who has been entrusted with the most glorious news in the universe is sitting in a Roman cell when he writes it. This is the pattern of the gospel: its glory travels in the most unlikely vessels. The imprisoned apostle, the persecuted church, the minority community that the world dismisses — these are the means through which the manifold wisdom of God is made known. When the church is most visibly weak, it is often doing its most significant cosmic work. The angels are watching — and what they see is the wisdom of God displayed in jars of clay.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begins to pray for his readers, but stops mid-sentence. He must first explain why he is in chains: he is not Rome’s prisoner by accident, but Christ’s prisoner, held because of his mission to bring the gospel to Gentiles like them.

For this reason. Because of everything in chapter 2: Gentiles have been brought near and are being built into God’s temple (2:19–22). Paul is about to pray that they will experience this reality. But he breaks off after “Gentiles” and only picks up the prayer again in verse 14 with the same words, “For this reason”. Verses 2–13 are a long digression, as if a man starting to pray suddenly thinks: they need to know why I can say this.

I, Paul. An emphatic, personal touch, used when Paul puts his own authority and story on the line (2 Corinthians 10:1; Galatians 5:2).

A prisoner of Christ Jesus. Humanly, Paul was a prisoner of Rome, under house arrest, chained to a soldier (Acts 28:16, 30). But he never calls himself Caesar’s prisoner. Christ is Lord of his circumstances: he is in prison because Christ placed him there, for Christ’s purposes (Philippians 1:12–14). The chain belongs to Christ.

On behalf of you Gentiles. This is literally true. Paul was arrested in Jerusalem when a mob accused him of bringing Gentiles into the temple, past the dividing wall (Acts 21:27–29; see 2:14). When he told the crowd that God had sent him to the Gentiles, they shouted that he should not live (Acts 22:21–22). He was imprisoned for the very truth of chapter 2. His chains are the price of their inclusion.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul is sorry for himself, or that his sufferings earn the Gentiles’ salvation. Only Christ’s sufferings save. Paul’s sufferings serve the spread of that salvation (Colossians 1:24).

In a sentence. Paul is in chains as Christ’s prisoner because he preached that Gentiles belong fully to God’s people.

On a Tuesday. Your hardest circumstances can be held, as Paul held his, under Christ’s lordship. You are not the prisoner of your situation, your illness or your employer, but a servant of Christ placed where he wants you.
verseByVerse.note: Paul was imprisoned because of his mission to the Gentiles; he breaks off here and resumes in verse 14.

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God's grace that was given to me for you, how the mystery was made known to me by revelation,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul explains his role: God entrusted him with a special responsibility, to manage and distribute God’s grace to the Gentiles, and for that purpose God revealed to him a secret that had been hidden, the “mystery”.

Assuming that you have heard. Or “surely you have heard”. A polite expression, not real doubt. Some readers of this circular letter (see 1:1) had not met Paul personally, but they would have heard of his calling.

The stewardship of God’s grace. “Stewardship” is oikonomia, from oikos (house) and nomos (law, management): the management of a household. A steward was often a trusted slave who ran a wealthy man’s estate, handling his goods for others (Luke 12:42). Paul is the steward of grace, not its owner (1 Corinthians 4:1–2). Grace is not his to keep or to change; he is entrusted with it to give it out.

That was given to me for you. The grace in view is the grace of his commission: his calling to be the apostle to the Gentiles (v. 8; Romans 15:15–16). It was given to him “for you”: not for his honour, but for their benefit.

The mystery. In everyday English a mystery is a puzzle that cannot be solved. In Paul it means almost the opposite: a secret of God, hidden until God chose to reveal it, which is now openly made known (Romans 16:25–26; Colossians 1:26). In the pagan “mystery religions” of the time, secrets were whispered only to initiates. Paul’s mystery is proclaimed to everyone.

Made known to me by revelation. Paul did not work this out by study, nor learn it from other apostles. The risen Christ revealed it to him (Galatians 1:11–12, 15–16), beginning on the Damascus road, where he was told that he was sent to the Gentiles (Acts 26:16–18).

What it does not mean. Not that the gospel is secret knowledge for a spiritual elite. That was the claim of later Gnostics. The Christian mystery is public, preached, and open to all.

In a sentence. God entrusted Paul with the grace of his calling to the Gentiles, and revealed to him the secret plan he now proclaims.

On a Tuesday. Whatever gifts and knowledge God has given you, you are their steward, not their owner. They are given to you for others.
verseByVerse.note: A stewardship is a trust given to a household manager.

verseByVerse.quote: as I have written briefly. When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has already written about this mystery briefly in chapters 1 and 2, and he says that when they read what he wrote, they will be able to see for themselves that he truly understands Christ’s mystery.

As I have written briefly. Paul refers back to this very letter, especially 1:9–10 (God’s plan to unite all things in Christ) and 2:11–22 (Jew and Gentile one in Christ). Not to an earlier, lost letter.

When you read this. Letters in the early church were read aloud in the congregation (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27). Paul expects his words to be read publicly and repeatedly.

You can perceive my insight. “Insight” (synesis) means understanding, the ability to put things together. Paul is not boasting. He is pointing out that the authority of his message can be tested by reading it: it hangs together, and it unlocks the Old Testament promises.

The mystery of Christ. The secret whose content is Christ: what God has done in him, including the joining of Jew and Gentile in one body (v. 6).

What it does not mean. Not that we need special visions or secret experiences to understand God’s purposes. What Paul received by revelation we receive by reading. The written word is how apostolic insight reaches us.

In a sentence. Paul’s understanding of the mystery is open to anyone who reads what he wrote.

On a Tuesday. If you want to understand God’s plan, read the letters he gave. Read Ephesians through in one sitting this week.

verseByVerse.quote: The mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This secret plan was not made known to earlier generations in the way it has now been revealed, by the Spirit, to Christ’s apostles and prophets.

Not made known to the sons of men in other generations. “Sons of men” simply means human beings. Before Christ, people did not grasp this mystery.

As it has now been revealed. The word “as” matters. Paul does not say the mystery was completely unknown, but not known as it is now. The Old Testament did promise blessing to the nations: in Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3), and the Servant would be a light for the nations (Isaiah 49:6; see also Isaiah 2:2–4; Amos 9:11–12). What was not clear was how: that Gentiles would be included not by becoming Jews, through circumcision and the law, but directly in Christ, as full and equal members of one new body. That was the surprise.

To his holy apostles and prophets. “Holy” means set apart by God for this task, not personally sinless. The apostles and prophets are the foundation of the church (2:20); this is why. They received the revelation of the mystery and passed it on. Again, prophets here are New Testament prophets, listed after the apostles (see 2:20; 4:11).

By the Spirit. The Holy Spirit is the revealer (1 Corinthians 2:10–13; John 16:13). The New Testament is the Spirit’s work through these men.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is irrelevant or contradicted. The New Testament reveals what the Old Testament promised in shadow. Christ is the key that opens the Old Testament (Luke 24:27, 44–47).

Where Christians differ: was the church entirely hidden? Classic dispensationalists teach that the church was completely unknown in the Old Testament, a “parenthesis” inserted into God’s programme for Israel, which will resume after the church is removed. Covenant theology holds that the church fulfils God’s promises to Abraham and the prophets, now revealed far more clearly. Paul’s word “as” (not known as it is now) implies that something was known before, and elsewhere he shows that the Gentiles’ inclusion fulfils the promise to Abraham (Galatians 3:8, 29) and the prophets (Romans 15:8–12). Verdict: the church is the fulfilment of God’s one plan, partially foreseen and now fully revealed.

In a sentence. What earlier generations only glimpsed, God has now made plain through his apostles and prophets by the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Read the Old Testament as Christians: look for the promises to the nations, and see how they come true in your own church.

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the mystery itself, stated plainly: through the gospel, Gentiles share fully and equally with Jewish believers in God’s inheritance, his body and his promise, in Christ Jesus.

This mystery is. Literally “that the Gentiles are”. Paul now defines what he has been talking about.

Three “fellow” words. Paul uses three Greek compounds beginning with syn (“with, together”), one of which he probably coins:

1. Fellow heirs. Synklēronoma: co-heirs. Gentiles inherit everything God promised Abraham and his descendants (1:11, 14, 18; Galatians 3:29). In the ancient world, an heir received the whole estate of the father. Gentile believers are not tenants or guests on Israel’s estate; they inherit it equally.

2. Members of the same body. Syssōma: co-bodied, a word not found before Paul. Not two bodies, one Jewish and one Gentile, side by side, but one body with one head, Christ (2:16; 4:4).

3. Partakers of the promise. Symmetocha: co-sharers. “The promise” is God’s great promise to Abraham and his offspring, summed up in the gift of the Holy Spirit (1:13; Galatians 3:14) and in God’s pledge to be their God.

In Christ Jesus. Everything they share is in union with him. He is the true offspring of Abraham (Galatians 3:16), and all who are in him share his inheritance.

Through the gospel. The means of inclusion is the good news believed, not ancestry, circumcision or law-keeping. This is why Paul fought so hard against those who wanted Gentiles circumcised (Galatians 2:3–5; 5:2–6).

What it does not mean. Not that Gentiles replace Jews, or that Jewish believers lose anything. It is “fellow” heirs: sharing, not taking over. Nor that ethnic identity is erased (see 2:14). The point is equal standing before God and equal belonging in his family.

In a sentence. The secret now revealed is that Gentiles, through the gospel, are equal heirs, equal members and equal sharers with Israel in Christ.

For worship. If you are a Gentile believer, you are an heir of the promises made to Abraham. Give thanks for an inheritance you were never born into.

verseByVerse.quote: Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul did not earn his role. God made him a servant of this gospel as a sheer gift, by his power, and gave him, the least deserving of all believers, the privilege of preaching to the nations the endless riches of Christ.

Of this gospel I was made a minister. “Minister” is diakonos, servant, the word from which “deacon” comes. It was used of a waiter at table. Paul’s highest title is servant. “I was made”: God appointed him; he did not apply.

According to the gift of God’s grace. His ministry is a gift, not a reward.

By the working of his power. The same language as 1:19–20: the power that raised Christ from the dead. It took resurrection power to turn Saul the persecutor into Paul the apostle (Acts 9:1–22), and it takes the same power to sustain his ministry (Colossians 1:29).

Though I am the very least of all the saints. Paul invents a word: he takes the Greek for “least” and adds a comparative ending, “leaster”, “less than the least”. He is not being falsely modest. He never forgot that he had persecuted the church (1 Corinthians 15:9; 1 Timothy 1:13–15). Notice the progression in his letters: least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9, about AD 55), least of all the saints (here, about AD 61), foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15, about AD 63). The older he grew in grace, the lower he saw himself.

This grace was given. Again grace. Paul cannot speak of his ministry without speaking of grace (1 Corinthians 15:10).

To preach to the Gentiles. To announce, as a herald announces good news.

The unsearchable riches of Christ. “Unsearchable” (anexichniaston) means literally “untrackable”, without footprints: like a land so vast that no explorer could ever trace all its paths to the end (Romans 11:33). Christ’s riches include forgiveness, adoption, wisdom, the Spirit, hope and an inheritance (chapter 1). However long a believer explores them, there is always more.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul’s sense of unworthiness made him timid. The man who called himself the least of the saints also wrote with full apostolic authority. Humility is not hesitancy; it is knowing that everything is grace.

In a sentence. By God’s grace and power, Paul, the least of the saints, was made a servant to preach Christ’s endless riches to the nations.

On a Tuesday. God uses people who know they are unworthy. Your past does not disqualify you from serving him; pride does. And never think you have exhausted Christ: there is more to find in him this week.

verseByVerse.quote: and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s task is not only to preach to the Gentiles but to make plain to everyone how God’s secret plan works: a plan hidden through all the ages in the mind of God, the Creator of all things.

To bring to light. To illuminate, to shine a light on what was in darkness. The gospel does not create the plan; it reveals it.

For everyone. Not only Gentiles, but all people. God’s plan is public.

The plan of the mystery. “Plan” is oikonomia again (see v. 2; 1:10): the arrangement, administration or working out of God’s secret purpose. Paul shows how the plan works in history.

Hidden for ages in God. The plan was not absent; it was in God, kept in his mind from eternity (1:4, 9–11). It was hidden from people, not from God. History unfolds what God had always intended.

Who created all things. Why mention creation here? Because the God who saves is the God who made everything. Redemption is not a repair job on a project that went wrong, but the Creator carrying through his original purpose: to unite all things in Christ (1:10). The new creation (2:10, 15) is the goal of the first.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “fellowship” (koinōnia) instead of “plan” (oikonomia), and add “by Jesus Christ” after “created all things”. Verdict: “plan” is original, supported by the earliest manuscripts, and “by Jesus Christ” is a later expansion. The truth it adds is biblical (Colossians 1:16), but it is not part of this verse.

In a sentence. Paul’s task is to show everyone the plan God hid in himself from the beginning and has now carried out in Christ.

On a Tuesday. History is not random. The God who made the world is working out his plan in it, and your small part in his church belongs to that plan.

verseByVerse.quote: so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the astonishing purpose of the church: through a united people of Jews and Gentiles, God is now putting his rich and many-sided wisdom on display before the angels and the spiritual powers of the unseen world.

So that. The purpose of Paul’s preaching (vv. 8–9), and of the mystery itself.

Through the church. Not through the stars, or through great events of world history, but through the church: ordinary people gathered in Christ. The Greek word ekklēsia means assembly, the gathered people of God. The church is God’s showcase, his visual aid to the universe.

The manifold wisdom of God. “Manifold” (polypoikilos) means many-coloured or richly varied, like an embroidered cloth or a meadow of flowers. God’s wisdom is seen in the variety of the people he gathers: Jew and Gentile, slave and free, rich and poor, every culture, joined in one body without losing their variety. Only God could make such different people one. A church of people who are all alike shows less of this wisdom.

Might now be made known. “Now”, in this age, before the end. The display is already happening.

To the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. Spiritual beings, angelic and demonic (1:21; 6:12; Colossians 2:15). Good angels watch with wonder: these are things into which angels long to look (1 Peter 1:12). Evil powers watch their defeat: the division and hostility they fostered (2:2) is undone. The church is a theatre, with heaven as the audience.

What it does not mean. Not that the church preaches to angels, or that we should try to address or command spiritual powers. The church makes God’s wisdom known simply by being what it is: a reconciled people. Nor does “wisdom” mean cleverness. God’s wisdom is his skill in achieving his good purposes, above all through the cross, which looks like foolishness to the world (1 Corinthians 1:18–25).

In a sentence. God displays his richly varied wisdom to the spiritual powers through the church, a people of every kind made one in Christ.

On a Tuesday. Your church’s unity across race, class, age and culture is a sermon preached to heaven. Guard it, and widen it. Every quarrel in the church hides that display; every reconciliation shows it.

verseByVerse.quote: This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this was God’s purpose from eternity, now fully achieved in Christ. And because of Christ, believers can now come to God freely and confidently, through faith in him.

The eternal purpose. Literally “the purpose of the ages”. The church is not an afterthought or plan B. God planned it before time (1:4, 11).

That he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord. “Realized” means carried out, accomplished, in Christ’s life, death, resurrection and ascension. The plan is not only foreseen; it has been done.

In whom we have boldness. “Boldness” (parrēsia) originally meant the freedom of speech of a citizen in the assembly, the right to speak openly without fear. Before God, it means freedom to speak to him frankly, without terror.

And access. Prosagōgē, the right of entry into the king’s presence (see 2:18).

With confidence. Assurance that we will be welcomed, not turned away. Those who were far off and without God (2:12–13) can now come into his presence boldly (Hebrews 4:16; 10:19–22).

Through our faith in him. The way to this confidence is faith: trusting Christ, not our performance. Our confidence is not self-confidence but Christ-confidence.

Textual and translation note. The phrase can be translated “through his faithfulness” (Christ’s own faithfulness), and some scholars argue for that. Verdict: the usual translation, faith in him, best fits Paul’s usage in Ephesians, where faith is the believer’s trust in Christ (1:15; 2:8). Either way, our confidence rests on Christ.

What it does not mean. Not casualness or presumption before God. Boldness is not irreverence. We come with reverence and awe (Hebrews 12:28), but without fear of rejection, as children come to a father.

In a sentence. God’s eternal plan is fulfilled in Christ, and in him we can come to God boldly and confidently through faith.

For worship. Approach God today with confidence, not timidity: not because you have had a good week, but because Christ is your access.

verseByVerse.quote: So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because his ministry is part of God’s eternal plan, Paul asks his readers not to be discouraged by his imprisonment. His suffering is for their benefit; it is a mark of their honour, not a sign of failure.

So I ask you. The digression of verses 2–13 ends where it began: with Paul’s chains (v. 1).

Not to lose heart. To become discouraged, to give up. The readers might have reasoned: if the apostle of this gospel is in prison, perhaps the gospel is failing. Paul says the opposite.

Over what I am suffering for you. Paul is in prison because he took the gospel to the Gentiles (see v. 1).

Which is your glory. His sufferings show how much their salvation is worth. If an apostle thinks it worth chains to bring Gentiles the gospel, they must be precious in God’s sight. And his suffering serves their eventual glory: it advances the gospel through which they will share Christ’s glory (2 Timothy 2:10; Philippians 1:12–14).

What it does not mean. Not that Paul’s sufferings add anything to Christ’s atoning work. Christ’s suffering alone saves. Paul suffers to bring that salvation to others.

In a sentence. Paul’s chains are no reason for despair, because his suffering serves the glory of those he preaches to.

On a Tuesday. Do not be discouraged when faithful Christian leaders or missionaries suffer. God often advances the gospel through the suffering of its messengers. Pray for them, and do not lose heart.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul kneels before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named. He asks that, out of his glorious riches, God will strengthen them with power in their inner being through his Spirit, so that Christ may make his home in their hearts through faith. Rooted and established in love, may they have power with all God’s people to grasp how wide, long, high and deep Christ’s love is, and to know this love that surpasses knowledge, so that they may be filled with all the fullness of God. To him who can do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine, by the power at work in us, be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus through all generations for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Indwelling Christ and the Fullness of God

The prayer of Ephesians 3:14–21 reveals the goal of the Christian life with startling clarity: not moral improvement, not doctrinal accuracy, not even evangelistic fruitfulness — but the fullness of God. "Filled with all the fullness of God" (v.19) is a goal so vast it cannot be reached in a lifetime, which is precisely the point. The Christian life is not a project with a completion date; it is a journey into an infinity that perpetually exceeds the traveller. Paul set no limit to his desires for the Ephesians — he asked for the infinite, because the infinite is what God offers.

The means of this fullness is the indwelling of Christ. "That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (v.17) — the verb "dwell" (katoikein) means to settle, to take up permanent residence, as opposed to merely passing through. This is not the occasional visitation of religious experience; it is the abiding presence of the living Christ in the interior life of the believer. The Reformers consistently emphasized that union with Christ — not merely forgiveness, not merely a changed record before God, but genuine, living union with the risen Lord — is the foundation of the entire Christian life. It is from this union that everything else flows: assurance, holiness, prayer, service, suffering, joy.

The doxology of vv.20–21 is also a theology of prayer. It teaches us that God is not limited by the smallness of our asking. The greatness of our petitions cannot exhaust his capacity to answer; the boldness of our faith cannot outrun his willingness to give. The God to whom we pray is the God who can do more than we can imagine asking — and the power by which he does it is "at work within us." It is the same resurrection power of Ephesians 1:19–20. Our prayers are small; his answers are not required to match them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The mystery religions of Ephesus promised spiritual fullness — union with the divine, access to hidden power — through initiation, through ritual, through the gradual ascent of the initiated. The costs were significant: financial, social, sometimes physical. And the fullness promised was always partial, always provisional, always requiring the next level of initiation. Paul prays for his readers to receive a fullness that no mystery religion could offer and no initiation could achieve: the fullness of God himself, freely given, received through faith, sustained by the Spirit. The contrast with what Ephesus was selling could not have been more pointed.

Now: "Far more abundantly than all that we ask or think" — this phrase has stood as one of the great encouragements of Christian prayer across the centuries. When we pray small, God answers large. When we cannot find words, the Spirit intercedes. When the situation seems beyond recovery, we serve the God who raises the dead. The doxology of Ephesians 3 is not merely a liturgical flourish; it is a declaration of the character of the God to whom we pray. He exceeds our prayers not because he is indifferent to them but because he is inexhaustibly generous. Every time this doxology is spoken in corporate worship, the church is reminding itself — and the watching powers — of who their God is.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now resumes the prayer he began in verse 1. He kneels before God the Father, the one from whom every family in heaven and on earth receives its existence and its name.

For this reason. The same words as verse 1, picking up the thought again. The reason is the whole of chapter 2 (and the explanation in 3:2–13): Gentiles are now part of God’s family and temple. Paul prays that they will experience the reality.

I bow my knees. Jews normally stood to pray (Mark 11:25; Luke 18:11, 13). Kneeling expressed special earnestness, humility or urgency (Luke 22:41; Acts 7:60; 20:36). Paul, chained, kneels. His posture shows the intensity of what he is about to ask.

Before the Father. Prayer is addressed to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit (2:18). Paul prays as a child to his Father, which is exactly the access he has just described (v. 12).

From whom every family in heaven and on earth is named. A wordplay in Greek: Father is patēr, family is patria (a family group descended from one father, a clan). Every family derives its existence from God, the original Father. “Is named”: in the Bible, to name something is to give it its existence and identity (Genesis 2:19–20), and to have authority over it. God is not called “Father” because human fathers exist; human fathers exist as faint copies of God’s fatherhood.

In heaven and on earth. Including families of angels as well as human families. Everything that exists in groups owes its being to the Father. Since Jew and Gentile are now one family (2:19), Paul prays to the Father of them all.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “of our Lord Jesus Christ” after “the Father”. Verdict: not original. The shorter reading is found in the earliest manuscripts and makes the wordplay with “family” clearer.

What it does not mean. Not that every human being is a child of God in the saving sense. All are God’s creatures and owe him their being (Acts 17:28), but adoption is through Christ (1:5; John 1:12). And kneeling is not required for prayer: posture is a help, not a law.

In a sentence. Paul kneels in earnest prayer to the Father from whom every family receives its being.

On a Tuesday. If your own father failed you, do not shape your picture of God by him. God is the original Father, of whom even the best earthly fathers are only shadows.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “family” renders patria, a word closely related to “father” (pater) in verse 14.

verseByVerse.quote: That according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s first request: that out of the limitless wealth of his glory, the Father would give them inner strength, power from the Holy Spirit working deep within them.

The shape of the prayer. Verses 16–19 are one sentence with a chain of requests, each leading to the next, like steps on a staircase: strengthened by the Spirit (v. 16), so that Christ dwells in your hearts (v. 17), so that you may grasp the dimensions of his love (v. 18), so that you know that love (v. 19), so that you may be filled with all the fullness of God (v. 19).

According to the riches of his glory. “According to” is important: not out of his riches, which could mean a small gift from a large fortune, but in proportion to his riches. A millionaire who gives a coin gives out of his riches; one who gives in proportion to his wealth gives generously. God gives in proportion to his glory: without limit. “Glory” here means the wealth of his whole character and power.

He may grant you. Paul asks for a gift. Inner strength is not achieved by self-effort; it is given.

To be strengthened with power. Two words for strength, piled up: made strong with might. Paul has already prayed that they would know God’s power (1:19); now he prays that they would be strengthened by it.

Through his Spirit. The Holy Spirit is the agent who applies God’s power in us (Romans 8:11; Galatians 5:22–23).

In your inner being. Literally “the inner man”: the inward self, the heart, the person as God sees them, as opposed to their outward body and circumstances. In believers, the inner being is renewed day by day even while the outward body wastes away (2 Corinthians 4:16; Romans 7:22).

What it does not mean. Not a prayer for outward strength, health or success, good as those things are to pray for. Paul, in prison, prays for strength within, which can be strong when the body is weak. Nor is it a prayer for spectacular experiences: the strength in view is the strength to know and love Christ, as the following verses show.
