In a sentence. Paul asks the Father to strengthen believers inwardly by his Spirit, giving out of the full measure of his glory.

On a Tuesday. Pray for inner strength, not only for changed circumstances. When you pray for a friend in trouble, pray for this too: that the Spirit would make them strong inside.

verseByVerse.quote: So that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, that you, being rooted and grounded in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The purpose of inner strength is that Christ himself would settle down and be fully at home in their hearts, through faith, so that their whole life would grow from and rest on love.

So that Christ may dwell. The word is katoikeō: not to visit or lodge, but to settle down and make one’s permanent home. Christ already lives in every believer (Romans 8:9–10). Paul prays that he would be more fully at home: welcomed in every room, not confined to one corner. The Puritans used the picture of a house: Christ enters at conversion, but we must open every room to him.

In your hearts. In the Bible the “heart” is not only the emotions but the centre of the person: thought, will, desire and feeling together (see 1:18). Christ’s dwelling there means he rules and shapes everything we are.

Through faith. Christ dwells in us as we trust him. Faith is the open door.

That you, being rooted and grounded in love. Two pictures. “Rooted” is from gardening: a tree whose roots go deep into good soil, drawing life from it (Colossians 2:7; Psalm 1:3). “Grounded” is from building: a house laid on a solid foundation (Matthew 7:24–25). Love is both the soil from which we grow and the foundation on which we stand. Here it is above all Christ’s love for us (vv. 18–19), which then produces our love for him and others. Grammatically the phrase leads into the next request (v. 18): those rooted in love are able to grasp love.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ enters and leaves believers depending on their mood or behaviour. His indwelling is permanent (John 14:23). Paul is praying for a deeper experience of it, not its beginning. Nor is “love” here a vague feeling: it is the self-giving love shown at the cross (5:2, 25).

In a sentence. Paul prays that Christ would be fully at home in their hearts through faith, and that their life would be rooted and founded in love.

On a Tuesday. Ask: is there a room of my life where Christ is not welcome? My money, my screen, my grudges, my ambitions? Open the door.

verseByVerse.quote: may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that, together with all of God’s people, they would have the strength to take in how vast the love of Christ is: wide, long, high and deep beyond all measuring.

May have strength to comprehend. “Comprehend” means to grasp, to seize hold of. It needs strength: our minds are too small and our hearts too cold to take in Christ’s love unless God strengthens us (v. 16).

With all the saints. We grasp the love of Christ together, not alone. No individual Christian sees all of it. The old saint who has suffered, the new believer full of joy, the church in another culture: each sees aspects of Christ’s love the others need. Private spirituality alone will always grasp less.

What is the breadth and length and height and depth. Paul does not say of what, but verse 19 makes clear he means the love of Christ. The four dimensions are not separate measurements to be analysed, but a way of saying: in every direction you look, it goes beyond you. Many interpreters have drawn applications from them, and they are helpful if held lightly:

Breadth. Wide enough to embrace Jew and Gentile and people of every nation (chapter 2).

Length. Long enough to stretch from eternity past, before the foundation of the world (1:4), to the ages to come (2:7).

Height. High enough to lift us to the heavenly places with Christ (2:6).

Depth. Deep enough to reach us when we were dead in sin (2:1), and to go down into death itself at the cross.

Background. Job 11:7–9 asks whether anyone can find out the deep things of God, which are higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol, longer than the earth and broader than the sea. Psalm 103:11 says that as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his steadfast love. Paul says that in Christ, this immeasurable love is now known.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ’s love is something we can finally measure and map. The point is the opposite. Nor is this a purely intellectual exercise: “comprehend” includes the heart. It is possible to describe the love of Christ accurately and not be moved by it at all.

In a sentence. Paul prays that all believers together would be strengthened to grasp the immeasurable size of Christ’s love.

On a Tuesday. Talk with another believer this week about how Christ’s love has met you. You will grasp it better together than alone.

parallels.desc: higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol

verseByVerse.quote: and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that they would truly know Christ’s love, a love so great that it goes beyond what anyone can fully know, and that knowing it, they would be filled up to all the fullness of God.

To know the love of Christ. “Know” (gnōnai) in the Bible means more than knowing about. It is personal, experiential knowledge, as one knows a friend (John 17:3). Paul prays not that they would learn facts about Christ’s love, which they already knew, but that they would experience it more deeply.

That surpasses knowledge. A deliberate paradox: to know what is beyond knowing. We can know Christ’s love truly but never fully. A child can truly know the sea by wading in it, though it will never cross the ocean. There is always more. Perhaps Paul also has in view the claims of false teachers who prized “knowledge” (gnōsis): love surpasses that kind of knowledge (1 Corinthians 8:1).

That you may be filled. The goal of the whole prayer.

With all the fullness of God. Literally “filled up to all the fullness of God”. “Fullness” (plērōma) is a key word in Ephesians and Colossians. In Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9), and the church is his fullness (1:23). Paul prays that believers would be filled with everything God is and gives: his life, love, holiness and presence, as fully as creatures can be filled. The aim is maturity, to be like Christ (4:13).

What it does not mean. Not that believers become God or lose their creaturely nature. The Creator–creature distinction is never erased. A cup filled from the ocean is full of the ocean, but it is still a cup. Some traditions speak of deification (theōsis); Reformed theology speaks rather of union with Christ and being conformed to his image (Romans 8:29). Nor is this filling a once-for-all experience that leaves nothing more to receive. It is a growing filling that continues throughout life and into eternity.

In a sentence. Paul prays that believers would know by experience Christ’s infinite love, and be filled with all that God is and gives.

For worship. Ask God to show you more of Christ’s love today, and to fill whatever in you is still empty.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having asked so much, Paul breaks into praise. God is able to do immeasurably more than everything we ask him for, or even imagine, and he does it by the very power already at work inside us.

Now to him who is able. A doxology, a short hymn of praise. Paul’s prayer has asked for staggering things (vv. 16–19). Now he says: God is able to do even more.

To do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think. Paul piles up words, using a doubled superlative (hyperekperissou): “super-abundantly beyond”. The thought climbs in steps: God is able to do what we ask; more than we ask; more than we can imagine; far more abundantly than all we can imagine. Our requests are limited by our words, our imagination by our minds; God is limited by neither.

According to the power at work within us. The power is not distant; it is already working in believers. It is the same power that raised Christ from the dead (1:19–20) and raised us with him (2:5–6). The God who did that can do anything he purposes.

What it does not mean. Not a promise that God will give us whatever we imagine, or that big prayers guarantee big blessings in the sense of health, wealth or success. Paul is still in prison. The context is the request of verses 16–19: being strengthened, knowing Christ’s love, being filled with God. God’s “more” is more of these things, and more of his good purposes for us than we could ever plan (Romans 8:28–32). Sometimes the “more” arrives as a “no” to what we asked, because God has something better.

In a sentence. God can do far more than anything we can ask or imagine, by the resurrection power already at work in us.

On a Tuesday. Pray bigger prayers for your spiritual life, your church and your unbelieving friends. And trust God when he answers differently from what you asked.

verseByVerse.quote: to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All glory belongs to God, and it is to be displayed in the church and in Christ Jesus, through every generation, for ever and ever.

To him be glory. “Glory” means the shining out of who God is: his weight, splendour and worth made visible. To give God glory is to recognise and declare it. This is the goal of everything in chapters 1–3 (1:6, 12, 14).

In the church and in Christ Jesus. A surprising pairing: the church appears alongside Christ. God is glorified in Christ, the head, and in the church, his body (1:22–23). The church shows God’s glory as it reflects Christ: a reconciled people of every nation, built into his temple. The church is not glorious in itself, but as the place where Christ’s glory shines.

Throughout all generations, forever and ever. Literally “to all the generations of the age of the ages”. Empires rise and fall; the church goes on, and the praise of God in it will never end.

Amen. A Hebrew word meaning “firm, true, so be it”. It was the people’s response in worship, saying yes to what was said (1 Corinthians 14:16; Nehemiah 8:6). Paul invites the readers to say it with him.

The turning point. This doxology ends the first half of the letter. Chapters 1–3 describe what God has done (doctrine); chapters 4–6 describe how we should live (duty). Between them stands praise. Right doctrine leads to worship, and worship leads to right living.

What it does not mean. Not that the church adds to God’s glory, as if he needed it. God’s glory is complete in himself. The church displays it, as a mirror displays the sun.

In a sentence. God deserves glory in Christ and in his church for ever.

For worship. Say the Amen aloud, and mean it.

3.overview:
Paul begins to pray (v. 1), then breaks off to explain his own role in God’s plan (vv. 2–13). God gave him, a prisoner for the Gentiles’ sake, a stewardship of grace: the revelation of the mystery of Christ, hidden in earlier generations and now revealed by the Spirit to the apostles and prophets. The mystery is that Gentiles are fellow heirs with Israel, members of the same body and sharers in the promise through the gospel. Paul, the least of all the saints, was given the task of preaching Christ’s unsearchable riches to the nations, so that through the church God’s many-sided wisdom might be displayed to the powers in the heavenly places. His sufferings are for their glory, so they must not lose heart.

Then he resumes his prayer (vv. 14–21), kneeling before the Father from whom every family takes its name. He asks that they be strengthened by the Spirit in the inner person, that Christ may dwell in their hearts by faith, and that, rooted in love, they may grasp the immeasurable dimensions of Christ’s love that surpasses knowledge, and be filled with all the fullness of God. The chapter ends in a doxology to the God who can do far more than we ask or imagine, to whom be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus for ever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Walk Worthy: The Unity of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As a prisoner for the Lord, Paul urges them to live worthy of their calling: completely humble and gentle, patient, bearing with one another in love, and working hard to keep the unity the Spirit gives through the bond of peace. There is one body and one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father of all, over all, through all and in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Unity of the Church as Theological Reality

The passage reveals that the unity of the church is not an aspiration or a programme — it is an ontological reality that precedes and grounds every effort to express it. The Spirit has already created one body. The question is not whether unity exists but whether our behaviour honours the unity that does. This distinction between the given reality and the required response is characteristic of Paul's ethical method throughout the letter: indicative first, imperative second. Be what you are. Express what is already true.

The four virtues through which unity is maintained — humility, gentleness, patience, forbearance — are a portrait of Christlike character applied to community life. They are not soft virtues; they are demanding ones. Humility means thinking of others' interests above your own (Philippians 2:3). Gentleness (prautēs) belongs to the word Jesus used of himself (“I am gentle and lowly in heart,” Matthew 11:29) — strength in service of love. Patience is the willingness to absorb rather than retaliate. Forbearance is the daily choice to keep choosing the person in front of you rather than withdrawing when they disappoint. Together these virtues create the environment in which the given unity of the Spirit can be made visible.

The Reformers consistently emphasised that doctrinal unity and relational unity are inseparable. The sevenfold “one” of vv.4–6 grounds the relational unity of vv.2–3 in doctrinal reality. We are not called to unity by ignoring our differences or pretending that doctrine doesn't matter. We are called to unity because there is genuinely one Lord, one faith, one baptism — and the body that confesses these things is, by that very confession, one. Preserving this unity is not sentimentality; it is theological faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church was the most socially diverse community in the city. Former Artemis worshippers, Jewish converts, Greek philosophers, slaves and freedmen, wealthy merchants and harbour workers — all brought together by the preaching of the gospel. The centrifugal forces were enormous. Every human instinct would have been to fracture along existing social fault lines. Paul's “therefore” connects the unity he calls for directly to the cosmic reality of chapter 2: the wall has already come down. The body is already one. Now: walk like it. Bear with one another. Choose the humility that makes room for people unlike you. This was not a small ask in first-century Ephesus.

Now: The church in our age is under intense pressure to fragment — along political lines, cultural lines, worship-style lines, theological nuance lines. The market logic of contemporary Christianity encourages us to shop for churches that suit our preferences, reinforcing the very homogeneity that Paul's vision challenges. Against this, Ephesians 4:1–6 calls the church to a costly unity rooted not in shared preference but in shared confession: one Lord, one faith, one baptism. The local church that perseveres through its internal differences — that chooses patient, humble, forbearing love over the easier path of fragmentation — is doing something more theologically significant than it knows. It is bearing witness to the one God who is over all and through all and in all.

verseByVerse.quote: I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now that Paul has shown what God has done, he urges his readers to live in a way that matches it: a life that fits the high calling God has given them.

Therefore. The hinge of the whole letter. Chapters 1–3 are almost all about what God has done: chosen, adopted, redeemed, raised, reconciled, built. There is only one command in them (2:11, “remember”). Chapters 4–6 are full of commands: about forty. The order matters. Paul does not say, “Live like this, and God will accept you.” He says, “God has accepted you; therefore live like this.” Christian ethics flows out of grace, never the other way round. Theologians call this the move from indicative (what is true) to imperative (what to do).

I … a prisoner for the Lord. Literally “in the Lord”. Paul repeats 3:1. He is not using his chains to win sympathy, but to show that he is asking nothing he has not paid for himself. The calling costs, and he has paid in chains.

Urge. Parakaleō: to call alongside, to appeal, to encourage. Not a cold order, but a pastor’s earnest plea. The same word is used for comfort.

To walk. Paul’s word for a whole way of life (see 2:2, 10). It appears five times in chapters 4–5 and organises them: walk worthy (4:1), not as the Gentiles walk (4:17), walk in love (5:2), walk as children of light (5:8), walk wisely (5:15). Walking is steady, daily, step by step: not occasional bursts of spiritual excitement.

In a manner worthy. “Worthy” (axiōs) originally meant “of equal weight”: as when one side of a scale balances the other. Our conduct should balance our calling. If a king’s son lives like a criminal, his life does not match his name. Not worthy in order to earn the calling, but worthy in the sense of fitting it.

Of the calling to which you have been called. In Paul, God’s “calling” is not a general invitation but his effective summons, by which he brings a person to Christ (1:18; Romans 8:30; 2 Timothy 1:9). We were called to be holy and blameless (1:4), to be his children (1:5), to be one body (4:4). The calling is not a job or career (though those matter), but the call to belong to Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that our conduct makes us worthy of being called, or that God calls those who are worthy. He calls the dead (2:1–5). Nor is it a life of grim effort under a heavy load: the same God who called also equips (4:7, 11–12) and works in us (3:20).

In a sentence. Because God has done all this for you in Christ, live a life that matches the calling he has given you.

On a Tuesday. Before the day starts, remember who God has called you to be. Then ask, at each decision: does this fit the name I bear?
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 1–3 set out what God has done; chapters 4–6 show the life that follows.

verseByVerse.quote: With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first marks of a life worthy of God’s calling are not great achievements, but humility, gentleness and patient love: the virtues that make it possible for very different people to live together as one church.

Why these come first. Paul is about to speak of the unity of the church (v. 3). The thing that most often destroys unity is not doctrine but pride. Humility, gentleness and patience are the virtues that hold people together.

With all humility. Tapeinophrosynē: lowliness of mind. In the Greek world it was not a virtue but a fault, the cringing attitude of a slave. Christ made it a virtue. He humbled himself, taking the form of a servant, to the point of death (Philippians 2:3–8). Humility is not thinking badly of yourself; it is thinking of yourself less, and seeing yourself truly before God: a sinner saved by grace (3:8). It counts others more significant than yourself.

And gentleness. Prautēs, often translated “meekness”. It was used of a horse that had been tamed: strong, but under control. It is not weakness. Jesus called himself gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29), yet drove the traders out of the temple. Gentleness is power held in check for the good of others: the strength not to retaliate, not to crush, not to insist on one’s rights.

With patience. Makrothymia: long temper, the opposite of short-tempered. It is the patience God shows toward us (Romans 2:4). It is especially patience with people rather than circumstances: with those who are slow, difficult or wrong.

Bearing with one another in love. To bear with is to put up with, to tolerate the faults and quirks of others without giving up on them. The church is not made of easy people. Every congregation includes the irritating, the awkward and the oversensitive, and each of us is one of them for someone else. Love is the reason and the strength to bear with them.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should tolerate sin or false teaching without a word: Paul will command speaking the truth in love (v. 15) and the confronting of wrong (5:11). Bearing with one another is about personal faults and differences, not about excusing evil. Nor is humility a pretended low opinion of oneself, or a refusal to use one’s gifts (v. 7). False modesty is still focused on self.

In a sentence. A life worthy of God’s calling shows itself first in humility, gentleness, patience and the love that puts up with others.

On a Tuesday. Think of the believer who irritates you most. Bear with them today in love, and remember that someone is bearing with you.

verseByVerse.quote: Eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians do not have to create unity: the Holy Spirit has already made all believers one. Their task is to guard that unity eagerly, with peace as the cord that ties them together.

Eager. Spoudazontes: making every effort, being diligent, hurrying to do it. Unity does not maintain itself. It takes work, intention and effort, like keeping a garden from being overgrown.

To maintain. To keep, guard, preserve. You can only keep something you already have.

The unity of the Spirit. The unity the Spirit creates. Every believer has the same Spirit (2:18, 22; 1 Corinthians 12:13). Christ has already made Jew and Gentile one (2:14–16). This unity is a fact, not a goal; it is God’s work, not a human agreement. What we can do is either display it or obscure it, guard it or damage it.

In the bond of peace. A “bond” is something that ties together, like a cord or a ligament. Peace is what binds believers to one another. Christ is our peace (2:14), and the peace he made at the cross must be lived out in relationships. Where there is quarrelling, grudges and factions, the bond is fraying.

What it does not mean. Not unity at any price, or unity that ignores truth. Paul immediately grounds unity in “one faith” (v. 5) and describes a unity of the faith and knowledge of Christ (v. 13). Unity with those who deny the gospel is not the unity of the Spirit. Nor does it require one worldwide church organisation, or uniformity in every practice. The unity of the Spirit is the shared life of all who truly belong to Christ, visible wherever they love one another, and kept by the virtues of verse 2.

In a sentence. The Spirit has already made believers one; we must work hard to keep that unity, bound together by peace.

On a Tuesday. If there is a rift between you and another believer, take the first step to repair it. And refuse to repeat the story that would widen a division in your church.

verseByVerse.quote: There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — one Lord, one faith, one baptism,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why must believers guard their unity? Because it rests on great realities that every Christian shares: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and (in v. 6) one God and Father. These seven “ones” are the foundation of Christian unity.

The shape. The seven “ones” are arranged around the Trinity. One Spirit, with the body and the hope he creates (v. 4). One Lord, with the faith and baptism that focus on him (v. 5). One God and Father, over all (v. 6). The unity of the church reflects the unity of God himself.

One body. The church, the body of Christ (1:23; 2:16). There are many congregations, but only one church, with one head. A Christian in Ephesus and a Christian in China today belong to the same body.

One Spirit. The Holy Spirit, who indwells every believer and makes them members of the body (1 Corinthians 12:13). There is no believer without the Spirit (Romans 8:9).

The one hope that belongs to your call. When God called us, he called us to a single future: the inheritance in Christ, his return, the resurrection, and the new creation (1:18). Christians may differ in temperament and culture, but they are all heading to the same destination.

One Lord. Jesus Christ, the one to whom every believer has bowed. In the Roman world “Lord” was used of Caesar; for Christians, there is only one Lord (1 Corinthians 8:6). This is the confession that makes someone a Christian: Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9).

One faith. Probably both the act of faith (all believers trust the same Christ in the same way) and the content of faith, the gospel believed (Jude 3). Christian unity is not shared feeling but shared truth.

One baptism. Baptism is the sign of entry into Christ and his body, given once (Romans 6:3–4; Galatians 3:27). Every believer is baptised into the same name, the name of the Father, the Son and the Spirit (Matthew 28:19). Some take it to mean Spirit baptism, but water baptism as the sign of union with Christ best fits the list.

What it does not mean. Not that all who call themselves Christians are thereby one, regardless of what they believe. The “one faith” sets a boundary: unity is among those who confess the one Lord and the one gospel. Nor does “one baptism” mean that baptism saves by itself: it is the sign of union with Christ by faith, not its cause.

Where Christians differ: one baptism, but whose? Christians disagree about who should be baptised and how. Paedobaptists (Presbyterian, Anglican and others) baptise the infants of believers as the new covenant sign, parallel to circumcision (Colossians 2:11–12). Credobaptists (Baptists and others) baptise those who profess faith, holding that baptism signifies a union with Christ by faith that infants cannot yet profess (Acts 2:41; 8:12). Sadly, many churches do not recognise each other’s baptisms. Verdict: credobaptist, held charitably. Believers’ baptism best fits the New Testament pattern, but paedobaptist Christians who trust Christ are brothers and sisters in the one faith and the one body. The disagreement is real, but it must not break the unity of verse 3.

In a sentence. Christians are one because they share one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism and one God and Father.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to write off another believer over a secondary matter, run through this list. Count how much you share before you count what divides you.

verseByVerse.quote: one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The climax of the list: over all, through all and in all is the one God and Father. The unity of the church rests ultimately on the oneness of God.

One God. The great confession of Israel: Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one (Deuteronomy 6:4). Paul, a Jew, has not abandoned this. The one God is now known as Father, Son and Spirit (vv. 4–6), without becoming three gods. The God who is one makes his people one.

And Father of all. In context, Father of all believers: his family of Jews and Gentiles (2:18–19; 3:14–15). There are no stepchildren in God’s family.

Who is over all. His transcendence: he rules above everything, sovereign over the church and the world.

And through all. His providence: he works through everything, sustaining and directing it.

And in all. His presence: he dwells in his people by his Spirit (2:22).

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “you” (“in you all”) or “us”. Verdict: the shorter text, “in all”, is original. The addition, however, gives the right sense: the “all” in view is God’s people.

What it does not mean. Not pantheism, the idea that God is everything or everything is God. God is over all, distinct from his creation. Nor universalism, that everyone is God’s child and will be saved: Paul has just described people as by nature children of wrath (2:3) and alienated from the life of God (4:18). God is Father of all who are in Christ.

In a sentence. Above, through and within the church stands the one God and Father, and his oneness is the root of ours.

For worship. Worship the one God whom the whole church, across the world and through history, worships with you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Each believer has received grace as Christ apportioned it. As the psalm says, the conqueror ascended with captives and gave gifts to people; the one who ascended first descended, and he ascended above the heavens to fill everything. He gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors and teachers, to equip his people for service and build up his body, until all reach unity in faith and knowledge of the Son, maturity and the full stature of Christ. Then we will no longer be like children tossed by every wind of teaching and human trickery, but, speaking the truth in love, will grow in every way into Christ, the head, from whom the whole body, joined and held together, builds itself up in love as each part does its work.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ascended Christ and the Equipping Ministry

The passage grounds all ministry in the ascension of Christ — a movement of Pauline theology that is often underemphasised. It is the ascended Christ who gives gifts to his church. The one who has “ascended far above all the heavens” (v.10) is also the one who “fills all things” — present everywhere, sovereign over all, distributing gifts according to his wisdom and his grace. Ministry is not primarily a human enterprise; it is a dimension of the ongoing, active reign of the risen and ascended King.

The list of gifted persons — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — has generated significant debate about which offices are permanent and which ceased with the apostolic age. The Reformed tradition has consistently held that the foundational offices (apostles and prophets, Ephesians 2:20) were unique to the founding of the church, while the equipping offices (evangelists, pastor-teachers) continue throughout the church's history. What remains constant in every age is the purpose: equipping the saints for ministry until the whole body reaches the fullness of Christ.

The metaphor of the body in vv.15–16 is Paul's most developed statement of mutual ministry. The body grows “when each part is working properly” — not when a few parts are exceptionally active while the rest remain passive, but when every member is fulfilling their function. This is the vision of a church in which every person is a minister — not because every person preaches, but because every person contributes the grace-gift they have received to the building up of the whole. The body that achieves this grows toward Christ in every way. The body that fails at this — where a few do everything and the many receive — stunts its own growth.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church had known extraordinary leadership — Paul himself had spent three years there, and the elders he had appointed knew the weight of shepherding a flock in a hostile city (Acts 20:28–31). Now Paul is gone, and his letter is itself an act of equipping: preparing the church to continue faithfully without his physical presence. The gifted leaders he describes in vv.11–12 are, in the first instance, the elders and teachers of the Ephesian church — men charged with the immense responsibility of preparing every member for a ministry that would build the body in Paul's absence. This was not a programme; it was a pastoral theology applied to a real community facing real challenges.

Now: The consumer church — where the congregation pays for spiritual services delivered by professional clergy — is the precise opposite of Paul's vision. It produces spiritual infants who cannot feed themselves, who are vulnerable to every wind of doctrine, who have no sense of their own giftedness or their own call to ministry. The equipping church — where gifted leaders deliberately, systematically invest in the ministry capacity of every member — produces a body that is robust, maturing, and growing in love. The question for every church leader is not “How well am I performing?” but “How well am I equipping?” And the question for every member is not “Am I being fed?” but “Am I contributing?”

verseByVerse.quote: But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unity does not mean sameness. Within the one body, Christ has given every believer a particular gift of grace for serving others, and he has decided what each person receives.

But. A turn from “all” (vv. 4–6) to “each”. The church is one, but it is not a uniform mass. Unity and diversity belong together, like the parts of a body (1 Corinthians 12:12–27).

Grace was given. Here “grace” means not saving grace, which all share equally, but grace for service: the gift and ability to serve in a particular way. Paul spoke of his own calling as a grace given to him (3:2, 7–8). Every believer has some version of the same thing.

To each one of us. No exceptions. There are no giftless Christians, no passengers in the church (1 Corinthians 12:7; 1 Peter 4:10). The gifts may be public, like teaching, or quiet, like helping, giving, showing mercy or administration (Romans 12:6–8).

According to the measure of Christ’s gift. Christ decides what each person receives and how much. This removes both pride and envy. If your gift is large, you did not earn it; if it is small, Christ chose it for you. He gives as he sees fit (1 Corinthians 12:11).

What it does not mean. Not that the gift is for the person’s own benefit or status. Gifts are given for the building up of the body (v. 12). Nor does it mean every believer has the same gift, or that we must have a spectacular one to be useful.

In a sentence. Within the church’s unity, Christ gives each believer a distinct gift for serving others, in the measure he chooses.

On a Tuesday. Ask: what has Christ given me to serve others with? If you do not know, ask a mature friend what they see in you, and start serving where there is need.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore it says, 'When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul supports his point from Psalm 68. Like a conquering king returning in triumph, the ascended Christ has defeated his enemies and now distributes the spoils of his victory, gifts for his people.

Therefore it says. Paul introduces Scripture. “It says” means God says it in the Scripture.

Psalm 68. A victory psalm. It celebrates God marching from Sinai and going up to his sanctuary on Mount Zion as a victorious king, with captives in procession behind him, receiving tribute from the defeated. When a king in the ancient world won a war, he returned to his capital in a triumphal procession, displaying his prisoners and receiving the spoils.

When he ascended on high. Paul applies the psalm to Christ. God’s ascent to Zion is fulfilled in Christ’s ascension to heaven after his resurrection (Acts 1:9–11), where he is seated far above every power (1:20–21).

He led a host of captives. Literally “he took captivity captive”. Two readings: either Christ’s defeated enemies, sin, death, Satan and the powers, paraded in his triumph (Colossians 2:15); or the people he freed from captivity to those enemies, now following him. The first fits the military picture best. In either case, the point is that Christ won.

And he gave gifts to men. Here is the puzzle. The Hebrew of Psalm 68:18 says the king received gifts among men; Paul says he gave gifts to men. Paul is not misquoting carelessly. The Aramaic paraphrase of the Psalms used in synagogues (the Targum) also read “gave”, applying it to Moses giving the law. And the psalm itself goes on to describe God giving to his people (68:10, 19, 35). A victorious king received tribute in order to share it out among his people. Paul draws out the full meaning: the King who received the spoils of victory now distributes them. Christ ascended to give.

The gifts. They are named in verse 11: not abilities in the abstract, but people. Christ gives the church gifted servants.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul changed Scripture to suit his argument. He interprets it, as Jewish teachers did, in the light of its fulfilment in Christ. Inspired by the Spirit, Paul shows what the psalm was pointing to all along.

In a sentence. Like a victorious king, the ascended Christ has triumphed over his enemies and now shares out the gifts of his victory with his people.

For worship. Every gift you have received in the church, every faithful pastor, every helper, is a spoil of Christ’s victory. Thank him for them.
verseByVerse.note: The psalm pictures God ascending Mount Zion in victory, receiving tribute; Paul applies it to Christ, who in triumph gives gifts. A Jewish Aramaic paraphrase of the psalm also reads “gave gifts.”

parallels.desc: you ascended on high, leading a host of captives

verseByVerse.quote: (In saying, 'He ascended,' what does it mean but that he had also descended into the lower regions, the earth? He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul pauses to explain the psalm. If Christ “ascended”, he must first have come down. The one who came down to the depths is the same one who has now gone up above all the heavens, so that he might fill the whole universe with his presence and rule.

The logic. To ascend implies a prior descent. The psalm speaks of God ascending; if it is fulfilled in Christ, then Christ must first have come down from heaven. This identifies Christ with God: he came from heaven before he returned there (John 3:13; 6:62).

The lower regions, the earth. The Greek is literally “the lower parts of the earth”. The question is what Paul means. There are three main views.

1. The incarnation. “The lower parts, that is, the earth”: Christ came down from heaven to earth. Grammatically, “the earth” explains what the lower regions are. This fits the contrast with “far above all the heavens”.

2. A descent into Hades. “The parts lower than the earth”: Christ went to the realm of the dead between his death and resurrection, perhaps to proclaim his victory (compare 1 Peter 3:19). This lies behind the phrase in the Apostles’ Creed, “he descended into hell”.

3. Pentecost. Christ ascended, then descended again in the Spirit to give gifts. This is less likely, because the descent comes before the ascent in Paul’s words.

Verdict: the incarnation, Christ’s coming down from heaven to earth, including the whole of his humiliation down to death and the grave (Philippians 2:6–8). Calvin and the Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 50) understand the Creed’s phrase in a similar sense: that Christ endured the depths of humiliation, including the agony of the cross and remaining in the state of the dead until the third day. The main point is clear on any view: the one who went lowest has been raised highest.

Far above all the heavens. Not merely into the sky, but beyond every created realm, to the throne of God (Hebrews 4:14; 7:26).

That he might fill all things. Christ ascended not to leave the world, but to fill it with his presence, power and rule (1:23). From the throne, he governs all things for his church and pours out his Spirit and gifts (Acts 2:33).

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “first” (“he also descended first”), as in the King James Version. Verdict: an early explanatory addition, not original, though it correctly states the order.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ’s ascension was a departure that left the church alone. He is more present to the whole church now, by his Spirit, than he was to the disciples in Galilee (John 16:7).

In a sentence. The Christ who came down to the lowest depths is the Christ who now reigns above everything, filling all things with his rule.

On a Tuesday. Whatever depths you are in, Christ has been lower, and he has come up. There is no place he does not fill.
verseByVerse.note: “The lower regions, the earth” may mean his coming down to earth in the incarnation.

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here are the gifts the ascended Christ gives: not things, but people. He gave the church apostles, prophets, evangelists, and shepherds who teach, to serve his people with his word.

And he gave. The emphasis is on “he”: Christ himself gave. These servants are not the church’s invention or its employees, but Christ’s gifts to it. To despise faithful leaders is to despise his gifts.

The apostles. Those personally commissioned by the risen Christ as his authoritative witnesses: the Twelve and Paul, with a few others in a wider sense (Acts 1:21–26; 1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:7–9). They laid the foundation of the church (2:20), and their teaching is preserved in the New Testament.

The prophets. New Testament prophets, who received and spoke revelation from God for the church in the foundation-laying period (2:20; 3:5; Acts 11:27–28; 13:1).

The evangelists. Those gifted to proclaim the gospel, especially where it has not been heard, and to plant churches. Philip is called an evangelist (Acts 21:8), and Timothy was told to do the work of one (2 Timothy 4:5). They are something like missionaries and church planters.

The shepherds and teachers. The Greek grammar links these two with one article: probably one group, pastors who teach. “Shepherd” (poimēn) is the word translated “pastor” (Latin pastor means shepherd). A shepherd feeds, leads, protects and seeks his flock, and in the church he does it chiefly by teaching God’s word (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2; John 21:15–17). In the New Testament these are the elders, also called overseers (Titus 1:5–7). Christ is the chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4); they are under-shepherds.

The common thread. Every gift listed is a ministry of the word. Christ builds his church by his word, spoken by the people he gives.

What it does not mean. Not a complete list of gifts (compare Romans 12:6–8; 1 Corinthians 12:8–10, 28). Nor does it mean that only these people serve: the next verse says they equip everyone else to serve.

Where Christians differ: apostles and prophets today. Some churches, especially in the newer charismatic and apostolic movements, recognise living apostles and prophets with authority to direct the church. Others hold that “apostle” may be used today in a weaker sense, of missionaries or church planters. Cessationists hold that the foundational offices of apostle and prophet ended with the apostolic age, because a foundation is laid once (2:20), and that Scripture is now complete. Verdict: cessationist, held charitably. No one today holds the apostles’ authority, and the prophetic foundation is complete in Scripture. Evangelists, pastors and teachers continue, and the church needs them as much as ever.

In a sentence. The ascended Christ gives his church people who minister his word: foundational apostles and prophets, and ongoing evangelists and pastor-teachers.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your pastors this week by name, that they would feed, lead and protect the flock with the word.
verseByVerse.note: “Shepherds” is the word often translated “pastors.”

verseByVerse.quote: to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why does Christ give these leaders? Not so that they can do all the ministry while everyone else watches, but so that they can equip all God’s people to do the work of ministry, and so build up the body of Christ.

To equip. Katartismos, a rich word. It was used of setting broken bones, of mending torn fishing nets (Mark 1:19), of fitting out a ship for a voyage, and of training someone for a task. Pastors and teachers mend, restore, train and fit out believers for service. Their chief tool is Scripture, which makes the person of God complete, equipped for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

The saints. All believers (see 1:1), not a special class.

For the work of ministry. “Ministry” is diakonia, service. The ministry of the church belongs to the whole church, not to professionals alone. Older translations (like the King James Version) placed a comma after “saints”, making three separate tasks for the leaders: equipping, ministry, and building up. Most interpreters now read it as a chain: leaders equip the saints, so that the saints do the work of ministry, so that the body is built up.

For building up the body of Christ. Two pictures merge: a building (2:20–22) and a body. The goal of all ministry is the growth of the church, in numbers and in maturity (v. 13).

What it does not mean. Not that pastors and teachers are unnecessary, or that everyone can do everything. The gift of pastor-teacher is distinct, and it matters. But the leaders’ job is not to be the only ones who serve; it is to make others able to serve. A church where only the pastor ministers is like a team where only the coach plays.

In a sentence. Christ gives pastors and teachers to train all his people for service, so that the whole church is built up.

On a Tuesday. What ministry has God equipped you for? Ask your elders, find a place to serve, and use it.

verseByVerse.quote: until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goal of all this ministry is a grown-up church: believers united in the faith and the knowledge of Christ, mature, measuring up to Christ himself, and no longer like children blown around by every new teaching and by clever deceivers.

Until. Ministry continues until the goal is reached. In full, that will be at Christ’s return; but the church is to move toward it now.

We all. Not a few spiritual heroes, but the whole church.

The unity of the faith. In verse 3 the church must guard the unity it has; here it grows into a fuller unity. The unity of the faith is shared conviction about the truth of the gospel. It grows as believers are taught the same truth and believe it together. Not agreement on the lowest common denominator, but agreement on the whole truth.

And of the knowledge of the Son of God. “Knowledge” is epignōsis, full, personal knowledge (1:17). The faith is not only a set of truths but knowledge of a person. The only time Paul calls Jesus “the Son of God” in Ephesians.

To mature manhood. Literally “to a complete man”, a full-grown adult, in contrast with “children” in verse 14. It refers to the whole church as one new man (2:15) growing up, not only to individual men. Women and men alike are included.

To the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. The standard is staggering: not the best Christian you know, but Christ himself. Maturity is measured by how far we have grown to be like him (Romans 8:29; Colossians 1:28).

So that we may no longer be children. Children in the bad sense: unstable, gullible, easily impressed. Not the childlike trust Jesus praised (Matthew 18:3), but childishness (1 Corinthians 14:20; Hebrews 5:13–14).

Tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine. A picture from the sea, familiar to a port city like Ephesus: a small boat without keel or anchor, thrown about by waves and blown wherever the wind goes. Immature believers chase every new teaching, trend or teacher, with no stable grip on the truth. Every new book or online preacher sends them in a new direction.

By human cunning. The word (kybeia) means dice-playing, and so trickery: the sleight of hand of a cheat at dice.

By craftiness in deceitful schemes. False teaching is often deliberate and organised. “Schemes” (methodeia) is the word used of the devil’s schemes in 6:11. Behind human deceivers stands the deceiver.

What it does not mean. Not that mature Christians never change their minds or learn anything new. Maturity is teachable. But it is stable: it grows deeper roots instead of being uprooted by each new idea. Nor is maturity measured by knowledge alone: verse 15 adds love, and the standard is the character of Christ.

In a sentence. Ministry aims at a united, mature church that has grown up into Christ and is no longer blown about by false teaching.

On a Tuesday. If every new trend in Christian books or online preachers moves you, ask for grounding in the whole counsel of God. Read the whole Bible, sit under faithful preaching, and learn the historic confessions of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead of being tossed about, the church grows up into Christ by speaking the truth in love. Christ, the head, supplies the whole body, and as each part does its work, the body grows and builds itself up in love.

Rather, speaking the truth in love. One Greek word (alētheuontes): “truthing”, living and speaking the truth. Against the deceivers of verse 14, the church holds to the truth. But it does so “in love”. Truth without love becomes harsh and proud; it wins arguments and loses people. Love without truth becomes sentimental and empty; it comforts people on their way to ruin. The church needs both together. Love tells the truth, and truth is told lovingly.

We are to grow up in every way into him. Growth in every area: knowledge, holiness, love, worship, service. The direction is “into him”: becoming more like Christ, and more fully united to him.

Who is the head, into Christ. In the ancient world, the head was seen as the source of direction and of life for the body. Christ rules the church and supplies its life (1:22; Colossians 1:18).

From whom the whole body. Growth comes from Christ. The church grows not by human techniques, but by drawing life from its head.

Joined and held together. The same builder’s word used in 2:21: fitted together, every part in its place.

By every joint with which it is equipped. “Joints” or ligaments are the points of contact between parts of the body, through which supplies pass. Christ’s life flows to the members through their connections with each other. No Christian receives all they need from Christ in isolation; much of it comes through other believers.

When each part is working properly. Every member has a function (v. 7). When some parts stop working, the body is weakened. A church in which only a few serve grows unhealthy.

Makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love. The body builds itself up, but only as Christ supplies it, and only in love. Love is the atmosphere of healthy growth. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up (1 Corinthians 8:1).

What it does not mean. Not that “speaking the truth in love” is only about confronting people with their faults. Above all, it means holding to and speaking the truth of the gospel, against error, in a loving way. Nor does church growth mean only numerical growth: Paul’s concern is maturity.

In a sentence. As believers hold to the truth in love and each member serves, the whole church grows up into Christ, its head, and builds itself up in love.

For worship. Thank Christ for the members of his body who have helped you grow, and ask how you can be a joint through which his life reaches someone else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Put Off the Old, Put On the New
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul insists they must stop living like unbelieving Gentiles, whose thinking is futile, whose understanding is darkened, and who are cut off from God’s life by ignorance and hardened hearts; having lost all sensitivity, they give themselves to sensuality and every kind of impurity. That is not how they came to know Christ, if they truly heard and were taught the truth that is in Jesus: to put off the old self, corrupted by deceitful desires, to be renewed in their minds, and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Renewal of the Mind and the New Humanity

The “old self” and “new self” of this passage are not psychological categories — they are eschatological ones. The old self is the Adamic humanity: the self that has inherited Adam's corruption, lives under the dominion of sin, and is “corrupt through deceitful desires” (v.22). The new self is the new humanity created in Christ — what Paul elsewhere calls “the last Adam” (1 Corinthians 15:45). To be “in Christ” is to have been transferred from the old humanity to the new, from the domain of the first Adam to the domain of the Second.

The renewing of the mind (v.23) is the cognitive dimension of this transfer. Romans 12:2 makes the same point: “be transformed by the renewal of your mind.” The mind that has been shaped by the world — its values, its assumptions, its desires — must be reshaped by the word and Spirit of God. This is not achieved in a moment; it is the work of a lifetime. Every act of sustained Bible meditation, every time truth displaces a lie, every time a Spirit-given desire overcomes a flesh-driven one, the mind is being renewed. This is the slow and glorious work of sanctification.

The goal of the renewal is “the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness” (v.24). This is the restoration of the image of God that was defaced at the fall. God made humanity in his image; sin corrupted that image; Christ has come to restore it. The new self is not merely morally better than the old — it is ontologically different, created anew after the very likeness of God. This is why the Christian life is not ultimately about rule-keeping but about becoming who you already are in Christ: the image-bearer of God, restored and renewed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus was a city of extraordinary sensual abundance. The temple complex of Artemis, the bath-houses, the theatre, the commercial district — pleasure was available in every form and at every price. To be a Christian in Ephesus was to swim against a powerful and relentless current. Paul does not tell the Ephesian Christians to try harder or to exercise greater willpower. He gives them something more powerful: a new identity. You are not the old self anymore. The garment of the old life is to be put off — not held on to, not worn occasionally for old time's sake, but removed and discarded. And in its place: the new self, created after God's own likeness.

Now: The pornified, entertainment-saturated, hyper-stimulated culture of the 21st century is Ephesus with better technology. The mechanisms of desire-manipulation are more sophisticated; the availability of darkness is more immediate; the cultural current against a holy life runs faster. Paul's answer is unchanged and still the most powerful available: not more discipline applied to the old self, but the daily renewal of the mind in the truth of the gospel — who you are in Christ, what you have been given, who you are becoming. The Christian who meditates daily on Scripture, who submits their thinking to the word of God, who asks the Spirit to renew their mind — this person is not swimming against the current on their own. They are being transformed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this I say and testify in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now gives a solemn charge: believers must stop living the way the unbelieving world around them lives, with minds that are empty of God and go nowhere.

Now this I say and testify in the Lord. A solemn tone, almost a legal oath. “Testify” means to declare as a witness. “In the Lord” means with Christ’s authority. This is not Paul’s opinion; it is Christ’s command.

You must no longer walk. “Walk” again (see v. 1). A change of way of life is required. “No longer”: they once did walk this way (2:1–3).

As the Gentiles do. The readers were Gentiles by birth, but Paul now uses “Gentiles” to mean unbelieving pagans. Their identity has changed so completely that they are no longer counted as Gentiles in this sense. They belong to God’s people; they must stop living like outsiders.

In the futility of their minds. “Futility” (mataiotēs) means emptiness, worthlessness, purposelessness: thinking that goes round in circles and arrives nowhere. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses in Ecclesiastes: vanity of vanities. The problem with the unbelieving mind is not lack of intelligence: the ancient world had great philosophers. It is that thinking cut off from God loses its true object and purpose (Romans 1:21). Clever people can build careers, theories and lives on emptiness.

What it does not mean. Not that unbelievers are stupid, or that everything they think is false. By God’s common grace, unbelievers discover much truth in science, art and wisdom. The futility is at the root: without God, the deepest questions of life (who am I, why am I here, how should I live, what happens at death) are left without true answers.

In a sentence. Believers must no longer live like the world around them, whose thinking, cut off from God, ends in emptiness.

On a Tuesday. Notice how many of your daily assumptions come from the culture rather than from Christ: about success, pleasure, money and what makes life worthwhile. Hold each up to the light of Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: They are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart. They have become callous and have given themselves up to sensuality, greedy to practice every kind of impurity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul traces how unbelief works. At its root is a hardened heart. This produces ignorance; ignorance cuts people off from God’s life; and in the end, the conscience goes numb and people abandon themselves to sensuality and an endless appetite for impurity.

The order. Read the chain from the inside out: (1) hardness of heart, which causes (2) ignorance, which leads to (3) alienation from the life of God and (4) darkened understanding; and then (5) callousness, (6) giving themselves up to sensuality, and (7) greed for impurity. The root problem is not in the head but in the heart. People do not reject God because they lack information; they lack understanding because their hearts are hard toward him.

Darkened in their understanding. The mind cannot see clearly, like a room with the lights off. They are in darkness about God, themselves and the meaning of life (5:8; Romans 1:21).

Alienated from the life of God. Cut off from the life God gives, and from the life God lives. This is the spiritual death of 2:1.

Because of the ignorance that is in them. Not innocent ignorance, as of someone who has never heard, but wilful ignorance: not knowing what one could know and should know.

Due to their hardness of heart. “Hardness” (pōrōsis) was a medical term for a callus or for bone setting hard; it was also used of marble. The heart grows stony and insensitive toward God (Mark 3:5; Romans 11:25). This is the root.

They have become callous. Literally “past feeling”. The conscience, which once protested, has gone numb. Like skin that has been burned so often it no longer feels pain. What once caused shame no longer does.

And have given themselves up to sensuality. “Sensuality” (aselgeia) means shameless indulgence: open, unrestrained self-gratification that no longer bothers to hide or blush. In Romans 1:24 Paul says God gave them up; here they give themselves up. Both are true: God’s judgment is to hand people over to what they have chosen.

Greedy to practise every kind of impurity. “Greedy” is pleonexia: wanting more, the same word translated “covetousness” in 5:3. Sin does not satisfy; it creates a hunger for more. The more one indulges, the less one is satisfied, and the further one must go.

What it does not mean. Not that every unbeliever is equally sensual or depraved. Paul describes where the road leads, and the direction of a life cut off from God. Many unbelievers are restrained by conscience, upbringing, law and God’s common grace. Nor does it mean that Christians cannot be affected: Paul warns believers precisely because they can drift back toward this pattern.

In a sentence. Unbelief begins in a heart hardened toward God, which darkens the mind, cuts people off from God’s life, numbs the conscience, and ends in a never-satisfied appetite for impurity.

On a Tuesday. Repeated sin numbs the conscience. Do not trust the fact that something no longer feels wrong. Test your conscience by Scripture, not your conscience by your habits.

verseByVerse.quote: But that is not the way you learned Christ!
verseByVerse.commentary:
In one short sentence Paul sets the believers apart from all that: that is not how you learned Christ. Christ himself was what they learned, and he does not lead to that way of life.

But that is not the way. The Greek is emphatic: “But you, not so.” The contrast is complete.

You learned Christ. An unusual phrase, found nowhere else in Greek literature. Paul does not say “you learned about Christ”, or “you learned Christianity”. Christ himself is the subject matter. To become a Christian is to be enrolled in Christ’s school, with Christ as both teacher and curriculum (Matthew 11:29). Learning a person is different from learning a subject: it means coming to know him, his character, his ways and his will, so that his life shapes yours.

The logic. If you have truly learned Christ, you cannot be comfortable with the life of verses 17–19. You cannot learn the pure, self-giving Christ and conclude that sensual, self-serving living is fine.

What it does not mean. Not that learning Christ is a purely intellectual exercise. It includes knowledge, but it is the knowledge of a disciple following a master.

In a sentence. Believers have learned Christ himself, and Christ does not teach a life of empty sensuality.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted, ask: is this what I learned in Christ? Would the one I have learned recognise himself in what I am about to do?

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard about him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul explains what it means to have learned Christ: they heard Christ himself in the gospel, they were taught within their union with him, and what they were taught is the truth as it is found in Jesus.

Assuming that you have heard about him. Or “surely you heard him”. The Greek can mean “heard him”: when the gospel was preached to them, Christ himself was speaking through his messengers (2:17). This is a high view of preaching: in faithful proclamation, Christ’s voice is heard (Romans 10:14, 17).

And were taught in him. They were instructed as people already in union with Christ, and their instruction was about him. Conversion leads into teaching (Matthew 28:20).

As the truth is in Jesus. The only place in Ephesians where Paul uses the human name “Jesus” alone, without “Christ” or “Lord”. The emphasis falls on the historical person, the man from Nazareth. Truth is not an abstract idea or an inner feeling; it is found in a real person who lived, died and rose. False teachers detached “Christ” from the real Jesus; Paul ties them together (1 John 4:2–3).

What it does not mean. Not that truth is relative or personal (“my truth”). There is truth, and it is found in Jesus (John 14:6). Nor that any teaching that uses Jesus’ name is true: the test is whether it matches the Jesus of the apostolic witness.

In a sentence. Believers have heard Christ in the gospel and been taught in him, and the truth they learned is anchored in the real person of Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Test what you hear about Jesus, online or anywhere, by the Jesus of the Gospels. If it does not match him, it is not the truth as it is in Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: to put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires,
verseByVerse.commentary:
What did they learn in Christ? First, to put off their old self, the person they were before Christ, like taking off filthy clothes, because that self belongs to their old life and is rotting from within, driven by desires that lie.

The grammar. Verses 22–24 give the content of what they were taught (vv. 20–21): to put off the old self, to be renewed, and to put on the new self. Scholars debate whether these are commands (“put off!”) or a description of what happened at conversion (“you have put off”). Colossians 3:9–10 speaks of it as having happened. Verdict: both. At conversion, the old self was decisively put off in union with Christ (Romans 6:6); now believers must keep living out that change, day by day (vv. 25–32 give the commands).

To put off. A picture of clothing: to take off and throw away old garments. Clothing in Scripture often pictures character (Isaiah 61:10; Zechariah 3:3–5). Converts in the early church may have taken off old clothes before baptism and put on new white ones, picturing this change.

Your old self. Literally “the old man”: not just bad habits, but the whole person we were in Adam, before union with Christ, ruled by sin (see 2:1–3). Paul says this old self was crucified with Christ (Romans 6:6).

Which belongs to your former manner of life. The old self belongs to the past. It is out of date, like clothes from a former life. It does not fit who we now are.

And is corrupt. Present tense: “is being corrupted”, decaying, rotting, like a corpse or spoiled food. The old way of life is not stable; it is in the process of falling apart.

Through deceitful desires. Literally “desires of deceit”. Sin is a liar. It promises happiness, freedom and life, and delivers misery, slavery and death (Hebrews 3:13; James 1:14–15). Every temptation is a false advertisement. The serpent’s lie in Eden still works the same way (Genesis 3:4–6).

What it does not mean. Not that Christians have two natures fighting equally inside them, or that they are still the old self with a new layer on top. The old self has been put off; believers are new people (2 Corinthians 5:17). But remaining sin still lives in us and must be fought (Romans 7:21–25; Galatians 5:17). The fight is real, but the identity is settled. Nor does “putting off” happen by willpower alone: it flows from union with Christ, by the Spirit (Romans 8:13).

In a sentence. In Christ, believers put off their old self, which belongs to the past and is rotting through sin’s lies.

On a Tuesday. When a temptation promises you happiness, ask: what has this ever actually given me? Sin always over-promises.
verseByVerse.note: The “old self” (literally “old man”) is the person we were in Adam, before union with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Between putting off the old and putting on the new stands the renewal of the mind: change begins on the inside, as God keeps renewing the very attitude and outlook that steer our thinking.

And to be renewed. The Greek verb is present tense and passive. Present: an ongoing, continuous process, not a single event. Passive: something done to us, by God, through his Spirit and his word. We do not renew ourselves; we are renewed. Yet we are commanded to be renewed, which means we must put ourselves in the way of God’s renewing work (Romans 12:2).

In the spirit of your minds. Not the Holy Spirit here, but our own inner spirit: the deep attitude, disposition or mindset that directs how we think. It is not just changing a few opinions, but changing the whole outlook from which opinions come. The futile mind of verse 17 is replaced by a mind being made new.

Why the mind? Because the problem began with darkened understanding (v. 18). Behaviour follows belief. What we think about God, ourselves and the world shapes what we desire and what we do. Lasting change in behaviour comes through changed thinking, and that comes through the truth as it is in Jesus (v. 21).

What it does not mean. Not that Christianity is merely intellectual, or that knowing the right things automatically produces holiness. The mind here includes the heart’s attitudes. Nor is renewal instant or complete in this life: it continues until we see Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18; 4:16).

In a sentence. God keeps renewing believers from the inside, changing the very attitude that shapes their thinking.

On a Tuesday. What you fill your mind with shapes who you become. Count the hours you give to screens and the minutes you give to Scripture, and adjust.

verseByVerse.quote: and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Positively, believers put on their new self, as new clothes. This new self is a new creation, made by God to be like him, in the righteousness and holiness that come from the truth.

To put on. The clothing picture again (see v. 22). It is not enough to strip off the old; one must be clothed with the new. Elsewhere Paul says to put on Christ himself (Romans 13:14; Galatians 3:27). The new self is Christ-likeness.

The new self. Literally “the new man”: the person we are in union with Christ. “New” (kainos) means new in kind, fresh, not merely more recent. It is the individual expression of the “one new man” of 2:15.

Created. God’s act, like the first creation (2:10). Becoming a Christian is not self-improvement but new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

After the likeness of God. Literally “according to God”. Humanity was made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27). That image was defaced by the fall, though not destroyed. In Christ, who is the perfect image of God (Colossians 1:15), the image is being restored: the new self is renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator (Colossians 3:10). Salvation does not make us less human, but truly human again.

In true righteousness and holiness. Literally “in righteousness and holiness of the truth”, in contrast with “desires of deceit” (v. 22). The old self was driven by lies; the new self is shaped by truth. “Righteousness” is right conduct toward others and before God. “Holiness” is purity and devotion to God. Together they describe a life that reflects God’s own character.

What it does not mean. Not that believers produce their new self by their own effort, or that putting on is a mere outward act, like a costume. The new self is God’s creation, and putting it on means living according to what God has made us. Nor does it mean believers are already perfect: the new self is real, but it grows into full maturity over a lifetime.

In a sentence. Believers put on the new self God has created, restoring his likeness in them in righteousness and holiness shaped by truth.

For worship. Thank God that he is remaking you in his likeness, and that the end of the process will be a person like Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So they must stop lying and speak truthfully to one another, for they are members of one body. In anger they must not sin, nor let anger outlast the day and give the devil a foothold. Thieves must stop stealing and work honestly, so as to have something to share with those in need. No unwholesome talk should come from their mouths, only what builds others up and gives grace to those who hear. They must not grieve the Holy Spirit, with whom they were sealed for the day of redemption. They must get rid of bitterness, rage, anger, brawling, slander and malice, and be kind and compassionate, forgiving one another as God forgave them in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Grieving of the Spirit and the Ethics of Grace

Verse 30 — “do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” — is one of the most searching statements in the New Testament about the nature of the Spirit. He can be grieved. The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal force that responds mechanically to human sin; he is a Person with genuine emotional sensibility who is affected by the moral life of the community he inhabits. The sins Paul has listed — falsehood, uncontrolled anger, stealing, corrupting speech, bitterness, wrath, malice — do not merely harm the community; they wound the indwelling Guest.

The phrase “by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” provides the context for the warning. The Spirit who can be grieved is the same Spirit who has sealed us for the final day — who is our guarantee of the inheritance (1:14), the deposit of our future glory. To grieve him is therefore not a trivial matter; it is to harm the very relationship that is the ground of our assurance and the means of our transformation. This is not a threat to the believer's salvation; Paul does not say “by whom you were sealed unless you grieve him.” The sealing is certain. But the quality of the Spirit's presence and work in the community is affected by how the community lives.

The climactic command — “forgive one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (v.32) — sets the standard for Christian forgiveness at the level of the cross: freely given, fully extended, without conditions. The Reformers consistently emphasised that forgiveness is not a feeling but a decision — the decision to release the debt, to no longer hold the offence against the offender, to treat them as God treats us in Christ: with kindness and grace. This is impossible from human resources. It is possible only for those who have received it from God and draw on the same source to extend it to others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church was extraordinarily diverse. With diversity comes friction. The command against falsehood (v.25) — “speak truth with your neighbour, for we are members of one another” — addresses the social lubricant of deception that holds many human communities together. In the body of Christ, truth-telling is not optional; it is structurally necessary. A body in which the members lie to one another cannot function. The command against corrupting speech (v.29) — only what builds up — addresses the tongue that tears down, the word that diminishes, the comment that cuts. In a diverse community under pressure, these are the sins most likely to do lasting damage.

Now: “Do not let the sun go down on your anger” is one of the most practically demanding commands in Scripture, and one of the most consistently violated in married life, family life, and church life. We carry grievances. We nurse wounds. We let distance harden into walls. The apostle's word cuts through all of it: move toward resolution before night falls.

This does not mean every conflict is resolved in an evening — some wounds take weeks of patient, humble work to heal. But the direction must always be toward each other, not away. The community that actually practices this — that refuses to let resentment calcify, that keeps short accounts, that forgives as God in Christ forgave — will be noticed. It will be extraordinary. It will be a sign of the Kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now shows what putting off and putting on look like in practice, in five pairs. First: because believers belong to one another, they must throw off lying and speak the truth.

The pattern. Verses 25–32 follow a simple pattern: stop doing this; start doing that; here is the reason. Each command has a negative (put off), a positive (put on), and a gospel motive. Christian morality is never only “don’t”.

Therefore. Because you have put off the old self and put on the new (vv. 22–24).

Having put away falsehood. “Falsehood” (pseudos) is the lie, everything that is false. It connects to the “desires of deceit” (v. 22) and contrasts with “the truth as it is in Jesus” (v. 21). Lying is a mark of the old self, and of the devil, the father of lies (John 8:44).

Let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbour. Paul quotes Zechariah 8:16, where God tells his restored people to speak truth to one another. “Neighbour” here means especially fellow believers, as the next phrase shows.

For we are members one of another. The reason. In a body, each part depends on the others telling it the truth. If the eye lied to the hand about where the fire was, the hand would be burned. Lying among believers damages the body itself. Trust is the nervous system of the church.

What lying includes. Not only outright falsehoods, but exaggeration, flattery, half-truths that leave a false impression, false excuses, breaking promises, and pretending to be what we are not.

What it does not mean. Not that we must say everything we think, or be tactless. Speaking the truth is done in love (v. 15). Silence is not always lying, and there are things we rightly keep private. The tradition has debated hard cases, such as the Hebrew midwives deceiving Pharaoh (Exodus 1:15–21) or Rahab hiding the spies (Joshua 2). Whatever one concludes about protecting the innocent from murderers, those cases do not license the ordinary lies of daily life.

In a sentence. Because believers are parts of one body, they must stop lying and speak the truth to one another.

On a Tuesday. Watch for small lies today: the exaggerated story, the flattering comment, the excuse for being late.

parallels.desc: speak the truth to one another

verseByVerse.quote: Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anger is not always wrong, but it is dangerous. Believers may be angry without sinning, but they must not let anger lead them into sin, and must not keep it overnight.

Be angry and do not sin. Paul quotes Psalm 4:4 from the Greek Old Testament. The grammar suggests not a command to get angry, but a concession and a warning: “When you are angry, do not sin.” There is such a thing as righteous anger. God himself is angry at evil (2:3), and Jesus looked on hard-hearted people with anger (Mark 3:5) and cleared the temple (John 2:13–17). Not to be angry at child abuse, cruelty or injustice would be a moral failure.

The danger. Yet most of our anger is not righteous. It springs from wounded pride, frustrated desire or a sense that our rights have been violated (James 1:20; 4:1–2). And even righteous anger turns sinful easily: it becomes vengeful, disproportionate, or bitter. How to tell the difference: righteous anger is concerned with God’s honour and others’ good, not with my own ego; it is controlled; it seeks to put things right rather than to hurt; and it lets go once it has done its work.
