Do not let the sun go down on your anger. The word for anger here (parorgismos) means irritation, provocation, the state of being stirred up. Deal with it quickly. In Israel, wages had to be paid before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:15); so here, the debt of anger should be settled the same day. Anger kept overnight hardens into resentment. Go to the person, confess your part, seek reconciliation if possible, and give the matter to God.

What it does not mean. Not a command to be angry, nor permission for rage, outbursts or sulking. Nor a strict rule that every conflict must be resolved before bed. Sometimes it takes longer, and a late-night argument may be better postponed. The principle is: do not nurse anger, and do not let it settle in.

In a sentence. Anger at real evil may be right, but never let it become sin, and do not keep it overnight.

On a Tuesday. Is there anger you have carried for more than a day? Ask yourself honestly what it is about: God’s honour or your pride? Then deal with it today.

parallels.desc: be angry, and do not sin

verseByVerse.quote: and give no opportunity to the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anger nursed and kept gives the devil a foothold, in the heart and in the church. Do not hand him the ground.

And give no opportunity. “Opportunity” is topos, literally “a place”: room, space, a foothold. Like a military beachhead or a squatter who moves into an empty room. Unresolved anger opens a space in the heart that the devil uses.

To the devil. Diabolos, “the slanderer, the accuser”: the one who divides. His aim in a church is division (see 2:14–16; 4:3). Anger kept and fed becomes bitterness, gossip and factions, which are his best work. He is a real, personal enemy (6:11–12).

How the foothold grows. First a small grievance, then repeated rehearsing of it in the mind, then talking about it to others, then taking sides, then a divided church. Each step gives the devil more ground.

What it does not mean. Not that every angry Christian is demon-possessed, or that the devil is to blame instead of us. We give the opportunity; he takes it. Our responsibility remains. Nor should we be afraid: the devil is defeated (1:20–21), and if we resist him, he will flee (James 4:7).

In a sentence. Unresolved anger hands the devil a foothold in your heart and your church.

On a Tuesday. Resentment you keep for weeks is ground you have handed to the enemy. Take it back by forgiving and seeking reconciliation.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labour, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace changes a thief into a worker, and a worker into a giver. The one who used to take what belonged to others must now work honestly, so that he has something to give to those in need.

Let the thief no longer steal. Some of the converts had been thieves. In the ancient world, theft was common, including among slaves, who might pilfer from their masters (Titus 2:10). The church was made up of real people with real pasts.

But rather let him labour. “Labour” means hard, tiring work. Greeks of the upper classes despised manual labour as fit only for slaves. Paul, a tentmaker, worked with his own hands (Acts 20:34; 1 Thessalonians 2:9), and honoured it.

Doing honest work with his own hands. Literally “working the good with his hands”. Work that is good in itself, done honestly.

So that he may have something to share with anyone in need. The great surprise. The purpose of work is not only to support oneself and one’s family (which matters: 1 Timothy 5:8; 2 Thessalonians 3:10–12), but to be generous. The thief took from others; the converted thief works to give to others. That is the full reversal: from taking to giving. Jesus said it is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35).

What theft includes. Not only shoplifting or burglary. Also padding expense claims, wasting paid time, unpaid debts, pirated software, cheating on taxes, failing to pay a fair wage, and misusing what belongs to an employer (Leviticus 19:13; James 5:4).

What it does not mean. Not that earning well, owning property, or saving is suspect. The command against stealing assumes that property is real and rightful. Paul assumes that work will produce more than you need; the question is what you do with the surplus. Stewardship is not covetousness. Wise saving, providing for one’s family and planning for the future are good. Covetousness is wanting more for its own sake, or trusting wealth instead of God (Luke 12:15–21; 1 Timothy 6:17–19). Nor is generosity a substitute for work: Paul expects those who can work to work (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

In a sentence. The gospel turns the taker into a worker and the worker into a giver.

On a Tuesday. Check your working day for small thefts: time, expenses, honesty. And plan to give from what you earn, as part of why you earn it.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christian speech must not be rotten. Instead, every word should build others up, fit the moment, and be a channel of God’s grace to those who hear it.

Let no corrupting talk. “Corrupting” (sapros) means rotten, decayed, putrid: used of rotten fruit or bad fish (Matthew 7:17–18; 13:48). Rotten speech spreads decay, like one bad apple in a barrel. It includes gossip, slander, crude jokes, cutting sarcasm, complaining, flattery and words that tear down.

Come out of your mouths. Words come from the heart (Matthew 12:34). Rotten talk reveals rot within; changing the speech requires a changed heart.

But only such as is good for building up. The test: does this word build up, construct, strengthen? Not only is it true, but is it helpful? The same word as in verses 12 and 16: speech is one of the main ways the body builds itself up.

As fits the occasion. Literally “according to the need”. The right word for the moment and the person: comfort for the grieving, encouragement for the discouraged, warning for the wandering, truth for the confused. A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver (Proverbs 25:11). The same word at the wrong time can do harm.

That it may give grace to those who hear. Words can be means of God’s grace. When we speak truth, encouragement and the gospel to one another, God uses our words to strengthen faith (Colossians 4:6; Hebrews 3:13).

What it does not mean. Not that Christians may only speak about spiritual things, or never joke. Humour that builds up and gives joy is good. Nor that we must always be gentle and never confront: sometimes building up requires a hard word, spoken in love.

In a sentence. Let every word you speak be fresh, timely and grace-giving, never rotten.

On a Tuesday. Before you post, send or say it, ask three questions: Is it true? Will it build up? Is it right for this moment?

verseByVerse.quote: And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behind all these commands stands a person. Sinful words and deeds grieve the Holy Spirit, who loves us and has marked us as God’s own until the day our redemption is complete.

And do not grieve. To grieve is to cause sorrow, pain, distress. The command is set in the middle of commands about speech and relationships (vv. 25–32). The sins that grieve the Spirit here are especially sins against other believers: lying, anger, stealing, rotten talk, bitterness. The Spirit who makes believers one (4:3) is grieved by what divides them.

The Holy Spirit of God. A full, solemn title. He is holy, so sin grieves him; and he is God’s Spirit, so to grieve him is to grieve God.

Only a person can be grieved. You cannot grieve a force, an energy or an influence. The Holy Spirit is a person, who knows, wills and loves (1 Corinthians 2:10–11; 12:11; Romans 15:30). Isaiah 63:10 says that Israel rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit in the wilderness. Paul echoes it: the church must not repeat Israel’s sin.

By whom you were sealed. The Spirit is God’s seal on believers (see 1:13–14). A seal marked ownership and guaranteed security, like a stamp on a document or a mark on goods being shipped, protecting them until delivery.

For the day of redemption. The day when redemption is complete: the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body, and full freedom from sin (1:14; Romans 8:23). Believers are redeemed now (1:7), but not yet fully.

What it does not mean. Not a threat that sin will cause the Spirit to leave, or that believers can lose their salvation. The very verse says they are sealed until the day of redemption: the seal holds. The Spirit grieves precisely because he stays. The appeal is not fear but love. A child does not obey a loving father merely to avoid being disowned, but because he does not want to hurt the one who loves him. Nor does grieving the Spirit mean that God is fragile or controlled by our actions: his grief is the grief of holy love, not weakness.

In a sentence. Do not bring sorrow to the Holy Spirit, the loving person who lives in you and has sealed you as God’s own until the final day.

On a Tuesday. Before the harsh word or the dishonest act, remember that the one who lives in you is grieved by it. Let love for him, not only fear of consequences, hold you back.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and security until delivery.

parallels.desc: they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamour and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every form of bitterness, rage and malice must be put away from the Christian life completely, like rubbish taken out of a house.

Let all … be put away from you. “All”: not some, or most, but every trace. “Put away” means removed, carried off, thrown out.

Bitterness. Pikria: a sour, resentful spirit. It is kept and fed: the grudge that is rehearsed, the hurt that is not let go. Hebrews 12:15 calls it a root that springs up and defiles many. It is the soil from which the rest grows.

Wrath and anger. Two words. Wrath (thymos) is the sudden boiling up of rage: the outburst, the temper. Anger (orgē) is a more settled anger, simmering and lasting.

Clamour. Kraugē: shouting, brawling, loud quarrelling. Anger that has found its voice.

Slander. Blasphēmia: speech that damages another person’s name. Gossip, character assassination, telling stories behind people’s backs. The same word is used for blasphemy against God.

Along with all malice. Kakia: ill will, wishing others harm, taking pleasure in their misfortune. The root that lies beneath all the others.

The progression. Read in order, the list shows how resentment grows when it is not dealt with: from an inner bitter spirit, to outbursts of temper, to settled anger, to shouting, to slander behind the back, to a settled wish for the other’s harm. It begins in the heart and ends by poisoning a whole church.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must pretend they have never been hurt, or must never feel the pain of injustice. Grief over wrong is not bitterness. Bitterness is refusing to let go of the wrong, and nursing it. Nor does it forbid naming wrong or seeking justice through proper channels; it forbids the inner poison and the destructive speech.

In a sentence. Throw out of your life every trace of bitterness, temper, shouting, slander and ill will.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you speak about with a bitter edge? Stop repeating the story, and bring the wound to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In place of bitterness, believers must be kind, tender-hearted and forgiving to one another, and the pattern and power for it is the way God has forgiven them in Christ.

Be kind to one another. “Kind” (chrēstos) means useful, good, generous: kindness in action, not just in feeling. God himself is kind, even to the ungrateful and evil (Luke 6:35), and he showed kindness to us in Christ (2:7).

Tenderhearted. Eusplanchnos: literally “with good bowels”. The ancients located deep emotion in the gut, as we might say “heart”. It means compassionate, moved with pity for others’ pain. Jesus was moved with this compassion for the crowds (Matthew 9:36).

Forgiving one another. The Greek word (charizomenoi) is related to charis, grace: “gracing one another”. To forgive is to give someone grace they do not deserve, releasing them from the debt they owe us.

As God in Christ forgave you. The measure and the motive. The measure: we forgive as God forgave us, freely, fully and at great cost. The motive: having been forgiven so much, we cannot refuse to forgive others so little (Matthew 18:21–35). The more clearly we see how much God has forgiven us, the more able we are to forgive. “In Christ”: God’s forgiveness came through the cross, where Christ paid the debt.

What it does not mean. Forgiveness does not mean pretending the wrong was not wrong, or calling evil good. God did not pretend; he dealt with our sin at the cross. It does not always mean restoring trust immediately: trust is rebuilt over time, and wisdom may require boundaries, especially where there has been abuse. It does not remove all just consequences: a forgiven thief may still need to repay, and crimes should be reported to the authorities (Romans 13:1–4). And it is not the same as reconciliation, which requires both sides. What forgiveness does mean is this: releasing the debt, refusing to take revenge, refusing to keep bringing the wrong up, and wishing the other person good. Forgiveness may need to be renewed many times as the hurt resurfaces.

In a sentence. Be kind, compassionate and forgiving to one another, just as God has forgiven you in Christ.

On a Tuesday. Who do you need to forgive today? Begin by remembering, in detail, what God has forgiven you.

For worship. Thank God for all he has forgiven you in Christ.

4.theology:
Ephesians 4 stakes out the great Reformed doctrine of the inseparability of justification and sanctification. The same grace that declares the sinner righteous also begins to make them righteous. Not simultaneously, not automatically — but inevitably. Where the root is real, the fruit will come. Paul’s commands in this chapter are not the conditions of acceptance; they are the evidence of it. The indicative always precedes and grounds the imperative.

The chapter also gives the church its most searching doctrine of common life. The body of Christ is not a collection of private spiritual journeys happening in the same building. It is an organism, with every member genuinely joined to every other — responsible for each other’s growth, dependent on each other’s gifts, harmed by each other’s sin. Falsehood in the body is not a private failure; it is a systemic wound. Unresolved anger is not a personal problem; it is a strategic opening for the enemy. This is the doctrine of the church made viscerally practical.

And at the centre stands the renewal of the mind — the hinge on which all change turns. Not willpower, not behaviour management, but transformation at the level where thinking happens. This is the Spirit’s sovereign work, received through the ordinary means of grace: the word, prayer, honest community, and obedience to what is already known. The Christian does not renew themselves. But they can position themselves daily in the hands of the One who does. cf. Rom. 12:1–2; 2 Cor. 3:18; Phil. 2:12–13.
4.examples:
Then: The Ephesian believers had come out of a culture saturated with the very patterns Paul describes in vv. 17–19 — a world of mystery religions, sexual licence, and moral relativism where the only sin was public embarrassment. To be told to “put off” this was not a minor adjustment; it was a complete reorientation of identity. And the alternative Paul offered — speaking truth, controlling anger, working honestly, forgiving freely — would have looked countercultural to the point of strangeness. The church in Ephesus was being asked to be a visible sign that a different humanity was possible.

Now: The culture has changed; the pressure has not. The same patterns Paul named are alive and well: the mind drifting, the conscience growing quieter, the appetite demanding more. The same temptations assault the same pressure points: to manage rather than truth-tell, to nurse grievance rather than forgive, to speak what entertains rather than what builds. And the same command stands: no longer walk as those who do not know God. Not because you must earn your standing — that is secured in Christ — but because you have been made new, and new creatures do not live in the old way.

You, reading this chapter on a Monday morning, can take one thing to work: the person sitting across from you is either a fellow member of the body or a neighbour made in God’s image. Either way, what you say matters, what you do with your anger matters, how you handle the truth matters. The renewal of the mind is not a mystical event. It is what happens when the Christian opens the Bible instead of the phone, prays instead of broods, speaks the honest word instead of the comfortable one — and does it again tomorrow. This is how the body builds itself up in love.
4.overview:
With chapter 4 Ephesians turns from what God has done (chapters 1–3) to how his people must live (chapters 4–6). The first call is to walk worthy of their calling, in humility, gentleness and patient love, keeping the unity the Spirit has created, for there is one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism and one God and Father of all. Within that unity, the ascended Christ has given gifts to each believer, and has given the church apostles, prophets, evangelists and shepherd-teachers to equip all God’s people for ministry, until the whole body reaches maturity, no longer tossed about by false teaching, but speaking the truth in love and growing up into Christ the head.

Then Paul describes the new life. Believers must no longer live like the Gentiles, darkened in understanding and hardened in heart, given over to impurity. That is not how they learned Christ. They have been taught to put off the old self, be renewed in mind, and put on the new self, created to be like God in righteousness and holiness. The chapter ends with practical examples: truthfulness, anger without sin, honest work that enables giving, speech that builds up, and the kindness and forgiveness that mirror God’s forgiveness in Christ, so as not to grieve the Holy Spirit.

5.title: Walking in Love and the Mystery of Marriage
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. <sup>2</sup>And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. <sup>3</sup>But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints. <sup>4</sup>Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving. <sup>5</sup>For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. <sup>6</sup>Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. <sup>7</sup>Therefore do not become partners with them; <sup>8</sup>for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light <sup>9</sup>(for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), <sup>10</sup>and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord. <sup>11</sup>Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. <sup>12</sup>For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret. <sup>13</sup>But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, <sup>14</sup>for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” <sup>15</sup>Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, <sup>16</sup>making the best use of the time, because the days are evil. <sup>17</sup>Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. <sup>18</sup>And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, <sup>19</sup>addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, <sup>20</sup>giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, <sup>21</sup>submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. <sup>22</sup>Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord. <sup>23</sup>For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. <sup>24</sup>Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands. <sup>25</sup>Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, <sup>26</sup>that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, <sup>27</sup>so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish. <sup>28</sup>In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies.
