verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As God’s dearly loved children, they must imitate him and live a life of love, following Christ, who loved us and gave himself as a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. Among God’s holy people there must be not even a hint of sexual immorality, impurity or greed, nor obscenity, foolish talk or coarse joking, which are out of place; instead there should be thanksgiving. No immoral, impure or greedy person, which is idolatry, has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. They must not be deceived by empty words, for these things bring God’s wrath on the disobedient, so they must not share in them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Cruciform Love as the Pattern of the Christian Life

“A fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (v.2) — Paul's description of Christ's self-giving at the cross is drawn directly from the Old Testament sacrificial language. The burnt offering was described as “a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (Leviticus 1:9; 8:21) — a sacrifice that God receives with satisfaction, that expresses the proper worship of creature before Creator. Paul applies this language to the cross: the death of Christ was the ultimate sacrifice, the perfect offering, the worship that satisfied the holiness of God and secured the salvation of his people.

The implication for ethics is profound: to walk in love in imitation of Christ is to participate in a form of worship. Every act of genuine, self-giving love — every moment of costly service, every forgiveness extended at personal cost, every preference of another's need over one's own comfort — is offered to God as a fragrant offering. The Christian life is not divided into sacred acts (prayer, church attendance) and secular acts (daily life, work, relationships). All of it is worship. The love that looks like Calvary, lived out in the ordinary texture of daily life, is received by God as the aroma of Christ himself.

Covetousness is identified in v.5 as idolatry — a striking identification that requires reflection. Covetousness is not merely wanting what others have; it is the orientation of the heart toward things rather than toward God, treating the creature as the source of satisfaction rather than the Creator. In this sense it is the root of sexual immorality as well: the sexualised culture is a culture of covetousness, of insatiable appetite, of treating persons as objects to be consumed. The gospel addresses this at the root by offering the only love that actually satisfies — the love of God in Christ, which surpasses knowledge and fills us with all the fullness of God (3:19).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Be imitators of God” — in the Greco-Roman world, this language had a specific resonance. The philosophical schools spoke of likeness to God as the goal of the spiritual life. But the path they offered was typically ascetic withdrawal, esoteric knowledge, ritual elevation. Paul offers a radically different path: imitate the God who descended, who gave himself up, who went to the cross for his enemies. The divine pattern to be imitated is not the god on the Olympian heights, remote and powerful, but the God who came down in love and poured himself out in death. The imitation called for is not upward escape but downward love.

Now: Sexual immorality has been rebranded in our age as liberation, as authentic self-expression, as the natural pursuit of desire. Covetousness is marketed as aspiration, ambition, the engine of economic progress. Paul's gospel cuts through all of it — not with a longer list of prohibitions, but with a higher vision. You are a beloved child of the God who gave his Son for you. You have been loved with a love that went to the cross. Now walk in that love: freely, lavishly, cruciformly, without counting the cost. This is not the moralism of a killjoy god; it is the invitation of a Father who wants his children to look like him and to know the joy of doing so.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God has forgiven them in Christ, believers are to copy their Father, the way loved children naturally copy the parent they love.

Therefore. The verse continues 4:32: “forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.” The chapter division hides the link. What God has done (forgiven us) becomes the pattern for what we do.

Imitators. Greek mimētai, from which we get “mimic”. The only place in the New Testament where we are told to imitate God directly (compare Matthew 5:48). How can creatures imitate God? Not in his power or knowledge, but in his character as he has shown it: his kindness, mercy, forgiveness and holiness.

As beloved children. Children copy their parents without being told: the way they speak, laugh and treat people. The motive matters. We do not imitate God in order to become his children or to win his love. We imitate him because we already are his children, adopted and loved (1:5). Love received becomes love reproduced.

The whole chapter. Paul goes on to describe this family likeness with one picture, “walk”: a way of life, step by step. Walk in love (v. 2), walk as children of light (v. 8), walk wisely (v. 15).

What it does not mean. Not that we can become divine, or earn our place by copying well. It is the family likeness of those already in the family.

In a sentence. You are God’s loved child; let your life look like your Father’s.

On a Tuesday. How would your Father treat the people you will meet today? Treat them that way.

verseByVerse.quote: And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The way God’s children imitate him is by love, and the measure of that love is Christ, who gave himself up for us as a sacrifice that delighted God.

Walk in love. “Walk” is Paul’s word for the whole of daily life. Love is not an occasional feeling but the direction of every step: words, decisions, money, time.

As Christ loved us. Not love as the world defines it (warm feelings, or giving people what they want), but love as Christ showed it. The word is agapē: love that chooses the other’s good at cost to itself.

Gave himself up for us. Christ did not only give things or time; he gave himself, to death, in our place (Galatians 2:20). That is the shape of Christian love: self-giving for another’s good, even when they do not deserve it.

A fragrant offering and sacrifice. Old Testament language. When an offering was burned, Scripture says it rose as “a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (Leviticus 1:9; Genesis 8:21): God accepted it with delight. Christ’s death was the sacrifice all those offerings pointed to, and the Father was fully pleased with it. Our sin was truly dealt with.

Why this matters for love. Our self-giving love for others, imperfect as it is, becomes in Christ a sacrifice pleasing to God too (Philippians 4:18).

What it does not mean. Not that love has no limits or must tolerate sin. Christ’s love aims at our holiness (v. 27). Love seeks the other’s true good, which sometimes means saying no.

In a sentence. Love people the way Christ loved you: by giving yourself for their good.

For worship. Thank Christ who gave himself up for you.
verseByVerse.note: A “fragrant offering” recalls the Old Testament sacrifices that pleased God.

verseByVerse.quote: But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sexual sin, every kind of moral uncleanness, and greed are so contrary to God’s holy people that there should not even be a hint of them among believers.

But. The contrast with v. 2. Love gives itself for another; these sins take from others for oneself. They are love’s counterfeits.

The setting. In first-century Ephesus sex outside marriage was widely accepted for men: with slaves, prostitutes and at pagan festivals. Christian sexual ethics were startlingly different.

Sexual immorality. Greek porneia: every sexual act outside marriage between a man and a woman, including adultery, sex before marriage, prostitution and homosexual acts.

All impurity. Greek akatharsia, uncleanness. A wider word: the moral filth of which sexual sin is one part. It covers impure thoughts, words, images and desires as well as acts (Matthew 5:28). “All” closes the loopholes: what never reaches the bed still defiles the heart.

Covetousness. Greek pleonexia, literally “wanting more”: the restless craving to have more than God has given, often at someone else’s expense. Why does Paul put greed beside sexual sin? Both are appetite out of control. Both treat people and things as ours to grab. And greed is the sin respectable people commit and rarely confess, which is why Paul names it so bluntly.

Must not even be named among you. Not that the words can never be said (Paul says them here), but that such things should never be associated with Christians: no reputation for them, no trace.

As is proper among saints. “Saints” means holy ones, people set apart for God. Every believer is one already (1:1). Paul does not say “become holy to be saints”; he says “you are saints, so live in the way that fits.”

What it does not mean. Not that owning, earning or saving is wrong. Working hard, planning ahead, providing for your family and managing money well are good stewardship (Proverbs 6:6–8; 1 Timothy 5:8). The line is crossed when getting more becomes what you trust, love and live for, when contentment disappears, or when you gain at others’ expense (1 Timothy 6:6–10, 17–19). A steward holds things for God and others; a covetous person holds them for himself. Likewise, desire for marriage and sex within it is good (1 Corinthians 7:2–5); impurity is desire outside God’s bounds.

What it does not mean: temptation is not the same as sin. Paul condemns sexual sin, not the experience of being tempted. The difference matters greatly, both to keep us from excusing sin and to keep tender consciences from despair.

Jesus was tempted. He “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). Being tempted, even strongly and repeatedly, cannot in itself be sin, or Christ would have sinned.

How temptation becomes sin. James traces the steps: “each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin” (James 1:14–15). A thought or image arrives, an attraction is felt: that is temptation. Sin is conceived when the heart says yes: when we welcome it, dwell on it, feed it, replay it, fantasise about it, or act on it. Jesus’ words about lust describe exactly this: looking at someone “with lustful intent” (Matthew 5:28), the look that keeps looking in order to desire. Luther put it plainly: you cannot stop the birds flying over your head, but you can stop them building a nest in your hair.

Where Christians differ: are the desires themselves sinful? Roman Catholic teaching holds that the inclination to sin left in us (concupiscence) is not itself sin until we consent. Reformed theology holds that the corruption remaining in believers, and its first stirrings, are truly sinful and need Christ’s forgiveness, though they are not deliberate acts (Westminster Confession 6.5; Romans 7:17–23). Verdict: the Reformed view is more faithful to Romans 7: our fallen desires are not neutral, and we never treat them as harmless. But three things must be kept distinct. First, temptation from outside, which Jesus himself faced, is no sin at all. Second, fallen desires that rise in us unbidden are the remnant of sin we fight, grieve over and bring to Christ, and for those in him there is “no condemnation” (Romans 8:1). Third, consenting to them, entertaining them or acting on them is sin committed, which needs repentance.

What this means in practice. A believer who feels sexual attraction to someone not his spouse, or who struggles with unwanted desires of any kind, including same-sex attraction, is not by that fact one of the “impure” Paul describes in v. 5. He is a soldier in a fight. The question is not “Did a tempting thought come?” but “What did I do with it?” Turn away at once (“flee youthful passions”, 2 Timothy 2:22), turn the mind to something good (Philippians 4:8), pray, tell a trusted believer, and remove what feeds the desire (Romans 13:14). God promises that with every temptation “he will also provide the way of escape” (1 Corinthians 10:13). And if you fall, do not hide: confess quickly and receive his forgiveness (1 John 1:9).

The other danger. Some excuse sin by calling it “just temptation” while they keep feeding it. Others drown in guilt for temptations they did not choose. The first needs repentance; the second needs the comfort of Christ, who was tempted as we are and helps those who are tempted (Hebrews 2:18).

In a sentence. God’s holy people are known by self-giving love, not by sexual sin or grasping greed.

verseByVerse.quote: Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The way Christians talk must fit their holiness too: no obscene talk, empty silliness or clever innuendo, but thanksgiving instead.

From deeds to words. Paul moves from what we do (v. 3) to what we say. Speech shows the heart (Luke 6:45) and also shapes it: what we joke about, we begin to take lightly.

Filthiness. Shameful, obscene talk.

Foolish talk. Greek mōrologia, literally “moron-talk”: empty, senseless speech, especially the kind that drifts into the indecent.

Crude joking. Greek eutrapelia. Greek writers used it of quick wit, a social skill admired at dinner parties. Paul means wit that turns to double meanings and innuendo, making sexual sin funny and normal.

Out of place. It does not fit who you are, like wearing muddy boots at a wedding.

Thanksgiving instead. The surprising cure. Why thanks, not simply “clean talk”? Crude humour cheapens God’s good gifts, especially sex, by mocking them. Thanksgiving honours the same gifts by receiving them gratefully in their proper place. The thankful heart does not need dirty jokes, because it enjoys God’s gifts as gifts.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must be humourless. Scripture is full of wit and joy (Proverbs 17:22). The target is humour that degrades.

In a sentence. Let your mouth be full of thanks, not filth.

On a Tuesday. When office banter turns crude, you do not need to preach; you do need not to join in. Look for the chance to be the grateful one.

verseByVerse.quote: For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul gives the solemn reason: people whose lives are ruled by sexual sin, uncleanness or greed have no share in the kingdom of Christ and God.

For you may be sure. Literally “knowing, know this”: emphatic. This is settled truth, not opinion.

Sexually immoral, impure, covetous. The same three as v. 3, now describing people whose lives are characterised by them.

Covetous, that is, an idolater. Why is greed idolatry? An idol is anything we trust, love and serve in God’s place. The greedy person looks to money and possessions for security, identity and joy: the things only God can give. He serves a different god (Matthew 6:24; Colossians 3:5). In a city full of idol temples, Paul says the most common idol is not in a temple but in a wallet.

No inheritance. An inheritance is what children receive from their father. God’s children inherit his kingdom (1:14, 18). Those who live as slaves to these things show that they are not his children, and so they receive nothing.

The kingdom of Christ and God. One kingdom, shared by the Son and the Father: God’s rule, now and in the new creation.

What it does not mean. Not that any believer who has ever sinned this way is lost. To the Corinthians Paul writes, “such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11). Nor that a Christian who stumbles has lost salvation. It means that a settled, unrepentant life given over to these sins marks a person as outside the kingdom, whatever they profess.

In a sentence. What rules your life shows which kingdom you belong to.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be fooled by people who say these sins do not matter: they are the very reason God’s wrath falls on those who disobey him.

Let no one deceive you. Some in and around the church taught that the body did not matter, or that grace made sin harmless. Every age has its voices saying, “God doesn’t care what you do with your body or your money.”

Empty words. Words with nothing true inside them: they sound kind but cannot deliver what they promise.

The wrath of God. Not a temper tantrum, but God’s settled, holy opposition to evil. A God who loves people cannot be indifferent to what destroys them. It is shown now (Romans 1:18) and will come in full at the judgment (Colossians 3:6).

Comes upon. Present tense: it is already falling, and will fall finally.

Sons of disobedience. A Hebrew way of saying people whose character is disobedience, as Paul described all of us before Christ (2:2–3).

What it does not mean. Not that believers should fear God’s wrath as their sentence. Christ has borne it for those who trust him (Romans 5:9). But they must not take lightly what God judges.

In a sentence. God takes these sins seriously; do not let anyone talk you into taking them lightly.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not become partners with them;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore do not become partners with them;

Setting and background. Paul has just warned that sexual immorality, impurity and covetousness bring the wrath of God on the sons of disobedience (v. 6). Converts in Ephesus lived among friends, family and guild members who still practised these things as normal parts of city life, in temple feasts, trade gatherings and private homes.

Therefore. Key words. “Therefore” (oun). Because these things bring God’s wrath (v. 6), believers must not take part in them.

Do not become partners with them. Key words. “Partners” (symmetochoi, co-sharers, joint participants). The same word Paul used in 3:6 for Gentiles who are now fellow partakers of the promise in Christ. You share in Christ’s promise; do not share in the world’s sin. “Become” (ginesthe, present tense): do not drift into becoming partners. Compromise usually happens gradually.

What it does not mean. It does not mean withdrawal from unbelievers. Paul says Christians must still live among the immoral and greedy of the world, or they would need to leave the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–10). Friendship, kindness and ordinary life with unbelieving neighbours are right; sharing in their sin is not.

In a sentence. So do not join in with people who live like that, or share in what they do.

On a Tuesday. You can sit with colleagues at lunch without sharing their gossip, their dishonesty or their jokes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Once they were darkness, but now they are light in the Lord, so they must live as children of light, whose fruit is all goodness, righteousness and truth, and find out what pleases the Lord. They must have nothing to do with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but expose them; it is shameful even to mention what the disobedient do in secret. Everything exposed by the light becomes visible, and so the call goes out: sleeper, wake up, rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.
verseByVerse.theology:
Light, Darkness, and the Prophetic Witness of Holiness

The ontological language of this passage — “you were darkness,” “you are light” — reflects the radical nature of regeneration. The new birth is not a moral improvement programme; it is a change of nature. What was dark has become light. What was oriented toward self and sin has been reoriented toward God and holiness. This is the consistent teaching of the Reformed tradition: regeneration is sovereign, total, and irreversible — a work of God in the interior of the person that creates a new appetite, a new orientation, a new capacity for the things of God.

The call to “take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them” (v.11) raises the question of the church's relationship to culture. The Reformed tradition has generally resisted both the temptation to total withdrawal (a pietism that disengages from the world) and the temptation to total accommodation (a liberalism that conforms to it). The middle path — engagement without assimilation, presence without compromise — is what it means to be light in the world. The church that is genuinely, visibly holy is not only doing something good for its own members; it is doing something necessary for the world, exposing by contrast what the world cannot see about itself.

The awakening hymn of v.14 — “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you” — is widely thought to be an early Christian baptismal hymn. It captures the eschatological urgency of the whole passage: the world is asleep, the darkness is presenting itself as normal and comfortable, and the church is called to be the community of the awakened, the risen, the enlightened. Not by shouting but by shining.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The darkness Paul describes in v.12 — “the things they do in secret” — was not merely a moral category. Ephesus had a fully developed underground of occult practice, of ritual darkness, of things done in the night that could not bear the daylight. The mystery religions operated precisely in the realm of secrets, of hidden things, of initiation into darkness. The church's commitment to transparency — to lives that could be lived fully in the open before God — was itself a form of witness against the culture of secrecy. You have nothing to hide because you have nothing to fear. You live in the light because Christ has shone on you.

Now: “Awake, O sleeper” has the ring of an alarm clock going off in a dark room. The world is sleeping — comfortable in its darkness, unaware of its danger, presenting its way of life as simply the normal and natural way to live. The church is called to wake up and to be awake — to see the world as it really is in the light of God's word, to live accordingly, and thereby to be the kind of community whose quality of life is itself an invitation: come and see what happens when Christ shines on you. In a culture that is drowsy with distraction and numbed by comfort, the church's wakefulness is among its most urgent callings.

verseByVerse.quote: for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers once were darkness itself, but in Christ they have become light, so they must live as what they now are.

At one time you were darkness. Not just “in the dark” but darkness itself. Darkness in Scripture means ignorance of God, sin and death. Before Christ, it was not only around us; it was our nature.

But now you are light. Not “you are in the light” or “you have some light”. You are light. Conversion is not a small improvement but a change of nature: from darkness to light, from death to life (2:1–5).

In the Lord. Not in ourselves. We are light as the moon is: shining with light received from Christ, the light of the world (John 8:12; Matthew 5:14).

Walk as children of light. Again the pattern: become what you are. A “child of” something in Hebrew idiom means someone marked by it. Live like people who belong to the light.

What it does not mean. Not that believers are sinless. The command to walk as light shows that we still need to grow into what God has made us.

In a sentence. You are no longer darkness; stop living as if you were.

verseByVerse.quote: (for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Light naturally produces goodness, righteousness and truth, and those who walk in it keep testing what pleases the Lord.

The fruit of light. Fruit grows; it is not manufactured. A life in Christ’s light naturally bears these things. Textual note. Later manuscripts read “fruit of the Spirit” (KJV), from Galatians 5:22. Verdict: “fruit of light” is original.

Good, right, true. Three sides of the light’s fruit. Goodness: generous kindness towards others. Righteousness: doing what is right before God and people. Truth: honesty and integrity, in contrast to the “empty words” of v. 6.

Try to discern. Greek dokimazō: test and approve, as a metalworker tests gold. The Christian life is not only following a list. It means thinking carefully, with Scripture, about what will please the Lord in each situation (Romans 12:2).

What is pleasing to the Lord. The goal is not “What can I get away with?” but “What would delight him?”

In a sentence. Light produces goodness, right living and honesty, and asks in every situation what will please Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must have nothing to do with the barren deeds of darkness, and instead must expose them for what they are.

Unfruitful works of darkness. Light bears fruit (v. 9); darkness produces only barren works. Sin promises much and gives nothing that lasts (Galatians 6:8).

Take no part. The same word root as “partners” in v. 7: do not be co-sharers.

Expose them. Greek elenchō: to bring into the open, convict, show something for what it is. This happens first by the contrast of a holy life, which shows darkness up simply by being different, and second, where right, by loving words (Matthew 18:15).

Shameful even to speak of. Some things done in secret are so degrading that dwelling on the details is itself corrupting. Exposing sin does not mean describing it with relish.

What it does not mean. Not a licence to police unbelievers, spread gossip or shame people publicly. The aim of exposing is repentance and healing, not humiliation (v. 13).

In a sentence. Do not join the darkness; let your life and your words show it for what it is.

verseByVerse.quote: But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, 'Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When light shines on darkness, it not only reveals but transforms, and so the gospel calls sleepers to wake up, rise from death, and let Christ shine on them.

Exposed by the light, it becomes visible. When sin is brought into God’s light, it is seen for what it is.

Anything that becomes visible is light. A difficult phrase. Its likely meaning: what is exposed and confessed does not stay darkness; it is changed into light. When a person’s sin is brought into the light and they repent, they themselves become light (1 John 1:7–9). Exposure is not the end but the door to conversion. That is why believers expose darkness: to see others rescued.

Therefore it says. Not an Old Testament quotation, but probably an early Christian hymn, perhaps sung at baptism, echoing Isaiah 26:19 and 60:1.

Awake, O sleeper. Sleep pictures a life unaware of God and of danger. Arise from the dead. More than sleep: spiritual death (2:1). Only God can raise the dead, which is why the call carries power.

Christ will shine on you. Like the sun rising on someone waking. The light that exposes is also the light that warms and gives life.

In a sentence. The light that shows sin up is the same light that heals: wake up and let Christ shine on you.

For worship. Pray for someone asleep in sin, that Christ will shine on them.
verseByVerse.note: These lines are not found in the Old Testament; they may come from an early Christian hymn, echoing Isaiah.

parallels.desc: awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust
arise, shine, for your light has come

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They must be very careful how they live, not as unwise but as wise, making the most of every opportunity, because the days are evil. They must not be foolish but understand the Lord’s will. Instead of getting drunk on wine, which leads to ruin, they must be filled with the Spirit: speaking to one another with psalms, hymns and songs from the Spirit, singing and making music from the heart to the Lord, always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fullness of the Spirit and the Worshipping Community

“Be filled with the Spirit” (v.18) is a present passive imperative — go on being filled, continuously, repeatedly. The fullness of the Spirit is not a one-time crisis experience; it is the ongoing reality of a life open to and dependent on God's Spirit. The passive voice is significant: we do not fill ourselves; we are filled. We create the conditions — prayer, the word, corporate worship, obedience — and God does the filling. The Spirit is given to those who ask (Luke 11:13), and the asking is to be persistent, humble, and expectant.

The triad of “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (v.19) has been the subject of considerable historical discussion about the nature of Christian worship. What matters more than the categorisation is the character: the worship is corporate, directed toward God, spirit-animated, joyful, and overflowing into the rest of life. Worship is not an event on Sunday that is unrelated to life on Monday; it is the expression of a fullness that shapes everything the Spirit-filled person does.

The closing imperative — “submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ” (v.21) — is the theological hinge on which everything that follows turns. Paul will apply mutual submission to wives and husbands, children and fathers, servants and masters. But the foundation is the mutual submission of the Spirit-filled community: a posture of other-centredness, of preferring one another, of deferring in love to the needs and preferences of those around us. This is the overflow of a life that has been filled with the Spirit of the One who “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6–7).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Several of the cults of Ephesus, above all that of Dionysus, were soaked in wine, in ecstatic states, in the pursuit of transcendence through altered consciousness. The Dionysian festivals were characterized by drunkenness and sexual abandon as means of communing with the divine. Against this entire religious culture, Paul offers the Spirit-filled community as the true alternative: not the dissipation of Dionysus but the fullness of the Holy Spirit, not the frantic ecstasy of the cult but the joyful, ordered, outward-facing overflow of a community that has been possessed not by wine but by God. The church was, in Ephesus, a genuinely countercultural gathering — a community whose worship looked and sounded like nothing else in the city.

Now: We live in an age of spiritual hunger and an age of extraordinary means for filling the void — entertainment, substance, distraction, the endless dopamine of the digital feed. None of it satisfies. The hunger returns, more insistent than before. Paul's word to a hungry generation is unchanged: be filled with the Spirit. The fullness he gives is not the temporary satiation of appetite but the genuine, overflowing, outward-directed joy of a life in which God himself has taken up residence. The church that is genuinely, visibly, joyfully full of the Spirit — that sings with gratitude, that submits in love, that gives thanks for everything — is offering the watching world a glimpse of what it was made for.

verseByVerse.quote: Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Living as light requires care and wisdom: watch how you live, and make the most of every opportunity, because the times are evil.

Look carefully then how you walk. Literally “see accurately how you walk”: like someone picking their way along a narrow path. Christian living is not careless.

Unwise and wise. In Scripture wisdom is not cleverness but skill in living God’s way, rooted in the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 9:10). The unwise are not necessarily ignorant; they simply drift with whatever the culture does.

Making the best use of the time. Literally “buying up the time”, like a merchant seizing a bargain. The word for time is kairos: opportunity, the right moment. Every day brings opportunities to do good, to speak of Christ, to love, which will not come back (Colossians 4:5).

Because the days are evil. The present age is under the influence of evil (2:2; 6:12). Time is short, and the pull of the world is strong. Drift is the default; wisdom requires intention.

What it does not mean. Not frantic busyness or guilt about rest. Jesus rested and withdrew. It means purposeful living, not wasting life.

In a sentence. Live on purpose, seizing the opportunities God gives, because evil days will not wait.

On a Tuesday. Look at your week: what is getting your best time and energy?

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So do not live thoughtlessly, but understand what the Lord wants.

Foolish. Greek aphrōn: senseless, without understanding. Not low intelligence, but living without thinking about God.

Understand. Grasp it, put it together. Christian obedience uses the mind.

The will of the Lord. Christians often worry about God’s hidden will for decisions such as jobs or marriage. Paul means mainly his revealed will in Scripture: holiness, thanksgiving, love (1 Thessalonians 4:3; 5:18). Know that, and the rest becomes much clearer.

What it does not mean. Not that God has hidden secret instructions you must decode. Within his revealed will, you have freedom to make wise choices.

In a sentence. Know what God has said he wants, and live by it.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead of letting wine take control, believers must keep being filled with the Spirit, so that he governs their lives.

The setting. Drinking was central to Greek social life, and at the festivals of Dionysus, god of wine, drunkenness was thought to bring people close to the divine. Paul says the true way to be filled with God is not wine but the Spirit.

Do not get drunk. Scripture consistently warns against drunkenness (Proverbs 23:29–35).

Debauchery. Greek asōtia: a life out of control, wasting itself. The word used of the prodigal son’s “reckless living” (Luke 15:13).

But be filled with the Spirit. Why compare wine and the Spirit? Both can fill a person and influence how they speak and act. Wine takes away self-control and leads to waste. The Spirit gives self-control (Galatians 5:23) and leads to praise, thanks and humble service (vv. 19–21).

Be filled. A present, continuous command: keep on being filled. Not a single experience but an ongoing life under the Spirit’s influence. And it is passive: you do not fill yourself; you yield to him.

Where Christians differ. Some Pentecostal teaching links filling with a second blessing after conversion, marked by tongues. Reformed theology holds that every believer is indwelt and sealed by the Spirit from conversion (1:13), and is called to be continually filled, that is, governed by him. Colossians 3:16 makes the parallel: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly”, followed by the same singing and thanks. Verdict: filling is the ongoing life of a Spirit-governed believer, nourished by the word and shown in the fruits that follow (vv. 19–21).

What it does not mean. Not a ban on wine, which Scripture treats as God’s gift (Psalm 104:15; John 2). The sin is being controlled by it.

In a sentence. Do not let anything but God’s Spirit control you, and let him shape everything.

verseByVerse.quote: addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Spirit-filled church sings God’s praise together, from the heart, and thanks God the Father for everything in Jesus’ name.

The first sign of the Spirit’s filling. Not spectacular experiences, but singing, thanksgiving and submission (vv. 19–21). In Greek these are all participles flowing from “be filled”: they are what Spirit-filling looks like.

Addressing one another. Singing is not only to God but to each other: teaching, encouraging and reminding one another of truth (Colossians 3:16).

Psalms, hymns and spiritual songs. Probably the psalms of the Old Testament, hymns of praise to God and Christ, and other songs prompted by the Spirit. Where Christians differ. Some Reformed churches sing only the biblical Psalms (exclusive psalmody), reading all three words as kinds of psalm. Most churches sing psalms alongside Christian hymns. Verdict: the psalms deserve a far larger place in our worship, but Scripture-filled hymns are also fitting (compare the songs of Revelation 5:9–10).

With your heart. From the inside, not just with the lips (Matthew 15:8).

Always and for everything. Not thanking God for evil itself, but giving thanks in every situation, because he rules over all things and works them for his children’s good (Romans 8:28; 1 Thessalonians 5:18).

To God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Trinity in worship: by the Spirit, through the Son, to the Father. We come in Jesus’ name because we come only through him.

In a sentence. Spirit-filled people sing God’s truth to one another and thank him for everything.

verseByVerse.quote: submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spirit-filled people humbly put others before themselves out of reverence for Christ, the principle behind the instructions to wives, husbands, children and servants that follow.

The hinge. Verse 21 completes the description of Spirit-filling and introduces the household sections (5:22–6:9). In Greek, v. 22 borrows its verb from v. 21.

Submit. Greek hypotassō: to arrange yourself under another, putting their good and their rightful leadership before your own way. It is chosen, not forced; no one is told to make others submit.

To one another. Every believer is called to humble, other-centred service. Pride, the demand for my rights, is the opposite of the Spirit’s work.

Where Christians differ. Egalitarians read “submitting to one another” as mutual submission that removes any distinct roles in marriage. Complementarians note that the following verses specify who submits to whom (wives to husbands, children to parents, servants to masters), and that the word means to arrange oneself under an authority. Verdict: the app’s complementarian view: all believers serve one another in humility, and within that God has given a particular order in marriage and family.

Out of reverence for Christ. Literally “in the fear of Christ”. The motive is not fear of people or social convention, but awe and love towards Christ, whom we serve by serving others.

In a sentence. Because you revere Christ, put others before yourself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wives should submit to their own husbands as to the Lord, for the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is head of the church, his body, of which he is the Saviour; as the church submits to Christ, so wives should to their husbands in everything. Husbands must love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself for her, to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, and to present her to himself radiant, without stain or wrinkle, holy and blameless. Husbands should love their wives as their own bodies; whoever loves his wife loves himself, for no one hates his own body but feeds and cares for it, as Christ does the church, for we are members of his body. That is why a man leaves his parents and is united to his wife, and the two become one flesh. This is a profound mystery about Christ and the church. But each husband must love his wife as himself, and the wife must respect her husband.
verseByVerse.theology:
Marriage, Headship, and the Gospel Mystery

Ephesians 5:22–33 is the most theologically freighted passage on marriage in all of Scripture. Its central claim — that marriage is a living image of the relationship between Christ and the church — elevates the institution beyond any merely human social arrangement. Marriage is a sign. Its structure (the husband's headship, the wife's willing embrace of it) is not arbitrary or culturally conditioned; it images something real and eternal: the self-giving authority of Christ over his church, and the church's joyful, trusting response to her Lord.

The husband's headship is defined entirely by the cross: “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (v.25). Any interpretation of headship that does not immediately move to sacrifice and self-giving has misread the passage. The head of the church is the one who died for it, who washed it, who nourishes and cherishes it (v.29). The husband who exercises headship in this mode is not dominating but descending — following the pattern of the One who “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28).

The wife's calling — to “submit to your own husband, as to the Lord” (v.22) — is the free, willing, graced response of a woman who is secure in Christ. It is not coerced compliance; it is the image of the church's joyful response to her loving Lord. This mutual imaging of the gospel — husband as Christ, wife as church — requires both partners to draw from wells deeper than themselves. No man can love his wife as Christ loved the church from his own resources; no woman can embody the church's response to Christ on her own. Both require the same Spirit who filled the community in v.18. Marriage is a Spirit-dependent vocation for both.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In the Greco-Roman world, the husband's authority over his wife was nearly absolute and assumed to be primarily for his benefit. The paterfamilias was the household's lord in every sense. Paul's command for husbands to love their wives sacrificially — to give themselves up for them, to nourish and cherish them as their own bodies — was not a reinforcement of existing cultural norms. It was their radical subversion. The Roman husband used his authority to be served. The Christian husband was to use his authority to serve. This was not a minor adjustment to the household code; it was a revolution grounded in the cross.

Now: Christian marriage swims against two powerful currents simultaneously. The first is the culture's dismissal of permanent covenant — the reduction of marriage to an expressive partnership that may be dissolved when it no longer meets individual needs. The second is the sometimes shallow version of complementarianism that invokes headship without the cross, demanding submission without offering service. Against both, Ephesians 5 offers the third way: covenant love, shaped by the cross, sustained by the Spirit, oriented toward the other's flourishing, and pointing always beyond itself to the love that holds the universe together. A marriage like this is a miracle — and miracles point to a Miracle Worker.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Christian wife freely places herself under her own husband’s leadership, and does it as part of her service to the Lord.

The setting. Ancient household codes told wives, children and slaves to obey the head of the household, but addressed only him. Paul speaks first to wives directly, as responsible persons who choose freely before God.

Submit. The verb comes from v. 21: arrange yourself under, support and follow his leadership. It is the wife’s own choice, offered to Christ.

Your own husbands. Not women to men in general, but a wife to her husband, within marriage.

As to the Lord. Both the motive and the limit. The motive: her submission is ultimately service to Christ. The limit: it never extends to sin, since no husband can ask what the Lord forbids (Acts 5:29).

What it does not mean. Not inferiority: husband and wife are equal heirs of grace (1 Peter 3:7). Not silence, passivity or giving up her judgment. And never submission to abuse. Abuse breaks the covenant God intended; a wife in danger should seek safety and the church’s help, and the church must protect her.

Where Christians differ. Egalitarians see headship as a first-century cultural arrangement now set aside. Verdict: the app’s complementarian view: Paul grounds the pattern in Christ and the church, not in culture, so it holds today; it is to be lived with gladness and humility, never used as a weapon.

In a sentence. A wife honours Christ by gladly following her husband’s loving leadership.

verseByVerse.quote: For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reason: a husband’s headship is meant to mirror Christ’s headship of the church, a headship that saves and serves, and wives are to follow it as the church follows Christ.

Head. In Paul, headship combines authority and responsibility (1 Corinthians 11:3). And Paul immediately defines it by Christ.

And is himself its Saviour. Christ’s headship is shown in rescuing and caring for his body, not in exploiting it. Headship is measured by what Christ did: leading by dying for his bride.

As the church submits to Christ. Willingly, trustingly, gladly, because his leadership is good.

In everything. In every area of married life, not only selected ones.

What it does not mean. Not in sin: no husband may require what Christ forbids. Nor does it mean the wife has no voice. Godly headship listens, consults and serves. A husband who uses this verse to dominate has missed the word “Saviour”.

In a sentence. Marriage is meant to picture Christ and his church: a loving, saving head and a trusting, responsive bride.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A husband’s calling is to love his wife the way Christ loved the church: by giving himself up for her.

Husbands, love. Ancient household codes told husbands to rule their wives. None told them to love them like this. Paul gives the husband the harder command.

Love. Agapaō: self-giving love that seeks the other’s good, not a feeling that comes and goes.

As Christ loved the church. The standard is not other husbands, or what she deserves, but Christ.

Gave himself up for her. The measure is the cross. Headship means going first in sacrifice: his comfort, preferences, time and if necessary his life for her good.

For whom did Christ die? Paul says he gave himself for the church, his bride: a pointer to the particular, effective love of the atonement (Acts 20:28; John 10:11).

What it does not mean. Not that a husband gives his wife whatever she wants. Christ’s love aims at his bride’s holiness and good (v. 26).

In a sentence. A husband leads by laying down his life for his wife.

On a Tuesday. Husbands: what could you give up this week for your wife’s good?

verseByVerse.quote: that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s love has a goal: to make his bride holy and beautiful, cleansing her by his word and one day presenting her to himself in perfect glory.

That he might sanctify her. To make her holy, set apart for him. Christ’s love does not leave us as we are.

Having cleansed her. Washed from sin’s guilt and stain.

The washing of water with the word. Two backgrounds. A Jewish bride took a ritual bath before her wedding (Ezekiel 16:8–14, where God washes his bride Israel). And Christians thought of baptism. Verdict: Christ cleanses his people through the gospel word, of which baptism is the sign. The cleansing is his work, not the water’s.

Present the church to himself. In weddings the bride was presented to the groom by her friends. Christ prepares and presents his bride himself.

In splendour, without spot or wrinkle. No stain of sin, no sign of age or decay. This is the church’s future glory at Christ’s return (Revelation 19:7–8; 21:2).

Holy and without blemish. The same goal as 1:4: what God chose us for, Christ brings to completion.

For husbands. A husband’s love aims at his wife’s growth in Christ: encouraging her faith, praying with her, protecting her from harm.

In a sentence. Christ loves his church to make her beautiful, and a husband’s love aims at his wife’s flourishing in Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Before a wedding the bride was washed and adorned.

parallels.desc: I bathed you with water

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Husbands should love their wives as their own bodies, because in marriage she has become one flesh with him.

In the same way. As Christ loves the church, his body.

As their own bodies. Not as possessions, but as part of himself: husband and wife are one flesh (v. 31).

He who loves his wife loves himself. In a sense, they share one life. To harm her is to harm himself; to care for her is to care for himself.

What it does not mean. Not that self-love is the goal or should be cultivated. Paul assumes we already care for ourselves (v. 29) and turns that natural instinct outward to the wife.

In a sentence. Care for your wife as naturally as you care for your own body.

verseByVerse.quote: For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, because we are members of his body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As people naturally feed and care for their own bodies, so Christ nourishes and cherishes his church, and husbands should do the same for their wives.

No one ever hated his own flesh. In ordinary life, people feed, protect and care for their bodies without thinking about it.

Nourishes and cherishes. Nourishing is feeding, providing what is needed to grow. Cherishing (literally “keeping warm”) is tender, affectionate care, as a mother bird warms her chicks.

Just as Christ does the church. Christ feeds his people through his word and the Lord’s Supper, and warms them with his love.

Members of his body. Every believer is part of Christ’s body and so cared for by him.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “of his flesh and of his bones” (KJV), from Genesis 2:23. Verdict: probably not original.

In a sentence. Christ feeds and warms his people; husbands, do the same for your wives.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s design for marriage from creation is that a man leaves his parents, holds fast to his wife, and the two become one flesh.

Genesis 2:24. The foundational text on marriage, quoted by Jesus when asked about divorce (Matthew 19:4–6).

Leave his father and mother. A new primary loyalty. Parents are still honoured, but the marriage now comes first.

Hold fast. To cling, to be glued to: a lifelong covenant commitment.

The two shall become one flesh. A union of the whole life (home, possessions, future), expressed and sealed in sexual union.

Where Christians differ. Some churches now affirm same-sex marriage. Verdict: the historic Christian view, held with compassion: Scripture defines marriage as the union of one man and one woman, and that pattern is part of its meaning, since it pictures Christ and his church.

In a sentence. Marriage is a new, lifelong, whole-life union of a man and a woman.

parallels.desc: a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Marriage carries a profound secret: from the beginning it was designed as a picture of the union between Christ and his church.

Mystery. In Paul, not a puzzle but a truth once hidden and now revealed by God (3:3–6).

It refers to Christ and the church. Paul is saying something remarkable. God did not first invent marriage and then find it a useful illustration. He designed marriage from creation to point to the greater marriage: Christ and his people, foretold in the prophets (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:19–20) and completed at the wedding feast of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9).

Why this matters. It explains the commands. Husbands are to love like Christ, and wives to follow like the church, because their marriage is meant to display the gospel to the watching world.

Where Christians differ: a sacrament? The Latin Vulgate translated “mystery” as sacramentum, one ground on which the Roman Catholic Church counts marriage among seven sacraments. The Reformers held that marriage is a holy creation ordinance for all people, not a sacrament of grace for the church. Verdict: marriage is honourable and holy, a living parable of the gospel, but not a sacrament.

For the single. Unmarried believers are not left out. The marriage that matters most, Christ and his church, includes every believer.

In a sentence. Every Christian marriage is meant to be a small picture of Christ’s love for his church.

For worship. Every wedding preaches the gospel of Christ’s love for his bride.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

parallels.desc: your Maker is your husband

verseByVerse.quote: However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In summary, each husband must love his wife as himself, and each wife must respect her husband.

However. After the great mystery of Christ and the church, Paul comes back down to everyday marriage: whatever else, do this.

Each one of you. Personal responsibility. Each answers to God for his or her own part, not the spouse’s.

Love his wife as himself. Self-giving care, as in vv. 25–29.

Respects. Literally “fears”: reverent honour, shown in trust, gratitude and support of his leadership, in how she speaks about him as well as to him.

What it does not mean. Not terror or blind agreement. And neither duty is conditional: his love does not wait for her respect, nor her respect for his love. Each obeys Christ first.

In a sentence. Husbands, love sacrificially; wives, honour respectfully; both of you, for Christ’s sake.

On a Tuesday. Husbands, say “I love you” with a sacrifice; wives, show respect in front of others. Both of you, ask forgiveness quickly.

5.overview:
Paul continues to describe the new life. God’s beloved children must imitate their Father and walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up as a fragrant sacrifice. That rules out sexual immorality, impurity and greed, crude talk and joking, all of which exclude people from Christ’s kingdom and bring God’s wrath. Once they were darkness; now they are light in the Lord, so they must live as children of light, producing goodness, righteousness and truth, exposing the works of darkness rather than sharing in them. Wise living makes the most of the time in evil days, understands the Lord’s will, and refuses drunkenness in favour of being filled with the Spirit, which shows itself in singing, thanksgiving and mutual submission out of reverence for Christ.

The household code that follows (5:22–6:9) applies this to marriage, family and work. Wives are to submit to their own husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is head of the wife as Christ is head of the church. Husbands must love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself for her, to make her holy and present her glorious; they must love their wives as their own bodies, nourishing and cherishing them as Christ does the church. Genesis 2:24 speaks of the one flesh of marriage, and Paul reveals its deepest meaning: it is a picture of the union of Christ and the church. Each husband must love his wife, and each wife respect her husband.

6.title: Household Duties and the Armour of God
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. <sup>2</sup>“Honor your father and mother” (this is the first commandment with a promise), <sup>3</sup>“that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.” <sup>4</sup>Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. <sup>5</sup>Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ, <sup>6</sup>not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, <sup>7</sup>rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man, <sup>8</sup>knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free. <sup>9</sup>Masters, do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him. <sup>10</sup>Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. <sup>11</sup>Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. <sup>12</sup>For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. <sup>13</sup>Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm. <sup>14</sup>Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, <sup>15</sup>and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace. <sup>16</sup>In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; <sup>17</sup>and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, <sup>18</sup>praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints, <sup>19</sup>and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, <sup>20</sup>for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak. <sup>21</sup>So that you also may know how I am and what I am doing, Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord will tell you everything. <sup>22</sup>I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts. <sup>23</sup>Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>24</sup>Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Children are to obey their parents in the Lord, for this is right. Honouring father and mother is the first commandment with a promise: that it may go well with them and they may live long. Fathers must not exasperate their children, but raise them in the Lord’s training and instruction. Slaves must obey earthly masters with respect and sincerity, as they would Christ, not only to win favour when watched, but as Christ’s servants doing God’s will from the heart, serving wholeheartedly as to the Lord, knowing the Lord will reward everyone for good done, slave or free. Masters must treat their slaves the same way, without threatening, knowing that their own Master and theirs is in heaven and shows no favouritism.
verseByVerse.theology:
Authority, Service, and the Lordship of Christ

The household codes of Ephesians 5:22–6:9 have sometimes been misread as Paul's accommodation to Roman social structures — a domestication of the gospel that reinforces existing hierarchies. The opposite is true. Paul takes every relationship in the household and transforms it from within by the same double principle: both parties have obligations, and both parties are accountable to Christ. This is not the endorsement of hierarchy for its own sake; it is the sanctification of ordered relationships by the presence of a Lord who stands above every human ordering.

The instruction to servants (vv.5–8) is particularly searching. “Obey... as you would Christ,” “doing the will of God from the heart,” “rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man, knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord.” Paul is not telling slaves that their situation is just; he is telling them that no situation, however unjust, is outside the reach of Christ's transforming presence. The servant who works faithfully for an unworthy master, doing it as for the Lord, is engaged in genuine worship — and will receive the Lord's commendation at the last day, whatever commendation or condemnation the human master gave or withheld.

The warning to masters — “do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him” (v.9) — is one of the most socially radical statements in the New Testament. The master has a Master. The one with authority is under authority. Before the throne of the impartial God, all distinctions of status dissolve. This truth, fully believed and consistently applied, has done more to dismantle unjust social structures than any legal or political programme. It was ultimately the logic of this verse, applied over centuries, that made slavery in the Christian world an untenable contradiction.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Roman paterfamilias held virtually absolute authority over his household — his wife, his children, and his slaves were all, in various degrees, subject to his legal control. Children had no independent legal standing; slaves were property. Paul's household code addresses children and slaves first, and addresses them as moral agents capable of genuine obedience to God — not as objects to be managed. This is itself a dignity-claim that the Roman household code did not make. And the commands to fathers (don't exasperate) and masters (treat them justly) placed obligations on the powerful toward the powerless that Roman law did not require. The Christian household was different — visibly, consistently, counter-culturally different.

Now: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord” and “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger” — both imperatives are needed in every age, and our age tends to violate both simultaneously. We live in a culture that simultaneously refuses to discipline children (producing entitled, poorly-bounded young people) and fails to give them the patient, encouraging, Christ-centred nurture that Ephesians 6:4 envisions. The Christian home where authority is exercised in love, where children are both appropriately disciplined and genuinely encouraged in the Lord, where the name of Christ is spoken and the word of God is read — this home is a counterculture, a community of formation in a world that has largely forgotten what formation is for.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul speaks directly to the children in the congregation. Their obedience to their parents is not just good manners; it is part of following Christ, and it is simply right.

The setting. Paul is in the middle of what are called the “household codes” (5:21–6:9): instructions for wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters. Greek and Roman moralists wrote similar codes, but they spoke only to the person with power: the husband, father and master. Paul speaks first to the weaker party in each pair, as full members of the church with their own calling before God. All of it flows from being filled with the Spirit (5:18) and submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ (5:21).

Children. Children were present when the letter was read aloud in church. Paul addresses them directly, as responsible disciples, not as an afterthought. Christianity takes children seriously. The word covers children still living under their parents’ authority, not adults.

Obey. Hypakouō: literally “to listen under”: to listen and do what is said. It is stronger than the “submit” used of wives (5:22). Children are to do what their parents tell them.

Your parents. Both, father and mother. In the Roman world, the father held legal power; Paul gives the mother equal standing as one to be obeyed.

In the Lord. Two meanings. First, as an act of service to Christ: a child’s obedience to parents is obedience to the Lord (Colossians 3:20 says this pleases the Lord). Second, within the Lord’s will: this is obedience as a Christian, which sets the limit of it.

For this is right. Paul’s first reason is not a promise or a threat, but simply that it is right: rooted in the way God made the world, not just in one culture’s customs. Every society that has flourished has honoured the bond between parents and children.

What it does not mean. Not obedience in sin. “In the Lord” rules out obeying a parent who commands what God forbids; then we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Nor does it require that abused children submit to abuse: parents who abuse betray the very authority they claim, and children should be protected. Nor does it mean that grown children who have left home must obey their parents for life: marriage creates a new household (Genesis 2:24; 5:31). But honour never ends (v. 2).

In a sentence. Children, obey your parents as part of following Christ, because it is right.

On a Tuesday. Parents: read this verse with your children and explain it. Children: obeying your parents today, without grumbling, is a way to please Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Honor your father and mother (this is the first commandment with a promise), that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul supports his command with God’s law: the fifth commandment tells us to honour our father and mother, and it is the first commandment with a promise attached, a promise of blessing and long life.

Honour. More than obedience. To honour (timaō) is to treat as weighty, to respect, value and give due regard. Obedience applies to children at home; honour applies for life. For adults, honouring parents includes respect in speech, gratitude, care and, when they grow old, providing for them (1 Timothy 5:4, 8). Jesus condemned religious people who used a loophole to avoid supporting their parents (Mark 7:9–13).

Your father and mother. Paul quotes the fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16). By quoting it, he shows that the moral law of the Ten Commandments still guides Christians (see 2:15).

This is the first commandment with a promise. The second commandment includes a statement of God’s steadfast love to those who love him (Exodus 20:6), but this is the first commandment with a specific promise attached to keeping it. Some take “first” to mean “first in importance” for children. Either way, God attaches blessing to it.

That it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land. In the original, the promise was long life in the land of Canaan, the land God was giving Israel. Paul’s Greek is the Greek Old Testament, where the word can mean either “the land” or “the earth”. Applied to Christians of every nation, it becomes a general principle: a society and a family where parents are honoured tend to flourish, and God blesses those who honour him by honouring their parents.

What it does not mean. Not a guarantee that every obedient child will live a long life, or that early death proves disobedience. Like the Proverbs, it states the way God normally works, not a mechanical rule. Faithful children sometimes die young, and the promise finds its final fulfilment in eternal life. Nor does honouring parents mean pretending their faults do not exist, or accepting abuse. It is possible to honour a parent while refusing their sin, keeping safe boundaries, and still treating them with respect.

In a sentence. Honour your father and mother all your life, for God commands it and promises to bless it.

On a Tuesday. Adult children: how do you honour ageing parents? A visit, a call, practical help, patience with their slowness. Plan one act of honour this week.
