verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fathers must not use their authority to crush or exasperate their children. Instead, they must bring them up with the discipline and teaching that come from the Lord.

Fathers. Fathers are named because, in Roman law, the father (paterfamilias) had almost absolute power over his children. He could decide whether a newborn lived or was abandoned to die; he could sell them into slavery or have them punished severely, even when they were grown. Into that world Paul speaks a revolutionary word: limit your power by love. The word can also mean “parents” (Hebrews 11:23), and the principle applies to mothers too; but fathers bear particular responsibility for the spiritual leadership of the home.

Do not provoke your children to anger. Do not exasperate them, drive them to resentment or despair. Colossians 3:21 adds the reason: lest they become discouraged. How fathers provoke: harshness and constant criticism, favouritism, mockery and humiliation, inconsistency (punishing one day what was ignored the next), rules without reasons, hypocrisy (demanding what they do not do), unrealistic expectations, neglect and absence, and refusal to admit their own wrong.

But bring them up. The word (ektrephō) means to nourish, to rear, to feed (it is used in 5:29 of nourishing one’s own body). Fathers are to nurture their children, with warmth and tender care, as a gardener tends a plant.

In the discipline. Paideia: training, including correction. It is the word used of God disciplining his children in love (Hebrews 12:5–11). Discipline means teaching by action: setting boundaries, correcting wrong, giving consequences, and praising what is right.

And instruction. Nouthesia: literally “putting in mind”: teaching by word, warning and explaining. Children need not only rules but reasons, and not only correction but understanding.

Of the Lord. This is the goal: not only well-behaved children, but children who know the Lord. The discipline and instruction come from him, follow his ways, and point to him. Israel’s fathers were commanded to talk of God’s words when they sat at home, walked by the way, lay down and rose up (Deuteronomy 6:6–7).

What it does not mean. Not a ban on firm discipline or on telling children “no”: lack of discipline is itself a failure of love (Proverbs 13:24; Hebrews 12:7–11). What is forbidden is discipline that is angry, humiliating, arbitrary or cruel. Nor does “of the Lord” mean that fathers can make their children Christians: only God gives new life (2:1–5). Fathers sow and water; God gives growth. And the verse does not mean that children’s faith or failures are entirely the parents’ fault: children are responsible persons too (Ezekiel 18:20).

In a sentence. Fathers, do not exasperate your children, but nurture them with the Lord’s correction and teaching.

On a Tuesday. Fathers: read the Bible and pray with your children this week. And if you have been harsh or unfair, apologise to them. It will teach them more about the gospel than many lessons.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul speaks to Christian slaves: they are to obey their earthly masters with serious care and an undivided heart, as if they were serving Christ himself.

Bondservants. Douloi: slaves. Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world; perhaps a third of the population of a city like Ephesus were slaves. Many of the first Christians were slaves (1 Corinthians 1:26; 7:21), and some were masters. Roman slavery was not based on race. People became slaves through war, debt, crime or birth. Some were household servants, teachers, doctors or managers; others laboured in mines and fields in terrible conditions. A slave was legally property, without rights.

Obey your earthly masters. Literally “masters according to the flesh”: their human, earthly masters. The phrase hints at a contrast: they have another Master in heaven (v. 9). The earthly master’s authority is real but limited.

With fear and trembling. Not cringing terror of the master, but conscientious seriousness, because the work is done before God. Paul uses the same phrase of working out our salvation (Philippians 2:12) and of his own ministry (1 Corinthians 2:3).

With a sincere heart. “Sincere” means single, undivided: without hidden motives, without one face for the master and another behind his back.

As you would Christ. The transforming motive. A slave’s work, even the lowest task, could be done for the Lord himself. Christ dignified the work of the lowest.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul approves of slavery or thinks it good. He addresses believers within a social system they could not change, and tells them how to live as Christians in it. Nor does it mean obeying a master who commands sin: obedience is “as to Christ”, and Christ never commands sin.

Where Christians differ: does the Bible endorse slavery? In the nineteenth century, slave-owners in the American South quoted texts like this to defend slavery. Paul does not endorse the institution. He regulates it while undermining it from within. He lists slave-traders, “enslavers”, among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10); he urges slaves to gain their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21); he tells masters that they and their slaves have the same Master who shows no favouritism (v. 9); and he asks Philemon to receive his runaway slave Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). In the church, slave and free were equals at the Lord’s Table (Galatians 3:28). Verdict: the gospel undermined slavery from within, and Christians such as William Wilberforce rightly led its abolition. Modern slavery and human trafficking are evils Christians must oppose.

Today. We do not have slavery in this form, but the principle applies to every employee: work sincerely, with diligence, as for Christ.

In a sentence. Christian slaves were to serve their earthly masters with whole-hearted sincerity, as if serving Christ himself.

On a Tuesday. Whatever your job, it can be done for Christ. Do today’s dullest task as if he had asked you to do it, because he has.
verseByVerse.note: Slavery was part of everyday life in the Roman world; many early believers were slaves or owned slaves.

verseByVerse.quote: not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christian work is not done only when the boss is watching, or only to please people. It is done from the heart, with goodwill, as service to the Lord, because it is God’s will.

Not by the way of eye-service. Ophthalmodoulia, a word Paul probably coined: “eye-slavery”, working only when the master’s eye is on you. The servant who slacks off when the supervisor leaves the room.

As people-pleasers. Working to win human approval rather than God’s. The motive is image, not integrity.

But as bondservants of Christ. The deepest identity of a Christian slave was not “slave of a master” but “slave of Christ” (Paul uses the same title of himself: Romans 1:1). Every Christian, slave or free, belongs to Christ.

Doing the will of God from the heart. Literally “from the soul”. Ordinary work is God’s will. Sweeping a floor, making a meal, building a wall, entering data: done well and honestly, it is obedience to God. The Reformers called this the doctrine of vocation: every lawful calling can be done for God’s glory (1 Corinthians 10:31), not only church work. Luther said the milkmaid and the farmer serve God as truly as the priest.

Rendering service with a good will. Not grudgingly, with resentment, but with a positive attitude toward the work and toward those served.

As to the Lord and not to man. The audience has changed. The worker serves the human employer, but ultimately works for Christ (Colossians 3:23).

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must accept unjust treatment without any protest, or never change jobs, or never speak up for fair conditions. Paul himself used his Roman rights (Acts 16:37; 22:25). The point is the inner attitude and integrity of the work itself.

In a sentence. Christians work wholeheartedly and with goodwill, not to impress people, but as service to Christ.

On a Tuesday. Work today as if Christ were your manager. He is. Notice when you slack off because no one is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord sees every good thing done, by slave or free, and will reward it. Even if no human master notices or thanks you, Christ does.

Knowing. Christians work with an eye on the future. This knowledge changes how we work now.

Whatever good anyone does. Every good thing, however small or hidden: the extra care, the honest report, the patient service. Nothing is too small for God to notice (Matthew 10:42).

This he will receive back from the Lord. God rewards faithful service (2 Corinthians 5:10; Colossians 3:24). A slave received no wages, often no thanks, and no hope of advancement. But the Lord is not unjust: he will repay. Earthly masters may cheat their workers; Christ never will.

Whether he is a bondservant or is free. Before the Lord’s judgment, social status makes no difference. A slave’s faithful work will be rewarded as fully as a free person’s.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn salvation by good works: salvation is by grace through faith (2:8–9). Rewards are God’s gracious recognition of the works he himself prepared and enabled (2:10). Augustine said that when God crowns our merits, he crowns his own gifts. Nor are the rewards necessarily material or in this life.

In a sentence. The Lord sees and will reward every good thing done for him, whatever a person’s status.

For worship. No faithful act is unseen by your Lord. Thank him that your hidden work matters to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Masters must treat those under them in the same spirit, without threats or abuse of power, because they too have a Master in heaven, who will judge them and their slaves with no favouritism.

Masters, do the same to them. A startling command in the ancient world. The same principles that govern the slave govern the master: sincerity, goodwill, service as to the Lord. Masters too must act from the heart before God.

And stop your threatening. Threats were the normal means of controlling slaves: beatings, being sold away from family, harsher work, death. Paul forbids them. Abuse of power is sin.

Knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven. The great leveller. The master is himself a slave of the Master in heaven. Both stand before the same Lord. The master will answer to Christ for how he treated his slaves. Colossians 4:1 adds: treat them justly and fairly.

And that there is no partiality with him. God does not favour the rich or the powerful (Romans 2:11; Job 31:13–15). In court, a slave had no standing; before God, slave and master stand equal. The Old Testament law had already told Israel not to rule over a fellow Israelite with harshness (Leviticus 25:43).

What it does not mean. Not that authority itself is wrong. The master is not told to stop being a master, nor the employer an employer. But all authority is held under Christ, accountable to him, and must be used for the good of those under it.

In a sentence. Those with power over others must use it without threats, knowing that they answer to the same impartial Master in heaven.

On a Tuesday. If you manage people, you will answer to Christ for how you treat them. Are your words, your demands and your pay fair? Would you be content to be treated as you treat them?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Finally, they must be strong in the Lord and his mighty power, and put on God’s full armour to stand against the devil’s schemes, for the struggle is not against human enemies but against the rulers, authorities and spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms. So they must take up the whole armour, to stand firm in the day of evil: truth as a belt, righteousness as a breastplate, readiness from the gospel of peace on their feet, faith as a shield to extinguish the evil one’s flaming arrows, salvation as a helmet, and the Spirit’s sword, God’s word. They must pray in the Spirit on all occasions, with every kind of prayer, staying alert and praying for all God’s people, and for Paul, that he may be given words to make known the gospel’s mystery fearlessly, as an ambassador in chains.
verseByVerse.theology:
Spiritual Warfare and the Victory of Christ

The passage grounds the doctrine of spiritual warfare in the victory already achieved by Christ. The Reformers consistently insisted that the Christian fights from victory, not toward it. At the cross and resurrection, Christ decisively defeated the powers: “He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). The “rulers and authorities” of Ephesians 6:12 are already defeated enemies — real, malevolent, and active, but operating under the authority of One who has conquered them. The Christian's warfare is not the decisive battle; it is the mopping-up operation conducted in light of a victory already won.

This context — victory already achieved — is what makes “standing” the characteristic posture of the Christian warrior rather than “advancing.” Paul does not say “take more territory.” He says “stand.” Hold what Christ has secured. Don't give ground to a defeated enemy. Don't abandon the position that grace has placed you in. This is not a passive posture; it requires every piece of armour, every act of faith, every prayer offered in the Spirit. But it is a posture of confidence, not of uncertainty — the confidence of those who know how the battle ends and who are fighting in the strength of its Victor.

Prayer (vv.18–20) is the atmosphere in which the armoured Christian stands. It is “at all times in the Spirit” — not occasional, not formal, but the constant, Spirit-sustained reaching toward the Commander. Paul's request for prayer for himself (vv.19–20) is among the most searching things in the letter. The apostle who has written the most magnificent theological letter in the New Testament asks his readers to pray that he would have the boldness to speak the gospel clearly. He is acutely aware that the proclamation of the gospel is itself a spiritual warfare activity, requiring not merely intellectual preparation but Spirit-given courage and divine enablement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus was a city saturated with occult practice. The book of Acts records that when the gospel came to Ephesus, it confronted demonic powers directly — the sons of Sceva, the burning of the magic books, the riot engineered by Demetrius the silversmith whose trade in Artemis-shrines was threatened (Acts 19). The Ephesian Christians knew, from personal experience, that spiritual warfare was real. When Paul tells them to stand against “the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places,” he is not speaking metaphorically to a congregation that has only ever faced theoretical opposition. He is arming people who have already been in the fight.

Now: The tendency in contemporary Christianity is to spiritualise spiritual warfare into invisibility (it's just a metaphor for human sin and social structures) or to sensationalise it into obsession (seeing demonic activity behind every difficulty). Paul's teaching steers between both errors. The powers are real — personal, intelligent, malevolent.

But they are defeated — operating under the authority of the risen Christ who has already triumphed over them. The Christian response is neither to ignore them nor to be paralyzed by them, but to stand — in the truth, in righteousness, in the gospel, in faith, in salvation, in the word of God, and in unceasing prayer. This is neither the naivety of the denier nor the anxiety of the obsessed. It is the steady, armoured confidence of those who know their Commander.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the letter reaches its climax, Paul calls believers to be strong. But the strength is not their own: it is the Lord’s strength, given to those who are in him.

Finally. The last section of the letter (vv. 10–20). It gathers up everything. The church, which is God’s new people (chapter 2), called to unity (chapter 4) and holiness (chapters 4–5), and living out the gospel at home and work (5:21–6:9), is engaged in a spiritual war. Everything in the letter will be opposed.

Be strong in the Lord. The verb is passive in Greek: “be strengthened”, “let yourselves be made strong”. Strength is something we receive. “In the Lord”: in union with Christ, as all the blessings of chapter 1 are “in him”.

And in the strength of his might. Paul uses three words for power that he used in 1:19 to describe the power that raised Christ from the dead and seated him above all powers. The same power is available to believers. They fight with resurrection power.

What it does not mean. Not “try harder” or “be strong in yourself”. Self-confidence is the first thing that falls in spiritual battle (1 Corinthians 10:12). The command is to rely on the Lord’s strength, which is made perfect in our weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9–10; Isaiah 40:29–31).

In a sentence. For the battle ahead, be strengthened by the Lord’s own mighty power.

On a Tuesday. When you feel weak, do not wait to feel strong before you obey. Ask for the Lord’s strength, and take the next step.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must put on the full armour God provides, because their real enemy is not people but the devil and his hosts of evil spiritual powers. Only God’s armour can stand against them.

Put on. The clothing picture again (4:22–24): putting on the new self, and now the armour. The armour is not something added to the Christian life; it is the Christian life itself, lived in Christ.

The whole armour of God. Panoplia: the full equipment of a heavily armed soldier, from which comes our word “panoply”. Paul may have looked at the Roman soldier chained to him (Acts 28:16, 20) as he wrote. But the picture comes first from Isaiah, where God himself puts on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation (Isaiah 59:17), and the Messiah wears righteousness and faithfulness as his belt (Isaiah 11:5). The armour of God is God’s own armour, worn first by Christ and now given to his people.

That you may be able to stand. The aim is to stand, to hold one’s ground, not to advance and conquer new territory. Christ has already won the victory (1:20–22; Colossians 2:15). The church must hold the ground he has won.

Against the schemes of the devil. “Schemes” (methodeia, our “methods”) are strategies, cunning plans (see 4:14). The devil rarely attacks head-on. He deceives (2 Corinthians 11:3, 14), accuses (Revelation 12:10), tempts (Matthew 4:1–11), divides the church (4:27), discourages, distracts, and twists Scripture (Matthew 4:6).

For we do not wrestle. “Wrestle” (palē) is the word for hand-to-hand combat, the Greek sport of wrestling. The fight is close, personal and exhausting.

Against flesh and blood. “Flesh and blood” means human beings. Our real enemies are not the people who oppose us: the persecutor, the critic, the false teacher, the hostile government. They are captives of the enemy, people to be won (2 Timothy 2:25–26). Paul himself had been a persecutor.

But against the rulers, against the authorities. The same words as in 1:21 and 3:10: ranks of spiritual beings.

Against the cosmic powers over this present darkness. Literally “world-rulers of this darkness”. Evil spirits who influence this fallen world system (2:2; John 12:31; 1 John 5:19). The word was used in magic texts of spirit beings. The Ephesians, who had practised magic (Acts 19:18–19), knew these fears well.

Against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. The heavenly places (see 1:3) are the unseen realm. Evil powers operate there, but Christ is seated far above them (1:20–21), and believers are seated with him (2:6).

What it does not mean. Not that every problem is directly caused by a demon, or that we are not responsible for our sins. The world, the flesh and the devil work together (2:1–3). Nor should the church be fascinated or terrified by the devil. C. S. Lewis warned of two equal errors: disbelieving in devils, and taking an excessive and unhealthy interest in them.

Where Christians differ: spiritual warfare. Some “deliverance” ministries focus on identifying, naming and binding territorial spirits over cities, or casting demons out of believers. Others, influenced by modern scepticism, neglect the spiritual battle altogether. Verdict: the battle is real, but the weapons Paul names are not special techniques. They are the ordinary means of grace: truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word and prayer. The church fights the devil by believing, living and proclaiming the gospel.

In a sentence. Put on God’s full armour, because your real enemy is not people, but the devil and his evil spiritual powers.

On a Tuesday. The colleague who opposes you, the family member who mocks your faith, is not your enemy. Pray for them, and resist the one behind the scenes.
verseByVerse.note: Paul may have written with a Roman soldier guarding him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the enemy is so powerful, believers must take up all of God’s armour, so that when the day of evil comes they can resist, and, having done everything, still be standing.

Therefore. Because the enemy is real and powerful (v. 12).

Take up. A military term: pick up your equipment, as a soldier does at the call to battle.

That you may be able to withstand. To resist, to stand against the attack. The same root as in James 4:7 and 1 Peter 5:9: resist the devil.

In the evil day. Two senses. The whole present age is evil (5:16; Galatians 1:4): we are always at war. But within it come particular days of evil, times of fierce temptation, persecution, crisis or grief, when the attack is concentrated. Jesus himself faced such hours (Luke 4:13; 22:53). We do not know when they will come; so we must be ready always.

And having done all. Having done everything needed: having put on the armour and fought.

To stand firm. Still on your feet when the battle is over. The goal is not glamour or spectacular victories, but endurance. Four times in verses 11–14 Paul uses the word “stand”. The Christian who stands at the end, still trusting Christ, has won.

What it does not mean. Not that believers can lose their salvation if they fail to stand. God keeps his people (1:13–14; John 10:28–29), and he keeps them precisely by giving them this armour and the will to wear it. But neither may believers be careless: God’s keeping works through our watchful perseverance, not apart from it.

In a sentence. Take up God’s armour so that in the day of evil you can resist and still be standing at the end.

On a Tuesday. Prepare for the evil day before it comes. The time to sharpen your sword is not in the middle of the battle.

verseByVerse.quote: Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first piece of armour is the belt of truth. Truth holds everything else together: the truth of the gospel, believed and held fast, and a life of honesty and integrity that matches it.

Stand therefore. The fourth “stand” (see v. 13). Now Paul describes the armour piece by piece. Each piece is introduced as already put on (“having fastened”): the soldier stands ready because he is dressed for battle.

Having fastened on the belt. Literally “having girded your loins”. A Roman soldier wore a tunic beneath his armour. Before fighting, he gathered it up and tucked it into a strong leather belt, so that he could move freely. The belt also held the sword and the lower armour in place. Without it, everything else would hang loose. In the Bible, “girding the loins” means getting ready for action (Exodus 12:11; 1 Peter 1:13).

Of truth. Isaiah 11:5 says the Messiah will wear faithfulness as the belt of his loins. Two sides of truth: objective truth, the truth of God’s word, the gospel (1:13; 4:21); and personal truthfulness, integrity, sincerity, honesty (4:25). They belong together. The devil is a liar (John 8:44); his first weapon is deception. He is defeated by people who know the truth and live it.

Why first? Because everything depends on truth. A Christian who doubts or does not know the truth, or who lives a lie, has nothing to hold the rest of the armour together.

What it does not mean. Not that we must have every theological question answered before we can stand. The belt is the central truth of the gospel, held firmly, and an honest life. Nor is it a cold intellectualism: truth is held in love (4:15).

In a sentence. Stand firm, held together by the truth of the gospel and a life of integrity.

On a Tuesday. Is there a lie you are living, a secret you are keeping, a gap between your public and private life? It is a loose belt. Bring it into the light.
verseByVerse.note: The soldier’s belt held his tunic and sword in place.

parallels.desc: righteousness shall be the belt of his waist

verseByVerse.quote: and having put on the breastplate of righteousness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second piece is the breastplate of righteousness, guarding the heart. It is both the righteousness of Christ counted to believers, which answers every accusation, and the righteous life that leaves the enemy no foothold.

The breastplate. Metal armour covering the chest and back, protecting the heart, lungs and other vital organs. A wound there was usually fatal.

Of righteousness. Again from Isaiah 59:17, where God puts on righteousness as a breastplate when he comes to save. Righteousness means being right with God and doing what is right. Which righteousness does Paul mean?

1. Imputed righteousness. The righteousness of Christ credited to believers by faith (Romans 3:21–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). The devil is the accuser (Revelation 12:10). He points to our sins and says, “You are guilty; God cannot accept you.” The answer is not our record but Christ’s: who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies (Romans 8:33–34). This breastplate protects the heart against despair.

2. Practical righteousness. A life of holiness and integrity (4:24; 5:9). Sin opens gaps in the armour; unconfessed sin gives the devil a foothold (4:27). A Christian living in deliberate sin is like a soldier fighting with an exposed chest.

Verdict: both. Imputed righteousness is the foundation: our standing before God rests on Christ alone. Practical righteousness flows from it and protects us in the daily fight. One answers the accuser; the other gives him no opening.

What it does not mean. Not that we must achieve a perfect life before we can resist the devil. The breastplate is first Christ’s righteousness, given as a gift. When we fail, the remedy is not to give up but to confess and to stand again in Christ’s righteousness (1 John 1:9; 2:1–2).

In a sentence. Guard your heart with the righteousness of Christ, which answers every accusation, and with the righteous life that flows from it.

On a Tuesday. When your conscience or the enemy accuses you, do not argue from your own record. Point to Christ’s. Then repent of the sin and walk in righteousness.

parallels.desc: he put on righteousness as a breastplate

verseByVerse.ref: v. 15 — The Shoes of the Gospel of Peace
verseByVerse.quote: and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third piece is the soldier’s footwear: the readiness, the firm footing, that the gospel of peace gives. Peace with God gives believers stable ground to stand on, and readiness to move with the good news.

As shoes for your feet. Roman soldiers wore the caliga, a heavy sandal-boot with thick leather soles studded with nails, giving grip on rough or slippery ground. A soldier who slipped in battle would fall; one with good footing could hold his position. Many battles were lost by bad footing.

Having put on the readiness. “Readiness” (hetoimasia) can mean preparation, preparedness, or a firm foundation. Two readings: (1) the stability, the firm footing, that the gospel gives, so that we can stand without slipping; or (2) readiness to go and share the gospel. Isaiah 52:7, which Paul likely has in mind, speaks of the beautiful feet of the messenger who brings good news and publishes peace (Romans 10:15). Verdict: the context of standing (vv. 11–14) favours firm footing first; but those who stand firm on the gospel of peace are also ready to share it.

Given by the gospel of peace. The gospel announces peace: peace with God through Christ’s death (2:14–17; Romans 5:1), and peace between people once divided (2:14–16). A soldier at war with God has no footing at all. A believer at peace with God stands on ground that cannot be shaken. The paradox: we fight our battle wearing the shoes of peace.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians are aggressive toward people: the gospel we carry is a gospel of peace. Our war is against the devil, not against human beings (v. 12).

In a sentence. Stand on the firm ground of the gospel of peace, ready to move with it.

On a Tuesday. Peace with God gives stability when everything else shakes: a diagnosis, a redundancy, a broken relationship. Stand on what God has said about your peace with him. And be ready to tell someone else about it.
verseByVerse.note: Roman soldiers wore sturdy studded sandals for a firm footing.

parallels.desc: the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace

verseByVerse.quote: In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In every situation believers are to take up the shield of faith. Trusting God and his promises puts out every burning arrow the evil one fires at us: his lies, accusations, temptations and fears.

In all circumstances. Or “above all”, “in addition to all”. Faith is needed in every part of the battle.

The shield. Not a small round shield, but the Roman scutum: a large rectangular shield, about four feet tall and two and a half feet wide, made of wood covered with leather. It covered the whole body. Soldiers could lock their shields together side by side and overhead into a wall, the “tortoise” formation, which protected the whole unit. Faith is not only individual: believers protect one another.

Of faith. Faith is trust in God: in his character, his promises and his Son. The shield is not faith in faith, or confidence in ourselves, but trust in God himself (Psalm 18:30; 1 John 5:4).

With which you can extinguish. Before battle, soldiers soaked the leather of their shields in water, so that burning arrows would be put out when they struck.

All the flaming darts of the evil one. Arrows tipped with cloth soaked in pitch and set alight. They did not only wound; they set things on fire and spread panic. The devil’s darts are the thoughts and impulses he throws at us: doubts about God’s goodness (Genesis 3:1), accusations that we are beyond forgiveness, sudden temptations, fears, despair, blasphemous thoughts. They come suddenly, and they burn. “All”: there is no dart that faith cannot put out.

How faith extinguishes. By answering the lie with God’s truth. When the dart says “God does not love you”, faith answers: he loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). When it says “you are too sinful”, faith answers: there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).

What it does not mean. Not that a believer who has fiery thoughts is failing. The darts are fired by the enemy; being attacked is not the same as sinning (see 5:3). The question is whether we raise the shield. Nor does it mean that faith must be strong to work: weak faith in a strong God holds the shield.

In a sentence. Faith in God and his promises puts out every burning lie, accusation and temptation the devil throws at us.

On a Tuesday. When a fiery thought comes, answer it with a specific promise of God. Write down three promises today and keep them ready.
verseByVerse.note: The Roman shield was large, about four feet tall, wood covered with leather; soldiers could lock shields into a wall.

parallels.desc: he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him

verseByVerse.quote: and take the helmet of salvation,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth piece is the helmet of salvation, guarding the mind. Believers receive it as a gift: the salvation God has given, and the sure hope of its completion, protect their thinking against doubt and despair.

And take. The verb means “receive”, “accept”. The helmet is handed to us; we do not forge it. Salvation is God’s gift (2:8).

The helmet. Made of bronze or iron, with cheek-pieces, protecting the head. A blow to the head could kill or stun a soldier, leaving him helpless.

Of salvation. Again from Isaiah 59:17. In 1 Thessalonians 5:8 Paul calls it the hope of salvation. Salvation has past, present and future aspects: we have been saved (2:5, 8), are being saved, and will be saved at the day of redemption (4:30). The helmet is the assurance that God, who began a good work, will complete it (Philippians 1:6).

Why the mind? The devil attacks the mind with doubt: “Are you really saved? Will you really make it? Is any of this true?” Discouragement and despair are among his chief weapons. The helmet guards the mind with the knowledge that salvation is God’s work, not ours, and is secure. A soldier who knows the outcome of the war is already settled fights differently from one who fears defeat.

What it does not mean. Not presumption or careless confidence. The assurance of salvation is held by faith and confirmed by a changed life (2 Peter 1:10). Nor does it mean that believers never struggle with doubt: the helmet is given precisely because they will.

In a sentence. Guard your mind with the salvation God has given you and the sure hope of its completion.

On a Tuesday. When the thought comes, “You will never make it”, answer it with this: my salvation does not depend on my grip on God, but on his grip on me (John 10:28–29).

parallels.desc: a helmet of salvation on his head

verseByVerse.ref: v. 17b — The Sword of the Spirit
verseByVerse.quote: and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The only weapon for attack in the list is the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. The Spirit who inspired Scripture puts it in our hands, and when it is spoken and applied, it cuts through the devil’s lies.

The sword. Machaira: the Roman short sword, about eighteen to twenty-four inches long, used for close combat, thrusting and cutting at short range. Not a weapon for a distant fight, but for hand-to-hand engagement (the “wrestling” of v. 12).

Of the Spirit. The sword is the Spirit’s. He inspired the word (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21), and he makes it effective in hearts. The word is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword (Hebrews 4:12). In Isaiah the Servant says that the Lord made his mouth like a sharp sword (Isaiah 49:2); in Revelation, a sharp sword comes out of Christ’s mouth (Revelation 1:16).

Which is the word of God. Here Paul uses rhēma, which often means a word spoken, a specific saying, rather than logos, the message as a whole. The point is Scripture used: a particular word of God, applied to a particular attack. Jesus showed how in the wilderness. Three times the devil tempted him, and three times Jesus answered with a specific text from Deuteronomy, introduced with “It is written” (Matthew 4:1–11). He did not argue or negotiate; he quoted Scripture, and the devil left.

Defensive and offensive. The sword parries attacks, as Jesus did. But it also advances: through the preaching of the word, captives are freed from the devil’s kingdom (Acts 26:18). Every time the gospel is preached and someone believes, the sword has struck.

What it does not mean. Not a magic formula, as if quoting verses works automatically. The devil himself quoted Scripture, out of context (Matthew 4:6). The sword must be understood and used rightly, in the Spirit, with faith. Nor does it mean that Christians may use the Bible as a weapon against people, to wound or win arguments. The enemy is the devil, not flesh and blood (v. 12).

In a sentence. The word of God, given and empowered by the Spirit, is the weapon that defeats the devil’s lies and frees his captives.

On a Tuesday. Memorise Scripture. You cannot use a sword you do not carry. Choose one verse this week for the temptation you face most often.
verseByVerse.note: The Roman sword was a short blade for close combat.

parallels.desc: he made my mouth like a sharp sword

verseByVerse.quote: praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The armour is worn and used in prayer. Believers must pray at all times, led and helped by the Spirit, in every kind of prayer, staying alert and persevering, and praying for all God’s people.

Praying at all times. The grammar links prayer to the whole armour: the soldier is to stand, armed, praying. Prayer is not a seventh piece of armour, but the way all the armour is put on and used. It is the atmosphere of the battle. “At all times” means in every situation and season: not only in crisis, and not only at fixed times, but as a constant habit of dependence (1 Thessalonians 5:17; Luke 18:1).

In the Spirit. Prompted, guided and helped by the Holy Spirit. We do not know how to pray as we ought, but the Spirit helps us in our weakness (Romans 8:26–27). Praying in the Spirit is praying in line with God’s will, in dependence on him, through Christ (2:18).

With all prayer and supplication. Every kind of prayer: praise, thanks, confession, and especially “supplication”, specific requests for particular needs.

To that end, keep alert. Stay awake, be watchful, like a sentry on duty at night. Jesus told his disciples in Gethsemane to watch and pray that they might not enter into temptation (Mark 14:38). They fell asleep, and they fell.

With all perseverance. Do not give up. Keep praying even when answers seem slow (Luke 18:1–8).

Making supplication for all the saints. The battle is fought together. Each believer prays for others, and is prayed for. A soldier who fights alone is easily picked off. Paul has modelled this in his own prayers for the readers (1:15–23; 3:14–21).

What it does not mean. Not that “praying in the Spirit” means only praying in tongues. Some read it so, but Paul’s phrase is general, and every believer is called to pray in the Spirit. Nor does “at all times” mean continuous words. It means a heart turned toward God through the day, and regular, persevering times of prayer.

In a sentence. Wear the armour in prayer: constant, Spirit-led, watchful, persevering prayer for all God’s people.

On a Tuesday. Make a short list of believers you will pray for this week, by name, with specific requests. The battle is won on your knees.

verseByVerse.quote: and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks them to pray for him too. Not for release from prison, but for words and boldness to proclaim the gospel, for he is Christ’s ambassador, even in chains.

And also for me. The great apostle asks ordinary believers to pray for him. He did not see himself as above needing their prayers. Every gospel worker needs the prayers of the church.

That words may be given to me. Even Paul needed help to speak. Effective proclamation is a gift from God (Colossians 4:3–4).

In opening my mouth boldly. “Boldly” (en parrēsia, see 3:12): with freedom, frankness, courage. Paul was facing trial before Caesar (Acts 25:11–12; 28:16–31). He might have been tempted to soften the message, to protect himself. He asks for courage to speak plainly.

To proclaim the mystery of the gospel. The mystery revealed in Christ, including the inclusion of the Gentiles (3:3–6).

For which I am an ambassador in chains. A striking paradox. An ambassador represented his king, spoke with his authority, and enjoyed diplomatic immunity: to insult an ambassador was to insult his king. Yet Christ’s ambassador is in chains (2 Corinthians 5:20). The word for chain (halysis) was sometimes used of the ornamental gold chains ambassadors wore as a sign of their office. Paul’s iron chain was his badge of office.

That I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak. He repeats the request for boldness: it is what he most needs. “As I ought”: preaching the gospel is a duty, not an option (1 Corinthians 9:16).

What it does not mean. Not that Paul did not care about his release or that praying for it is wrong (Philippians 1:19; Philemon 22). But his first concern was the gospel, not his comfort. God answered: Paul preached in Rome with all boldness and without hindrance (Acts 28:30–31), and his imprisonment advanced the gospel even in the imperial guard (Philippians 1:12–14).

In a sentence. Paul, Christ’s ambassador in chains, asks for prayer not for release but for boldness to proclaim the gospel.

On a Tuesday. Pray this for your pastor and for missionaries you know, by name: for words, for boldness, for clarity. And pray it for yourself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tychicus, a dear brother and faithful servant, will tell them all Paul’s news and encourage them; that is why Paul is sending him. Paul ends with peace to the brothers and sisters, and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, and grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with undying love.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace as the Alpha and Omega of the Christian Life

Ephesians begins with grace (1:2: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ”) and ends with grace (6:24: “Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ”). The entire letter is enclosed within this grace — and this is not merely a rhetorical device. It is a theological statement: the Christian life from first to last, from election before time began to the consummation of all things, is entirely an affair of grace. There is no moment in the Christian's experience that is not sustained by grace, no achievement that is not the fruit of grace, no prayer that is answered by anything other than grace.

The Reformed tradition has consistently defined grace as God's undeserved favour — not merely his assistance added to human effort, but his sovereign initiative in the face of human helplessness. Ephesians 2:8–9 defines salvation by grace through faith, with the explicit denial that this is our own doing. But grace is not only the initial gift; it is the sustaining reality of the entire Christian life. “I am what I am by the grace of God,” Paul writes to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 15:10). The letter to the Ephesians is the fullest exposition of what that grace is, what it has done, and what it looks like in the life of those who have received it.

Tychicus — the letter-carrier, the beloved brother, the faithful minister — is himself a theological figure in the ending of the letter. He represents the ordinary, faithful, unglamorous work of ministry that keeps the church alive between the apostolic moments: the friend who carries the letter, who brings the news, who comforts the worried flock. Every church is sustained by Tychicuses — people whose names are not famous, whose ministry is not spectacular, who are simply faithful. The letter that contains the most magnificent theology in the New Testament is delivered by one such person. Grace works through the ordinary.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul is in a Roman prison when he writes these final words. He may never see the Ephesians again. His benediction — “peace... love... faith... grace be with you” — is spoken over people he cannot reach with his hands or his presence, people he is releasing into the care of the God about whom he has been writing for six chapters.

This is what pastoral love looks like at its most costly and most beautiful: the shepherd who cannot be with his flock entrusting them to the Chief Shepherd, speaking blessing over them, sending them a trusted friend, and then releasing them in faith. Paul's imprisonment did not imprison his hope. The chains on his wrists did not chain the word of God (2 Timothy 2:9). The letter reached Ephesus. The grace it describes reached its readers. It reaches us still.

Now: “Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.” The word translated “incorruptible” (aphtharsia) is the same word used for the resurrection body — imperishable, undying, not subject to decay. The love of the true believer for Christ is not a passing emotion or a seasonal feeling; it is something that has been planted by God in a soul that has been made alive in Christ, and it partakes of the imperishable quality of its Object.

This love will outlast every earthly thing. It will survive death, outlast time, and find its perfect and eternal fulfilment at the Marriage Supper of the Lamb. The letter ends with this love — and this love, in its countless expressions across the centuries, has carried the gospel from Rome to Ephesus to the ends of the earth, and to us. Grace to you. And peace. And love incorruptible.

verseByVerse.quote: So that you also may know how I am and what I am doing, Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord will tell you everything. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul sends Tychicus, a dear and faithful brother, to bring news of him and to encourage the churches. The letter ends, as Christian fellowship always does, with real people caring for each other.

So that you also may know how I am. The readers would be anxious about Paul in prison. He wants them to know how he is: not to draw attention to himself, but because Christians care about one another.

Tychicus. A believer from the province of Asia (Acts 20:4), the region around Ephesus. He travelled with Paul, carrying the collection for the poor in Jerusalem, and became one of his most trusted messengers. He carried this letter and the letter to the Colossians, which uses almost the same words about him (Colossians 4:7–8), and probably travelled with Onesimus, carrying the letter to Philemon. Later Paul sent him to Ephesus again (2 Timothy 4:12) and possibly to Crete (Titus 3:12).

The beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord. Three descriptions: beloved (loved by Paul and the church), a brother (family in Christ), and a faithful minister (diakonos, servant). Not famous, but faithful. Paul’s ministry depended on many such people.

Will tell you everything. Some news was better carried by word of mouth than written, especially for a prisoner whose letters might be read.

That he may encourage your hearts. The aim of the news was encouragement. Knowing that Paul was well and that the gospel was advancing would strengthen their faith.

What it does not mean. Not that these closing personal notes are unimportant because they contain no doctrine. They show that the great truths of chapters 1–3 are lived among real people, with names, journeys and concerns.

In a sentence. Paul sends a faithful brother to share news and encourage the churches, showing that Christian truth lives in loving relationships.

On a Tuesday. Be a Tychicus: faithful, dependable, and an encourager. Who could you send a word of news or encouragement to this week?
verseByVerse.note: Tychicus came from the province of Asia and carried this letter and Colossians.

verseByVerse.quote: Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter ends with a blessing: peace, love and faith from the Father and the Son for the brothers, and grace for everyone who loves the Lord Jesus Christ with a love that will never die.

Peace be to the brothers. “Brothers” includes sisters: the whole church family. Peace with God and with one another has been one of the great themes of the letter (2:14–17; 4:3).

And love with faith. Faith and love go together: faith in Christ, love for all the saints (1:15). Faith works through love (Galatians 5:6).

From God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The same two persons named in the opening greeting (1:2), as the single source of every blessing. The letter begins and ends with the Father and the Son.

Grace be with all. The last word of the letter, as of most of Paul’s letters, is grace. Grace began it (1:2), grace has run through it (1:6–7; 2:5–8; 3:2, 7–8; 4:7), and grace ends it. Everything is grace.

Who love our Lord Jesus Christ. The mark of a true believer is love for Jesus. Not mere outward religion, but love for a person (1 Corinthians 16:22; 1 Peter 1:8).

With love incorruptible. “Incorruptible” (aphtharsia) means imperishable, undying, not subject to decay. It is used of the resurrection body (1 Corinthians 15:42). The phrase may describe the love itself, a love for Jesus that does not fade or decay; or it may describe the sphere of the grace, “grace in immortality”. Verdict: the ESV’s reading, an undying love for Jesus, is most natural. Remarkably, Ephesus later received a warning from the risen Christ that it had abandoned the love it had at first (Revelation 2:4). Undying love must be guarded.

What it does not mean. Not that grace is earned by love. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). The blessing describes those to whom grace has come: they love the one who gave it.

In a sentence. Paul ends with peace, love, faith and grace for all who love the Lord Jesus with a love that will never die.

For worship. Ask God for a love for Jesus that does not fade, and thank him for the grace that began, sustains and will complete your salvation.

6.overview:
The household code continues. Children are to obey their parents in the Lord, honouring father and mother as the commandment with a promise requires, and fathers must not provoke their children but bring them up in the Lord’s discipline and instruction. Slaves are to serve their masters sincerely, as serving Christ, knowing the Lord will reward every good deed, and masters must treat them likewise, without threats, for both have the same Master in heaven, who shows no favouritism. Paul does not endorse slavery here; he puts master and slave under one Lord, and plants the truth that would later undo the institution.

Then comes the famous call to spiritual warfare (vv. 10–20). Believers must be strong in the Lord’s might and put on the whole armour of God, because the real enemy is not flesh and blood but the devil and the spiritual powers of evil. The armour is God’s own (Isaiah 11:5; 59:17): the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, shoes ready with the gospel of peace, the shield of faith that quenches the evil one’s fiery arrows, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, the word of God, all taken up in constant prayer in the Spirit for all the saints, and for Paul, an ambassador in chains, to speak boldly. The letter ends with news through Tychicus and a blessing of peace, love, faith and grace on all who love the Lord Jesus with undying love.
